Chylothorax can occur because of a “leaky vessel” (known as the thoracic duct), which can cause accumulation of fluid (chyle) in the chest cavity. This excess of fluid within the chest cavity can impair the lungs during breathing and result in potentially life-threatening situations. Treatment of chylothorax in cats typically requires surgery to close the thoracic duct, preventing fluid from leaking into the chest cavity. Traditionally, surgical intervention of chylothorax requires opening the abdominal and chest cavities, causing a considerable amount of discomfort and even pain after surgery. Minimally invasive approaches have been developed, like thoracoscopic thoracic duct ligation where closure is performed through small incisions with the use of a camera and specialized instruments. The addition of another technique, known as pericardiectomy (removal of the pericardium, which is a sac-like organ surrounding the heart) along with thoracic duct repair is often performed to reduce the chance of recurrence. Even with these techniques in combination, recurrence rates of up to 30-50% have been reported. Additionally, more recent studies suggest that pericardiectomy may not be necessary in all patients, but rather proper identification of the location of the thoracic duct before surgery by way of a CT scan and in surgery by way of contrast can improve outcomes for cats. Currently, there are no prospective studies for cats with idiopathic chylothorax using standardized preoperative diagnostics and surgical techniques for each patient. This includes the use of contrast material before and during surgery to better identify the thoracic duct and stop its flow at the proper location, which is highly dependent on each cat. 	The aim of this project is to assess the outcome of cats with idiopathic chylothorax undergoing thoracoscopic thoracic duct ligation who have a standardized diagnostic workup preoperatively and successful preoperative and intraoperative thoracic duct visualization. Cats are invited to participate in this study if they are at least 6.6 lbs (3 kg) or greater, greater than 2 years of age, and have been diagnosed with idiopathic chylothorax. Prior to inclusion into this study cats will undergo physical examination and be diagnosed with chylothorax using pleural effusion fluid analysis (abnormal buildup of fluid in the pleural space, which is a thin cavity between the lungs and the chest wall). If not already completed within two weeks of their planned surgery date, cats will undergo a complete physical examination, and blood will be collected for complete blood count and serum biochemistry prior to admittance in this study. Additionally, cats will receive a complete work-up for chylothorax including an echocardiogram (heart ultrasound), heartworm testing, chest x-rays, and pleural effusion fluid analysis. If cats have undergone surgery previously for chylothorax or if they have an identified underlying cause of chylothorax (e.g. cancer, heart disease, lung lobe torsion, etc.), they will be excluded from participation in this study. Cats will be placed under general anesthesia for their first procedure. A CT scan will be conducted first, where a contrast solution (iohexol) will be injected underneath the skin around the anus and/or into the metatarsal paw pads, to highlight the thoracic duct. Under the same anesthetic event, your cat will also have a small incision made into its neck and a catheter will be placed in the jugular vein to measure pressures at the level of the heart. At a later date, cats will be placed under anesthesia again for surgery. Three very small (5-10mm) incisions will be made near the ribs for insertion of special surgical instruments (thoracoscopic camera and instruments) to allow the surgeon to see inside the chest cavity and close the thoracic duct branches. The thoracic duct will be visualized using a dye injected around the anus prior to surgery. If the thoracic duct is unable to be visualized with this minimally invasive technique, an incision will be made into the chest cavity between two of the ribs and the surgery will proceed as an “open” thoracic duct ligation. A chest tube will be placed to monitor post-operative fluid production in all patients, as is standard of care for chylothorax patients. All enrolled cats will be hospitalized post-operatively in the intensive care unit for a minimum of 48 hours for monitoring. Cats will be sent home once they are voluntarily eating and drinking, and their pain is deemed appropriately controlled with oral medications. All cats must be re-evaluated at the UF Small Animal Hospital at 1-, 3-, and 6 months after surgery for physical exam and chest x-rays to confirm occlusion of the thoracic duct and resolution of chylothorax. In dogs, a type of malignant tumor called a glioma accounts for approximately 35% of all spontaneous primary brain tumors. Even with treatment, the prognosis for both dogs and humans with gliomas is poor, and there is no cure. Current therapies such as radiation aim at extending quantity and improving quality of life. In this clinical trial, we are testing the safety and effectiveness of molecularly targeted cytotoxins, which are chemotherapeutic drugs, delivered directly to the patient's brain tumor. Developed by researchers at the Thomas K. Hearn Brain Tumor Research Centerat the Wake Forest School of Medicine, the unique chemotherapeutic drugs used in this trial are designed to affect only cancerous cells, and not normal brain tissue. Earlier generations of these molecularly targeted cyotoxins have been used safely and effectively in dogs with gliomas. Using specialized catheters the cytotoxins are infused directly into the tumor over a several hour period. The drug treatment is monitored continuously with MRI to allow the neurosurgeon to precisely track the drug delivery. **As a dog owner, how can I participate in this trial? **
If you suspect that your dog may have a brain tumor, you should arrange for an appointment with your local veterinarian. They will perform a complete neurological examination, which is the first and fundamental step in establishing a diagnosis in animals with brain disease. It is also a prerequisite for them to determine which additional diagnostic tests to recommend. However, advanced imaging studies of the brain, such as MRI, interpreted in conjunction with the neurological examination and other supporting tests, are usually necessary to best characterize diseases of the brain. If your local veterinarian cannot perform an MRI, they will often refer you to a veterinary neurologist who offers this service. Our Neurology and Neurosurgery Service works on a referral only basis, which means that your local veterinarian must first evaluate your pet and arrange for an appointment to see one of our specialists. In order to be eligible for this specific clinical trial, your dog must have an MRI of the brain that demonstrates an abnormality consistent with a glioma. Clinical Trial Inclusion Criteria: 
- Dogs of any age, breed, or sex between 3-45 kg in body weight
- Clinical signs of mild to moderate neurologic dysfunction referable to the brain
- MRI evidence of a single telencephalic intra-axial mass lesion consistent with a glioma
- No clinical or other diagnostic evidence of other significant systemic disease. 
- Dogs must have gross, measurable disease (> 1cm in diameter) on a current MRI We are happy to evaluate clinical and imaging findings to determine patient eligibility for this clinical trial. The iNKT cells directly kill the tumor (cancer cell) and  they also boost the patient's own anti-tumor (cancer-killing) immune responses. In this study, we will genetically modify these natural killer T cells (NKT) cells to express a protein known as a chimeric antigen receptor (CAR). The CAR directs the genetically modified CAR-iNKT cells to a target protein (known as B7H3) on the bone cancer cell. The CAR-iNKT cells kill the bone cancer cells and activate the immune system to do the same. The purpose of this study is to determine i) the safety of CAR-iNKT cells, ii) their ability to traffic to the bone tumor in your dog’s leg and exert an anti-cancer effect there, iii) their ability to delay or prevent metastatic disease and iv) how long the CAR-iNKT cells remain in your dog’s body. This clinical trial is fully funded and at no cost to owners. "Primary field"}], "description": "WHY IS THIS STUDY BEING DONE? Immunotherapies are a class of anti-cancer treatments that work by activating a patient’s own immune system to fight specific diseases, including cancer. A number of immunotherapies have been approved by the United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for use in humans in a wide range of diseases, including cancer. While these therapies have shown positive results in cancers of blood cells, they have had more limited successes in solid tumors like soft tissue sarcoma. This is thought to be in part because it is hard to get enough of the drug into the tumor when it is given through the blood stream (intravenously) without causing serious side effects. To overcome this limitation, this research study will use injections of immunotherapies directly through the skin into the tumor (intra-tumoral injections). The primary goal of this research study is to test whether it is safe and feasible to treat tumors by injecting them with a certain type of immunotherapy called T-cell engagers (TCEs).  A T cell is a special kind of white blood cell that attacks sick cells in your body, including virus-infected cells and cancer cells. TCEs are a new kind of cancer immunotherapy that helps a patient’s own T cells find and kill cancer cells. They work like a connector: one end sticks to a cancer cell, and the other end sticks to a T cell. By pulling the two cells together, the TCE helps the T cell recognize the cancer cell and activate its killing response. In this research study, two different TCEs will be tested together (TCE combination). They work in much the same way, but each one attaches to different markers on cancer cells and T cells. Because they target different markers, the two treatments can help T cells kill cancer cells more effectively, even at lower doses of each TCE, which helps reduce the chance of harmful side effects. The goal is to make the therapy work better while still keeping patients safe. The study will test different doses of TCEs per injection, different numbers of injections placed into the tumor itself, and the product used to dilute the TCEs. The TCE combination will be diluted either in sterile saline (a solution of salt and water) or in hydrogel (a water-based gel). The hydrogel’s job is to slowly release the drugs into the tumor, with the goal to keep the cancer cells exposed to the drugs for a longer time. This may help the treatment work better and could also reduce side effects. The TCE combination will also be mixed with sterile fluorescent dye(s) that will help researchers track where the injections were placed in the tumor. The fluorescent dye(s) have already been used in multiple canine and human clinical trials with no known side effects. The “investigational” part of the study are the intratumoral injections of the TCE combinations diluted in sterile saline or hydrogel. These TCEs are investigational drugs, which means they have not yet been approved by the FDA or the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA) for use in dogs or other species. The purpose of this study is to test the safety and the biological effect of the TCE combination in canine patients with soft tissue sarcoma (STS), rather than to specifically provide medical treatment to the enrolled patient."}, {"id": 28143, "name": "Single Radiation Treatment for Dogs with Transmissible Venereal Tumor", "url": "https://veterinaryclinicaltrials.org/s/single-radiation-treatment-for-dogs-with-transmissible-venereal-tumor-422595/?ref=gallery", "status": "Recruiting", "tags": [{"tag_path": "financial-incentive_fully-funded-including-initial-screening-47", "label": "Fully funded including initial screening", "parent_label": "Financial incentive"}, {"tag_path": "species-20_canine-21", "label": "Canine", "parent_label": "Species"}, {"tag_path": "intervention-type_radiation-60", "label": "Radiation", "parent_label": "Intervention type"}, {"tag_path": "primary-field-19_oncology-1_urogenital-tumors-349", "label": "Urogenital tumors", "parent_label": "Oncology"}, {"tag_path": "primary-field-19_oncology-1", "label": "Oncology", "parent_label": "Primary field"}], "description": "Canine transmissible venereal tumor (TVT) is an infectious cancer that can be spread between dogs, often through grooming behaviors or sexual contact. This cancer can be found worldwide, but is most common in Central and South America, Africa, and Asia. In the United States, this cancer is most commonly seen in animals rescued from other parts of the world, or in free-roaming pets in very remote areas. Treatment for this cancer involves once-weekly injections of chemotherapy, which are given until the cancer is resolved. For patients who cannot undergo this chemotherapy treatment, finding alternate therapies can be invaluable. We know that this cancer responds well to older forms of radiation therapy; however, we aim to determine if a single treatment with modernized radiation can provide similar treatment outcomes with fewer visits compared to chemotherapy. Dogs enrolled in this study will receive a single dose of radiation therapy, followed by recheck visits 7 days and 28 days after treatment. At each of these visits, patients will have tumor measurements and small samples of their masses collected with a needle for analysis. Patients complete the study on day 28 or if their tumor progresses after radiation treatment. "parent_label": "Primary field"}], "description": "Oral squamous cell carcinoma is a very difficult cancer to treat in cats and is often fairly advanced before it is detected. This clinical trial will be examining the effectiveness of a new type of immunotherapy  for treating this disease in cats, which is based on very promising data from two squamous cell carcinoma trials conducted recently in horses at CSU. This new treatment is designed to stimulate the body’s own immune defenses to attack the tumor cells and cause tumor regression or elimination. In this particular trial, even stopping the tumor from growing (rather than full elimination) would be considered a success. This immunotherapy drug has been tested previously in cats, and is generally well-tolerated, with few side-effects, but it has only been evaluated in one cat with oral squamous cell carcinoma previously. The treatment has however been extensively evaluated in horses with squamous cell carcinoma, with a high degree of success. In this study, we will evaluate this novel immunotherapy in cats with oral SCC to determine how well the treatment works and how well it is tolerated by cats. Cats will receive four injections of the LTN immunotherapy into their tumor, which are given once every three weeks. Cats must be put under anesthesia for these injections. While under anesthesia, cats will have CT scans and tumor biopsies performed prior to starting treatment, at the time of the third injection, and 3 weeks after the 4 th injection (CT only). Blood tests (complete blood count and chemistry profile) will also be performed at these visits. Study participation is completed after the visit that is 3 weeks after the last injection. Established definitive treatment options include surgery, radiation therapy, or a combination of these treatments. Surgical resection alone does not improve survival times achieved with supportive care alone, and is therefore not recommended. Radiation therapy provides an average of 14 months of survival time. The purpose of this study is to investigate a novel treatment option with the goal being to improve outcomes for dogs with high grade gliomas. Treatment in this study consists of injections of nanoparticles (NPs) that target brain tumor cells and result in their death. This is a single site, prospective, three arm clinical trial with no control (placebo) group. Each patient will be randomly assigned into one of these three groups. The treatment arms are: 1) surgical resection + nanoparticle administration 2) surgical resection + stereotactic radiation therapy 3) surgical resection + stereotactic radiation therapy + nanoparticle administration"}, {"id": 28602, "name": "PRISM Trial: Precision Research Integrating Symptoms and Molecular Biology in Canine Glioma", "url": "https://veterinaryclinicaltrials.org/s/prism-trial-precision-research-integrating-symptoms-and-molecular-biology-in-canine-glioma-715789/?ref=gallery", "status": "Recruiting", "tags": [{"tag_path": "financial-incentive_fully-funded-after-initial-screening-48", "label": "Fully funded after initial screening", "parent_label": "Financial incentive"}, {"tag_path": "species-20_canine-21", "label": "Canine", "parent_label": "Species"}, {"tag_path": "intervention-type_other-65", "label": "Other", "parent_label": "Intervention type"}, {"tag_path": "primary-field-19_oncology-1_brain-or-spinal-tumor-338", "label": "Brain or spinal tumor", "parent_label": "Oncology"}, {"tag_path": "primary-field-19_oncology-1", "label": "Oncology", "parent_label": "Primary field"}], "description": "High-grade gliomas are aggressive brain tumors that are difficult to treat in dogs. While surgery, radiation therapy, and chemotherapy may help some dogs, we still have much to learn about why some tumors respond better to treatment than others. The purpose of this study is to better understand brain tumors in dogs by collecting information about each dog's health, MRI findings, tumor characteristics, and in some dogs, how they respond to radiation treatment. By studying many dogs with naturally occurring brain tumors , we hope to identify patterns that will help veterinarians diagnose these tumors more accurately, predict how they may behave, and develop more effective treatments in the future. Although participation in this study may not directly benefit every dog, the information gained will help improve the care of dogs diagnosed with brain tumors and advance the development of new treatment options. Every dog that participates helps us learn more about brain tumors and brings us one step closer to improving treatment and quality of life for future dogs facing this disease. This study is investigating a gold nano-particle-based, ablative (removal) technique that aims to destroy tumor cells while limiting damage to healthy tissue. Purpose To assess the ability of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to differentiate between benign and metastatic (cancerous) lymph nodes Background Current methods of diagnosing and staging head and neck neoplasia (cancer) in dogs are invasive, and the biopsy samples required to determine if the cancer has spread to surrounding lymph nodes can be difficult to obtain. This study aims to characterize the appearance of regional lymph nodes using diffusion weighted MR sequences in a group of canine patients with confirmed head or neck neoplasia, and evaluate the ability of these sequences to differentiate non-metastatic from metastatic lymph nodes. Such a method of lymph node characterization could prove useful in the staging of tumors, leading to improved prediction of expected outcome and appropriate treatment recommendations. AuroLase Therapy is comprised of three components: 1) an off-the-shelf near infrared laser source, 2) an off-the-shelf interstitial fiber optic probe for delivery of the laser energy to a site near or inside the tumor, and 3) the investigational gold nanoparticles (AuroShell particles), a near infrared absorbing, physiologically inert material designed to absorb and convert laser energy into heat. Intravenously administered AuroShell particles have previously shown efficacy and high selectivity over surrounding healthy tissues in a variety of animal models. Human clinical trials are now progressing utilizing AuroLase Therapy for a number of clinical presentations and tumor types such as refractory head and neck, prostate, lung, and brain cancers. The purpose of the proposed study is to evaluate this therapy in dogs and cats with easily accessible spontaneous tumors. Dogs and cats will receive one AuroLase Therapy treatment and will then be followed for one month after treatment to observe anticancer activity and side effects. Dogs or cats that have been diagnosed with a malignant tumor that is easily accessible will be eligible for this study. Required study visits include pretreatment, day 0 (which may be the same day as pretreatment), day 1, 14, and 28. A physical examination and a small blood sample will be collected pretreatment, and days 1, 14, and 28. The AuroShell particles will be administered intravenously on study day 0. On study day 1 (approximately 24 hours after AuroShell particle infusion), your pet will be anesthetized for approximately 30 minutes for application of the laser treatment. While under anesthesia a tumor biopsy will be performed. Tumor biopsies will be repeated on study day 14 and 28 under mild sedation. Your pet may experience some local pain at the site of the biopsy and laser application. If this occurs, the clinician will prescribe pain medication. After study day 28 (or sooner if your pet is removed from this study for any reason), the study will be completed and the oncology clinician will discuss additional follow-up and treatment options with you. The study will cover all costs related to AuroLase Therapy treatment and required recheck examinations, blood tests and tumor biopsies. The first 21 dogs treated in the SRCBST study at the University of Minnesota showed that a bispecific targeted toxin (sarcoma bispecific targeted toxin, or SRCBST) is safe and doubles the expected survival time. SRCBST2 continues the research by Dr. Jaime Modiano, Dr. Antonella Borgatti and Dr. Michael Henson to determine the safest dose of SRCBST which is still effective. Results of this study will provide information to develop a therapy for both dogs and humans with this incurable disease. Dogs eligible for the study: 1. Diagnosed with HSA 2. Spleen removed by surgery either prior to study or at the Veterinary Medical Center 3. No evidence of metastasis (on chest x-ray, ultrasound) but if gross metastasis removed at time of splenectomy, may still be eligible 4. No concurrent kidney, liver or heart disease, or problems with blood clotting 5. No previous chemotherapy (prednisone is ok), cyclophosphamide, or alternative medications The study involves: PET-CT prior to start of treatment (optional but desired). This imaging will allow us to look for micro-metastasis but will not exclude dogs if any are found. PET-CT is performed under general anesthesia at a nearby University facility and requires an overnight stay following the procedure. Day 1, 3, 5 visit the VMC for SRCBST administration and follow up blood testing Day 8 chemotherapy begins, continues for total of 5 treatments, 3 weeks apart Day 21 - 2nd PET-CT (if first one was done and we saw no evidence of micro-metastasis Day 25-29: second round of SRCBST treatment, coincides with 2nd round of chemotherapy Day 88-92: Possible 3rd round of SRCBST at the time of the 5th chemotherapy, depending upon restaging results (bloodwork, X-ray, ultrasound) Month 6 follow up The owner is responsible for the initial oncology exam fee and staging diagnostics (approx $900-$1,100). Stereotactic radiotherapy (SRT) is the use of this very precise technology to deliver high doses of radiation in fewer treatments compared to conventional protocols. A conventional radiation protocol for nasal tumors involves 10 radiation treatments, given as one treatment per day for 10 days. To take advantage of the extreme accuracy of stereotactic radiation therapy, we are investigating the efficacy of a shorter protocol in which only 3 treatments are delivered over one week (on Monday, Wednesday and Friday). Since 2004 over 400 energy focused cancer treatments have been provided to patients with unresponsive skin based cancers at the Mercy University Hospital, Cork. Over 85% of the tumors treated have been reduced in size by more than 50% after one treatment. The treatment involves the application of a brief electrical pulse (under local anesthetic in people) directly to the tumor tissue. This causes the tumor cells to become temporarily porous and results in a significant increase in the tumor cells absorption of the chemotherapeutic drug. This treatment is extremely suitable for animals particularly in cases where the cancer is considered inoperable. In animals, the device is attached to an existing endoscope and during a standard endoscopic procedure the tumor is enveloped (sometimes in several locations due to tumor size) and treated after IV administration of chemotherapy with the intent that circulating chemotherapy will drive into the open cancer cells, effectively killing them. A newer device is now available to treat tumors using thoracoscopy or laparoscopy as minimally invasive options. The therapy is effective at the location where the electrodes are placed on the animal i.e. the visible tumor mass; provided contact can be made endoscopically the tumor mass can be reduced if not eliminated with minimal side effects 2) How long does the treatment take? The procedure is completed under anesthesia (isoflurane/sevoflurane). Injection of a low dose of chemotherapy (the total is 5% of what would be used conventionally) and application of electrodes directly to the tumor with pulses used taking less than 1/10th of a second to deliver. The pet is treated and able to go home the same day. 3) What chemotherapy drug is used? Is the chemotherapy toxic? The drug used in combination with the electric pulses is Bleomycin. On its own, bleomycin is very poorly absorbed by cells and is considered a poor drug for the treatment of cancer. However, by making the tumor cells porous (because they receive an electrical pulse), the drug can enter locally (but not to other cells in the body), and this results in the tumor cells dying. It also means that the toxicity is limited to the site of where the electrodes are placed which means side effects are truly unlikely. 4) Will my pet lose its hair from the chemo? No. A very low concentration of drug is used and is only toxic at the location the electrodes are placed i.e. on the tumor tissue. 5) Does anesthetic need to be used? Will my pet feel pain or discomfort? Human patients who receive local anesthetic feel the electric pulse and have described it as a dull thud. The anticipation is apparently worse than the discomfort of the pulse which it is important to point out subsides virtually immediately (the pulse lasts 1/10th of a second). In animals, the easiest solution is general anesthetic (isoflurane/sevoflurane) normally for between 15-30mins in total. In this case no discomfort is felt by the pet. 6) Is it an invasive treatment, does it involve surgery and stitches afterward? Unless surgery is needed to approach the tumor, no surgery is involved and therefore the therapy does not involve stitches. For extremely large tumors that are operable a possible combination treatment is to deliver the treatment to the healthy tissue margins afterward to minimize the risk of residual cancer cells escaping. 7) What side effects does the treatment have? No side effects have been reported from the drug or the electric pulses in humans. Some inflammation may occur in larger tumors but this can easily be managed with medication or with many cases subsides without additional therapy needed. 8) What should happen after treatment? How long will it take to see a response? The tumor is not surgically removed; it shrinks and regresses in size over a period of a few weeks after treatment. The speed at which this happens can vary depending on the type and size of the tumor. Normally a reduction in size can be seen within 2 weeks and regression can continue for up to 2 months. Aggressive cancers can be retreated after 4-6 weeks to improve the speed of regression. 9) Which patients are best for treatment? Any animal with a solid tumor can be treated. Dogs, Cats, and Horses have all been treated successfully. 10) Which cancers are best for treatment? Any solid tumor can be treated. Those located on the skin are the most straightforward to identify, diagnose and treat. Internal cancers can be treated during open surgery or via this specially designed endoscopic/internal equipment developed at the Cork Cancer Research Center. Particularly suited are those cancers considered inoperable or that involve invasive surgery e.g. to the head, legs or internal organs. Recent studies indicate that blocking XP01 can induce death of cancer cells as they cannot recover function when the shuttling of proteins is disrupted; in contrast, normal cells appear to be less sensitive to this effect, likely because they are not growing in an uncontrolled manner. The novel compound Verdinexor is an inhibitor of XP01 that is given orally twice per week. Verdinexor has been studied in 2 separate clinical trials in dogs with lymphoma with over 75 dogs treated to date. Approximately 30-40% of dogs with both newly diagnosed and relapsed lymphoma appear to benefit from Verdinexor treatment staying on therapy for over 8 weeks. The main side effect of Verdinexor is loss of appetite and weight loss, with other side effect such as intestinal upset (vomiting, diarrhea) and liver value elevations occurring less frequently. RV1001 is a novel inhibitor of a cell protein called PI3K delta. This drug, like verdinexor, is given orally. PI3Kdelta has an important role in both T and B cells, providing signals for cell survival. Recently, RV1001 was evaluated in a clinical trial of dogs with both T and B cell lymphoma. The overall objective response rate was 62% (3 complete and 10 partial responses) demonstrating very high biologic activity. Increases in liver enzymes were the primary side effect observed, and this was prevented in most dogs by giving the drug Monday through Friday with the weekends off, rather than daily without a break. While the activity of RV1001 was very high, the average time on drug was only 4 weeks indicating that the dogs rapidly developed resistance. Given the potential for both RV1001 and verdinexor to have activity in dogs with lymphoma and the non-overlapping side effects of each drug, the purpose of this study is to evaluate the effects of both drugs in combination. Objective of the trial: To evaluate the biologic activity when verdinexor is administered in combination with RV1001 in dogs with lymphoma, and to assess the clinical toxicities in dogs with lymphoma receiving verdinexor in combination with RV1001."}, {"id": 15272, "name": "Clinical trial in dogs with sarcoma.", "url": "https://veterinaryclinicaltrials.org/s/clinical-trial-in-dogs-with-sarcoma-920726/?ref=gallery", "status": "Completed", "tags": [{"tag_path": "financial-incentive_fully-funded-including-initial-screening-47", "label": "Fully funded including initial screening", "parent_label": "Financial incentive"}, {"tag_path": "intervention-type_drug-334", "label": "Drug", "parent_label": "Intervention type"}, {"tag_path": "species-20_canine-21", "label": "Canine", "parent_label": "Species"}, {"tag_path": "primary-field-19_oncology-1_soft-tissue-sarcoma-28", "label": "Soft tissue sarcoma", "parent_label": "Oncology"}, {"tag_path": "primary-field-19_oncology-1", "label": "Oncology", "parent_label": "Primary field"}], "description": "Purpose and Brief Explanation of Study: Heat shock protein 90 (Hsp90) is a chaperone protein that is important in maintenance of several proteins needed to promote cancer cell growth and survival. Hsp90 activity has been shown to be increased in cancer cells. Hsp90 inhibitor drug conjugates (HDCs) are small molecules that link an anti-cancer drug to an Hsp90 inhibitor. The Hsp90 inhibitor helps bring the anti-cancer drug inside the cancer cells. The anti-cancer drug can then be slowly released inside the cancer cells. Synta Pharmaceuticals has developed STA-12-8960, an Hsp90 inhibitor linked to SN-38, an active metabolite of the anti-cancer (chemotherapy) drug irinotecan. A recently completed clinical trial in dogs with cancer identified a dose of 15 mg/kg given intravenously weekly as the maximum tolerated dose. In this study, several responses to therapy were noted including dogs with lymphoma and mast cell tumors. Side effects were mild in most dogs and consisted of appetite loss and diarrhea, although these were well controlled with additional medications. Objective of the trial: The objective of this study is to compare the plasma and intratumoral concentrations of SN-38, the active metabolite of irinotecan, in dogs with soft tissue sarcoma receiving first irinotecan followed by STA-12-8960 to determine whether STA-12-8960 does result in greater intratumoral drug concentrations."}, {"id": 15275, "name": "Evaluating a targeted her2/neu cancer vaccine for the stimulation of anti-tumor immunity and prolonging survival times in dogs wit", "url": "https://veterinaryclinicaltrials.org/s/evaluating-a-targeted-her2neu-cancer-vaccine-for-the-stimulation-of-anti-tumor-immunity-and-prolonging-survival-times-in-dogs-wit-741440/?ref=gallery", "status": "Completed", "tags": [{"tag_path": "financial-incentive_unfunded-53", "label": "Unfunded", "parent_label": "Financial incentive"}, {"tag_path": "intervention-type_biologic-vaccine-58", "label": "Biologic/Vaccine", "parent_label": "Intervention type"}, {"tag_path": "species-20_canine-21", "label": "Canine", "parent_label": "Species"}, {"tag_path": "primary-field-19_oncology-1_osteosarcoma-or-bone-tumor-29", "label": "Osteosarcoma or bone tumor", "parent_label": "Oncology"}, {"tag_path": "primary-field-19_oncology-1", "label": "Oncology", "parent_label": "Primary field"}], "description": "The study will test whether an adenovirus based vaccine followed by a DNA plasmid administered via electrogenetransfer can elicit anti-tumor immunity and increase survival times. Most dogs undergo amputation and chemotherapy for bone cancer with median survival of about 1 year due to metastatic spread to the lungs. The vaccine will be an additional therapy to standard of care treatment. Up to 60% of dogs with osteosarcoma will express the Her2/neu genetic marker. Telomerase and HER-2/neu as targets of genetic cancer vaccines in dogs. Peruzzi D, Mesiti G, Ciliberto G, La Monica N, Aurisicchio L. Vaccine. 2010 Feb 3;28(5):1201-8. Epub 2009 Nov 26. The vaccine targets this Her2/neu pathway of tumorigenesis allowing the body's immune system to battle the cancer in addition to standard therapies. PROCEDURE: Vaccine is a series of 5 treatments (2 adenovirus/Her2/neu) followed by 3 DNA/plasmid administered via electrogenetherapy (EGT). The first two (2) adenovirus vaccines (prime) are administered via simple intra-muscular injection. The last three (3) of the series (boosters) are administered under a short anesthesia via EGT. Owners are alsop responsible for all other costs associated with their dog's treatment and participation in this study."}, {"id": 15284, "name": "Lymph Node Mapping in dogs with Mast Cell Tumors", "url": "https://veterinaryclinicaltrials.org/s/lymph-node-mapping-in-dogs-with-mast-cell-tumors-103110/?ref=gallery", "status": "Completed", "tags": [{"tag_path": "intervention-type_diagnostic-57", "label": "Diagnostic", "parent_label": "Intervention type"}, {"tag_path": "species-20_canine-21", "label": "Canine", "parent_label": "Species"}, {"tag_path": "primary-field-19_oncology-1_mast-cell-tumor-27", "label": "Mast cell tumor", "parent_label": "Oncology"}, {"tag_path": "primary-field-19_oncology-1", "label": "Oncology", "parent_label": "Primary field"}], "description": "Purpose of Study: Mast cell tumors are a very common skin tumor in dogs, and a common mechanism of spread in the body (metastasis) is to nearby lymph nodes. If tumor spread to lymph nodes is identified (as part of staging), this is important information that often influences treatment recommendations. Currently, standard protocols for looking for metastasis in lymph nodes most commonly include aspiration cytology. Aspiration cytology is minimally invasive, but may miss a diagnosis of lymph node metastasis in a concerning number of patients. Early literature suggests metastatic disease may be missed by lymph node aspiration in up to 40% of patients! The concern is that not only does aspiration cytology only sample a very small amount of a given lymph node, but that it is difficult to ensure that we have correctly predicted the optimal lymph node to sample for any given mast cell tumor. Lymph node mapping, a technique to visualize the lymphatic drainage of tumors by which tumor cells might spread, is increasingly used to improve cancer staging and treatment protocols in the treatment of cancer in humans. Efforts are made to identify the sentinel lymph node or primary lymph node that is most likely to demonstrate evidence of metastatic disease if it is present. This lymph node can then be surgically removed with the primary tumor, in order to be evaluated microscopically for spread of cancer. However the common method of sentinel lymph node mapping performed in people is not widely available to veterinarians. This trial is being performed to hopefully identify an alternative method of sentinel lymph node mapping that can be more widely accessible to a greater number of veterinary practitioners. By doing so, we hope that this will improve the accuracy of cancer diagnoses and treatment recommendations we make for dogs with mast cell tumors and other cancers, improving their quality of life and lifespan. Contact: Email Dr. Stephanie Majeski (smajeski@ucdavis.edu) or Dr. Michele Steffey (masteffey@ucdavis.edu) Call (530) 752-1393 to make an appointment Participation Requirements: Dogs must have been diagnosed with a peripheral mast cell tumor, have been evaluated by or received a consult from a clinician the Soft Tissue Surgery service to determine if LN mapping is viable for your individual dog, and you have elected surgical excision of this tumor both for diagnostic and treatment purposes. Initial Evaluation for Participation: Evaluation by the U.C. Davis V.M.T.H. Oncology or Soft Tissue Surgery services. Specific preoperative diagnostic tests to ensure that your pet is safe for surgical removal of the mast cell tumor will be recommended by the clinician that you consult with on these services. Procedures: If you choose to enroll your dog, lymph node mapping procedures will be performed the day before and the day of surgery. These will be discussed in more detail at the time of your appointment. Benefits: The study will cover costs associated with the sentinel lymph node mapping imaging. There is no charge to you for these procedures. Possible benefits of participating in this study for your dog include more sensitive identification of metastasis (spread of cancer) if it is present. If early metastasis is more sensitively identified, we can then make more accurate treatment recommendations for your pet. It is our hope that in addition to benefiting your dog, we will benefit future patients by advancing the standard of care offered when treating this type of cancer, improving care provided to larger numbers of veterinary cancer patients. If you are calling to schedule an appointment and already know that you are interested in having your dog participate in this study, please inform the coordinators so that they can make sure to schedule appropriately for the mapping procedures."}, {"id": 15286, "name": "Dasatinib Phase I Pharmacokinetics and Pharmacodynamics in Dogs", "url": "https://veterinaryclinicaltrials.org/s/dasatinib-phase-i-pharmacokinetics-and-pharmacodynamics-in-dogs-273333/?ref=gallery", "status": "Completed", "tags": [{"tag_path": "financial-incentive_fully-funded-after-initial-screening-48", "label": "Fully funded after initial screening", "parent_label": "Financial incentive"}, {"tag_path": "intervention-type_drug-334", "label": "Drug", "parent_label": "Intervention type"}, {"tag_path": "species-20_canine-21", "label": "Canine", "parent_label": "Species"}, {"tag_path": "primary-field-19_oncology-1_multiple-tumor-types-343", "label": "Multiple tumor types", "parent_label": "Oncology"}, {"tag_path": "primary-field-19_oncology-1", "label": "Oncology", "parent_label": "Primary field"}], "description": "Purpose of the study: To evaluate the safety, metabolism, and appropriate dosing of dasatinib in dogs. VTH credit given at completion of trial to be used towards additional treatment of $750."}, {"id": 15289, "name": "Immunolight Therapy for Canine Cancer - Phase II (Solid Tumors & Lymphoma)", "url": "https://veterinaryclinicaltrials.org/s/immunolight-therapy-for-canine-cancer-phase-ii-solid-tumors-lymphoma-156021/?ref=gallery", "status": "Completed", "tags": [{"tag_path": "financial-incentive_fully-funded-including-initial-screening-47", "label": "Fully funded including initial screening", "parent_label": "Financial incentive"}, {"tag_path": "intervention-type_drug-334", "label": "Drug", "parent_label": "Intervention type"}, {"tag_path": "species-20_canine-21", "label": "Canine", "parent_label": "Species"}, {"tag_path": "primary-field-19_oncology-1_multiple-tumor-types-343", "label": "Multiple tumor types", "parent_label": "Oncology"}, {"tag_path": "primary-field-19_oncology-1", "label": "Oncology", "parent_label": "Primary field"}], "description": "Purpose and Brief Explanation of Study With the support of the Immunolight team, doctors in the department of Radiation Oncology at North Carolina State University's College of Veterinary Medicine are working with researchers at Duke University's School of Medicine to develop Immunolight Therapy as a treatment option for dogs with various tumors. The goal of this therapy is to provide an alternative treatment for cancer; the hallmark of Immunolight Therapyis a non-invasive, immune-based treatment that does not involve the introduction of cytotoxic agents used in conventional chemotherapy, thus eliminating the potentially life altering side effects of current therapies. Immunolight Therapy involves the use of psoralen, a naturally-occurring compound found in broccoli and figs, as well as phosphors, tiny particles that absorb energy from X-rays to emit UV light in and around cells. For decades, psoralen has been used to treat skin disorders, cancer and autoimmune disease. Immunolight Therapy converts penetrating forms of energy, such as low-dose radiation therapy, into energies that are capable of activating the drug inside the body. This activation generates light inside the tumor to induce an immune response against cancer akin to a related technology (photopheresis) that has been successfully used to treat people with lymphoma of the skin. Immunolight Therapy has shown great promise in laboratory models of human breast cancer. Its short term safety has been documented in dogs; in that safety study, Immunolight Therapy also showed great promise as treatment for some kinds of cancer. Enrolling dogs with: - Lymphoma (newly diagnosed, or if chemotherapy is no longer working) - Oral Melanoma or othertumor types (e.g., dogs with tumors of the skin, toes, mouth, perineum and other sites MAY be eligible). - Most internal tumors will NOT be eligible. - Patients may not receive anyother treatments for their tumor prior to, or during enrollment in study. Immunolight Therapy will be given spanning 3-5 weeks for: - Lymphoma patients - 15 treatment sessions, with follow-up visits at 1 and 2weeks after finishing treatment. If your pet is benefiting from Immunolight Therapy, then additional recheck visits will be required once a month for 5 more visits. - Solid tumor patients - 15 treatment sessions, with follow-up visits at 3 & 6 weeks, and 3 & 6 months. Study Benefits Include: - Variety of free initial staging tests - Free Immunolight Therapy sessions - Free follow-up visits - Compensation available (up to $250) This study is financially supported by Immunolight, LLC., and NC State CVM. More information about Immunolight Therapy, and study eligibility can be found at www.immunolight.com."}, {"id": 15290, "name": "Clinical trial for dogs with mast cell tumor.", "url": "https://veterinaryclinicaltrials.org/s/clinical-trial-for-dogs-with-mast-cell-tumor-899699/?ref=gallery", "status": "Completed", "tags": [{"tag_path": "financial-incentive_medication-costs-included-other-costs-go-to-owner-52", "label": "Medication costs included, other costs go to owner", "parent_label": "Financial incentive"}, {"tag_path": "intervention-type_drug-334", "label": "Drug", "parent_label": "Intervention type"}, {"tag_path": "species-20_canine-21", "label": "Canine", "parent_label": "Species"}, {"tag_path": "primary-field-19_oncology-1_mast-cell-tumor-27", "label": "Mast cell tumor", "parent_label": "Oncology"}, {"tag_path": "primary-field-19_oncology-1", "label": "Oncology", "parent_label": "Primary field"}], "description": "Purpose and Brief Explanation of Study: Tyrosine Kinase Inhibitors (TKIs), including toceranib (Palladia), are a class of drugs that are being used with increased frequency in both human and veterinary oncology. In both populations side effects occur in a large percentage of patients, with many requiring dose reductions or drug holidays, potentially impacting treatment success. Toceranib is used frequently in veterinary medicine and has been demonstrated to have a clinical benefit for dogs with a variety of tumor types including mast cell tumors, anal gland anal sac adenocarcinoma, thyroid carcinomas, head and neck carcinomas, nasal tumors, and metastatic osteosarcoma among others. The most commonly encountered side effects in dogs receiving toceranib are reported to be gastrointestinal (GI) in nature and include diarrhea, vomiting, reduced appetite and weight loss. The frequency and severity of these side effects is variable among individual dogs and currently there are no clinical or molecular makers to identify those dogs that would benefit from the use of medications to prevent GI side effects. This is critical as the development of GI side effects significantly impacts patient treatment. Importantly, dogs that develop GI side effects are less likely to remain on toceranib therapy due to a negative impact on quality of life. "description": "Brief Explanation of Study: Diabetic cats usually require insulin injection to survive although after a period of treatment with insulin they sometimes recover enough and are able to survive without it (i.e. they experience clinical remission). However, the disease process that causes diabetes is still present and most cats that go into remission eventually relapse and become dependent again on insulin injections. Exenatide extended-release (Bydureon) is the first drug to be FDA approved as a once-weekly injection for the treatment of diabetes in people. Exenatide mimics the action of GLP-1, a hormone that augments secretion of insulin from the pancreas in response to elevations in blood sugar levels. Exenatide also enhances the ability of cells that produce insulin to withstand damage caused by disease and increases their chances of survival. It also simulates their growth and proliferation. As such, exenatide has the potential to treat the underlying disease process that leads to diabetes and maintain the cat in a state of clinical remission. We recently tested the effects of Bydureon in healthy cats, finding that Bydureon improves the control of blood sugar for more than 4 weeks after a single injection with no apparent side effects. Here we will compare the effect of Bydureon and placebo in diabetic cats in remission. All cats will receive an injection (of Bydureon or placebo) once every month for 12 months or less if their diabetes recurs. At each monthly recheck, a thorough history will be obtained, a physical exam performed, and blood glucose concentrations measured. Serum fructosamine concentrations will be measured if the blood glucose is high (>180 mg/dl), if clinical signs of diabetes are noted by the owners, or if significant weight loss is recorded. If serum fructosamine is high the cat will be considered out of remission. All cats will be fed a high protein, low carbohydrate diet throughout the study diet (dry or canned; meal fed or ad lib). Concurrent diseases will be treated as needed with standard protocols. Patients will be withdrawn from study if owners do not comply with the study protocol, if excessive weight loss occurs (>2% per week), if the cats body condition score is below ideal, if the cats appetite is persistently decreased or if any other adverse events that may be associated with drug administration are noted. Objective of the trial: To evaluate the benefit of Bydureon for maintaining diabetic cats in remission (in an insulin-independent state). What qualifies my cat for enrollment in this in this trial? To be eligible for participation in this study: 1. Your cat must be a diagnosed diabetic with a recent onset of remission according to the following criteria: Previous diagnosis of diabetes mellitus based on clinical signs and a high serum fructosamine Treated with insulin (any type) for at least 2 weeks. Has not required insulin treatment for at least 4 weeks but no more than 12 weeks Has no current evidence of diabetes relapse (normal serum fructosamine and no clinical signs such as increased drinking, urination or appetite) 2. Your cat must be routinely fed a diabetic diet (a high protein, low carbohydrate diet such as Hills m/d, Purina DM etc.). 3. Your cat must be in good body condition (cannot be under-weight). 4. Cats that have the following are NOT eligible to participate: Recent administration (previous 2 months) of oral hypoglycemic agents Significant concurrent disease (any disease that may require exogenous steroid administration, reduce life-expectancy to <12 months or require intensive management, e.g. gastrointestinal, pulmonary, cardiac, hepatic, neoplastic, or renal disorders \"CKD IRIS Stage 3 or higher\") Overt evidence of peripheral neuropathy (plantigrade stance, inability to jump). Overt evidence of acromegaly Untreated for hyperthyroidism. Cats will not be excluded if have controlled hyperthyroidism or are receiving methimazole and/or ACE-inhibitors. 5. You must agree to return with your cat for rechecks after the initial visit once a month (every 27-32 days). These rechecks will include:An injection of either placebo (sterile saline) or BydureonA complete physical exam and history taking What does enrolling my cat in this clinical trial involve? The study duration is 1 year (12 month). Before entering the study we will draw blood and urine from your cat to screen for concurrent diseases. Your cat will then be allocated randomly into one of the two treatment group: Bydureon or placebo. Because this is a blinded study (i.e. you are should not be aware to which group your cat is allocated) and because the syringes used to inject the two treatments are visibly different, your cat will receive all injections while you are not present. After receiving the injection we will schedule your next recheck for the next month (in 27-32 days).In each subsequent recheck, a blood sample will be drawn from your cat and blood glucose will be measured. If high, a serum fructosamine will be measured as well. If the serum fructosamine is high or if your cat has been showing signs consistent with diabetes since the last recheck (increased drinking, urination, appetite, etc.) your cat will be considered out of remission and will not continue in the trial. Resuming insulin therapy at that time will be considered and discussed with you and with your referring veterinarian.Throughout the duration of the study, decisions regarding your cats health will be made in consultation with your regular veterinarian as usual. Those decisions shall not and will not be affected by participation in the study. Client Compensation They study will pay for one third of the cost of the first office visit as well the full cost of screening tests (including urinalysis and blood tests CBC, Chem, T4, fPLI and IGF-1). All drug expenses (12 months worth of Exenatide-ER injections, roughly equivalent to $1500) and all follow-up rechecks (including office visits, blood glucose measurements and fructosamine concentrations) will be covered by the study."}, {"id": 15335, "name": "Genetic basis of two immune-mediated diseases in dogs", "url": "https://veterinaryclinicaltrials.org/s/genetic-basis-of-two-immune-mediated-diseases-in-dogs-802473/?ref=gallery", "status": "Completed", "tags": [{"tag_path": "financial-incentive_partially-funded_partially-funded-owner-cost-expected-500-49", "label": "Partially funded (owner cost expected <$500)", "parent_label": "Partially funded"}, {"tag_path": "financial-incentive_partially-funded", "label": "Partially funded", "parent_label": "Financial incentive"}, {"tag_path": "intervention-type_none-sample-collection-only-351", "label": "None - sample collection only", "parent_label": "Intervention type"}, {"tag_path": "primary-field-19_internal-medicine-3_urinary-renal-ureter-244", "label": "Urinary – renal/ureter", "parent_label": "Internal medicine"}, {"tag_path": "primary-field-19_internal-medicine-3", "label": "Internal medicine", "parent_label": "Primary field"}, {"tag_path": "species-20_canine-21", "label": "Canine", "parent_label": "Species"}], "description": "Purpose: The purpose of this study is to determine how amino acid status and markers of inflammation are affected in dogs with PLN. We will evaluate plasma amino acid concentrations and markers of inflammation \"C-reactive protein (CRP); tumor-necrosis factor- (TNF- ); interleukin-6 (IL-6)\" in order to then develop novel medical and dietary therapeutic strategies for dogs with PLN. Background: Protein-losing nephropathy (PLN) is a common disease in dogs and can be difficult to treat. Although nutritional therapy is one of the main components of managing this disease, optimizing nutrition is extremely challenging. Dietary protein restriction is recommended to reduce proteinuria. However, at the same time, these dogs have accelerated loss of lean body mass and also may have alterations in amino acids. Additionally, inflammation has been shown to be inversely correlated with amino acid status in people with chronic kidney disease (CKD). All of these factors can contribute to loss of lean body mass and subsequent harmful effects on strength, immune function, morbidity and mortality. An optimal nutritional approach would reduce dietary protein enough to decrease proteinuria without contributing to lean body mass loss. Our hypothesis is that dog with PLN will have altered amino acid profiles and that this will be correlated with increased inflammation as compared to healthy control dogs.The ultimate goal of this study is to determine if we can better optimize nutritional management of PLN in dogs. In people with PLN, feeding low protein diets with concurrent supplementation of keto acids or essential amino acids can improve whole body protein status but minimize nitrogen load. It can also improve hypoalbuminemia and reduce proteinuria. Amino acid supplementation may have some anti-inflammatory properties that may benefit dogs with PLN. If we can identify consistent amino acid imbalances in dogs with PLN, we may be able to tailor nutritional management to improve overall survival and outcome. Conventional chemotherapy protocols typically include one or sometimes multiple chemotherapeutic agents, that are directly toxic to the cancer cells, administered at maximally tolerated doses and intervals. Newer metronomic (low-dose continuous) chemotherapy protocols exert their anti-cancer activity differently, impacting the tumor microenvironment, angiogenesis and immune system. Furthermore, the mechanisms of acquired resistance to chemotherapy seem different when comparing high-dose conventional chemotherapeutic agents and metronomic agents. This is all strong evidence to support a combined treatment regimen.Toceranib phosphate ( Palladia ) was the first veterinary anti-cancer agent to obtain FDA approval based on demonstrable safety and efficacy in the treatment of canine mast cell tumors. Toceranib has subsequently demonstrated benefit in the treatment of numerous canine malignancies. Toceranib has direct anti-cancer, as well as anti-angiogenic activity, and recent research suggests a role in immune system modulation. Previous studies at the University of Wisconsin-Madison have clearly demonstrated that toceranib can be safely administered in combination with piroxicam, resulting in antitumor responses in canine carcinomas and sarcomas, in combination with CCNU, and doxorubicin, and vinblastine resulting in additive and synergistic effects in canine mast cell disease. Objective: The primary purpose of this study is to establish the safety and maximum tolerated dose of carboplatin when administered in combination with toceranib ( Palladia ) in dogs with malignant tumors. The secondary objective of this study is to demonstrate the efficacy/clinical benefit of this chemotherapeutic combination protocol in treating dogs with malignant tumors. What does enrollment into this trial involve? All dogs enrolled in this study will receive toceranib administered by mouth every other day for the duration of the study, and carboplatin administered intravenously every 21 days for a total of four treatments. Blood and urine samples will be collected at baseline, immediately prior to each subsequent dose of carboplatin, and 7, 14, and 21 days post-each dose of carboplatin. Imaging studies will be required for those patients with internal tumors only measurable with x-ray or ultrasound at least twice, but up to four times, during the study.After study day 84 (or sooner if your dog is removed from this study for any reason), the study will be completed and the oncology clinician will discuss additional and / or ongoing treatment options with you as the dogs owner and primary care giver. Client Compensation: The cost of the toceranib phosphate ( Palladia ) and carboplatin will be paid for by the study. Also covered will be the required recheck appointments, monitoring blood tests, urine tests, blood pressure evaluations and any imaging studies deemed necessary by the clinician. Treatment required for unanticipated side-effects will also be covered by the study up to $100. "Primary field"}], "description": "Background: Currently, there is no well-defined study regarding the survival and quality of life for dogs with lymphoma treated with prednisone, an orally administered, inexpensive steroid, despite the drug's inclusion in almost every treatment protocol for lymphoma. Why prednisone? Chemotherapy for canine lymphoma is costly, time-consuming, and has a risk of serious complications. Prednisone is thought to improve quality of life and reduce lymph node size. But the benefit of this inexpensive, orally administered drug has not been formally studied. Purpose of Study: The Canine LYmPhoma Steriod Only (CALYPSO) is a multi-center study involving 100 dogs with high grade lymphoma from approximately 15 contributing veterinary schools and specialty practices.We are interested in determining the response to therapy, how long does it last, if certain types of lymphoma respond better than others to prednisone, and most importantly, how quality of life is improved. Does my dog qualify for the study? Participant dogs need a confirmed diagnosis of intermediate to high-grade lymphoma. Your veterinarian can send aspirates or tissue samples for analysis to the laboratory of her/his choice or we can do this for you at the hospital. Dogs with lymphoma in peripheral lymph nodes qualify for the study. Dogs with skin or gastrointestinal lymphoma are not eligible for the study.Dogs with lymphoma in the spleen and liver only without peripheral lymph node involvement are not eligible.Dogs receiving any chemotherapy or prednisone before they visit our hospital are not eligible. What happens during the study? On the first day, your dogs quality of life at home will be assessed by having you answer questions about how he/she is feeling. This questionnaire will be repeated on Day 7, Day 14, and then monthly thereafter.Someone will contact you at home and review the questions with you if you do not revisit the hospital. Because the response to prednisone may differ between dogs based on the type of lymphoma (T-cell or B-cell), a fine needle aspiration of a lymph node will be obtained at the beginning of the study so it can be sent to a lab for special staining. After routine lab tests and a thorough physical exam including lymph node measurements are completed, your dog will start taking prednisone daily by mouth at home.All dogs get the same dosage."}, {"id": 15409, "name": "Evaluation of the effectiveness of intranasal midazolam administered via a mucosal atomization device and rectal diazepam as first", "url": "https://veterinaryclinicaltrials.org/s/evaluation-of-the-effectiveness-of-intranasal-midazolam-administered-via-a-mucosal-atomization-device-and-rectal-diazepam-as-first-788182/?ref=gallery", "status": "Completed", "tags": [{"tag_path": "primary-field-19_neurology-neurosurgery-5", "label": "Neurology/Neurosurgery", "parent_label": "Primary field"}, {"tag_path": "primary-field-19_neurology-neurosurgery-5_epilepsy-355", "label": "Epilepsy", "parent_label": "Neurology/Neurosurgery"}, {"tag_path": "financial-incentive_not-specified-66", "label": "Not specified", "parent_label": "Financial incentive"}, {"tag_path": "intervention-type_drug-334", "label": "Drug", "parent_label": "Intervention type"}, {"tag_path": "species-20_canine-21", "label": "Canine", "parent_label": "Species"}], "description": null}, {"id": 15431, "name": "Clinical trial for dogs with chronic gastrointestinal upset", "url": "https://veterinaryclinicaltrials.org/s/clinical-trial-for-dogs-with-chronic-gastrointestinal-upset-312856/?ref=gallery", "status": "Completed", "tags": [{"tag_path": "primary-field-19_internal-medicine-3_gi-esophagus-stomach-intestine-234", "label": "Gi – esophagus/stomach/intestine", "parent_label": "Internal medicine"}, {"tag_path": "primary-field-19_internal-medicine-3", "label": "Internal medicine", "parent_label": "Primary field"}, {"tag_path": "financial-incentive_fully-funded-including-initial-screening-47", "label": "Fully funded including initial screening", "parent_label": "Financial incentive"}, {"tag_path": "intervention-type_none-sample-collection-only-351", "label": "None - sample collection only", "parent_label": "Intervention type"}, {"tag_path": "species-20_canine-21", "label": "Canine", "parent_label": "Species"}, {"tag_path": "primary-field-19_oncology-1_osteosarcoma-or-bone-tumor-29", "label": "Osteosarcoma or bone tumor", "parent_label": "Oncology"}, {"tag_path": "primary-field-19_oncology-1", "label": "Oncology", "parent_label": "Primary field"}], "description": "Purpose and Brief Explanation of Study Osteosarcoma is the most common bone cancer in dogs. Even after surgical tumor removal and chemotherapy, the cancer often spreads (metastasizes) and dogs usually die of metastatic disease within an average of 12 months after diagnosis, despite aggressive therapy. However, interestingly, survival times have been shown to sometimes double in osteosarcoma patients who develop infections associated with surgical removal of the primary tumor. These infections may be capable of activating white blood cells such as monocytes to promote anti-tumor activity. The role of monocytes needs to be better understood in general in order to exploit their anti-tumor capabilities. Study Objective The purpose of this study is to characterize differences of monocytes between normal dogs, and osteosarcoma dogs. This will help us define changes that occur in monocytes of an osteosarcoma dog and enhance our understanding of the monocytes ability for tumor suppression. Our long-term goal is to harness the anti-tumor potential of monocytes to develop new therapies using these cells to increase survival in osteosarcoma. What qualifies my dog for enrollment in this trial? We are recruiting dogs in five different categories: 1.Dogs that have been diagnosed with osteosarcoma and have underwent limb amputation and full course of standard chemotherapy (no clinical trial dogs), one or more months after final chemo, no maximum amount of time. These dogs must be free of pulmonary metastasis. 2. Dogs that have been diagnosed with osteosarcoma and have underwent a limb-sparing surgery and have been diagnosed with a limb-spare associated infection. Samples that qualify for this category can be collected off-site and shipped to NCSU. This study will cover the cost of overnight shipping. 3. Dogs that have been diagnosed with osteosarcoma and not yet undergone treatment. These dogs can be enrolled at any time after diagnosis, just prior to treatment to include amputation. These dogs must be free of pulmonary metastasis. What does enrolling my dog in this clinical trial involve? To enroll in this study, you must sign an informed consent for venipuncture. Blood will be drawn from each patient, either at time of diagnosis prior to commencement of any therapy (surgery, chemotherapy, radiation) orafter definitive treatment (amputation/stereotactic radiation + chemotherapy) has been completed. This study requires only a one-time participation blood will be drawn during a single hospital visit. No other obligations will be required. Client Compensation Following determination of your dog's eligibility, costs associated with this study will be provided, to includea complete blood count. Dogs may leave the study at any time, especially in case of progression, to receive another treatment."}, {"id": 15455, "name": "Cancer pain in dogs", "url": "https://veterinaryclinicaltrials.org/s/cancer-pain-in-dogs-180753/?ref=gallery", "status": "Completed", "tags": [{"tag_path": "financial-incentive_fully-funded-including-initial-screening-47", "label": "Fully funded including initial screening", "parent_label": "Financial incentive"}, {"tag_path": "intervention-type_drug-334", "label": "Drug", "parent_label": "Intervention type"}, {"tag_path": "species-20_canine-21", "label": "Canine", "parent_label": "Species"}, {"tag_path": "primary-field-19_oncology-1_multiple-tumor-types-343", "label": "Multiple tumor types", "parent_label": "Oncology"}, {"tag_path": "primary-field-19_oncology-1", "label": "Oncology", "parent_label": "Primary field"}], "description": "Background - Recognition and alleviation of pain in oncology patients is essential for maintaining quality of life. Pain in these patients may be due to the cancer itself, a treatment modality being used (e.g., radiation or surgery), or a concurrent disease (e.g., osteoarthritis). To adequately control pain, a combination of more than one pain medication (NSAIDs, opioids, and adjuvant drugs such as gabapentin) is routinely required. Practitioners have at their disposal comprehensive sources of information on pain management. Most notably, the recently updated AAHA/AAFP Pain Management Guidelines for Dogs and Cats provide current recommendations for a multimodal approach to preempting and controlling pain. However, too much is often as deleterious (if not more) than not enough, in pain management! Aim - To put in adequacy pain management with pain mechanisms in cancerous canine patients, while establishing a pain mechanisms-based approach for analgesia in canine oncology. Design - Prospective, longitudinally open, baseline-controlled clinical trial. Methodology - Client-owned dogs affected by cancer (exclusion: lymphoma, mastocytoma, visceral hemangiosarcoma, and multiple myeloma) will be refereed to CVRS Oncology service for entering in an original study establishing pain mechanisms in cancerous dogs requiring palliative care. In addition to physical examination, clinical pathology tests, and global (visual analogue scale - VAS) pain assessment by the oncologist, global assessment by the owner (VAS, and canine health-related quality of life index - CHQLI), cinematic assessment (static stance weight-bearing and accelerometry), quantitative sensory tests (QST) will characterize the pain profile of the cancerous dog: * Primary punctate mechanical threshold, primary dynamic tactile threshold, secondary mechanical threshold, and conditioned pain modulation would respectively establish the presence of peripheral and/or central sensitization, as well as the value of diffuse nociceptive inhibitory control. * Analgesia would follow a step-wise approach, including NSAID (cimicoxib), anticonvulsant (gabapentin), and tricyclic antidepressant (amitriptyline). Cimicoxib is expected to target inflammatory peripheral / central sensitization. Gabapentin, as calcium channel blocker, would counteract spinal windup. Amitriptyline, as serotonine / noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor, would re-enforce descending inhibitory controls. The whole duration of follow-up would be less than one month, including 5 consultations for assuring animal welfare assessment, detection of potential drug side effects. and potential requirement to rescue analgesia. Potential benefits - To improve the quality of care provided to patients affected with cancer."}, {"id": 15463, "name": "Trial for dogs with newly diagnosed B cell lymphoma", "url": "https://veterinaryclinicaltrials.org/s/trial-for-dogs-with-newly-diagnosed-b-cell-lymphoma-686240/?ref=gallery", "status": "Completed", "tags": [{"tag_path": "financial-incentive_partially-funded_partially-funded-owner-cost-expected-500-49", "label": "Partially funded (owner cost expected <$500)", "parent_label": "Partially funded"}, {"tag_path": "financial-incentive_partially-funded", "label": "Partially funded", "parent_label": "Financial incentive"}, {"tag_path": "intervention-type_biologic-vaccine-58", "label": "Biologic/Vaccine", "parent_label": "Intervention type"}, {"tag_path": "species-20_canine-21", "label": "Canine", "parent_label": "Species"}, {"tag_path": "primary-field-19_oncology-1_lymphoma-or-leukemia-31", "label": "Lymphoma or leukemia", "parent_label": "Oncology"}, {"tag_path": "primary-field-19_oncology-1", "label": "Oncology", "parent_label": "Primary field"}], "description": "Objective: The primary purpose of this study is to demonstrate the safety and efficacy of a combination therapeutic protocol, incorporating chemotherapy and immunotherapy (ECI-LYM-1) which utilizes an autologous tumor vaccine and also infusion of autologous tumor specific T-cells, in dogs with naturally-occurring B cell lymphoma. What does enrollment into this trial involve? All dogs will undergo lymph node removal with blood sample collection (for confirmation of diagnosis and vaccine development) and three doses of doxorubicin chemotherapy for treatment of their lymphoma. Two weeks following the final doxorubicin treatment, a course of three vaccinations will be administered at weekly intervals. At the time of the last vaccination, a skin test will be performed to assess the immune response to the vaccine which will require 2 nights of hospitalization. Apheresis will be performed to extract tumor-specific T lymphocytes from the blood one week after the final vaccination. Your dog will remain hospitalized for two nights following this procedure and receive an additional skin test to assess their immune response to the vaccine. Low-dose, oral chemotherapy (cyclophosphamide) will be administered over 2-4 days at home in the week following apheresis. The T cells extracted during apheresis will be expanded at ELIAS Animal Health and will be re-infused 1 week after apheresis. Low-dose IL-2 will be administered starting 24 hours after the T cell infusion and will continue for 5 total injections under the skin on an every other day basis. A post treatment follow up visit will occur on day 93. Client Compensation: Once informed consent is obtained and preliminary diagnosis and staging is performed, this trial provides full funding for all treatment-related costs including surgery and all subsequent re-evaluations while on trial, all necessary diagnostics (bloodwork, radiographs), treatment, vaccine administration, apheresis, T cell infusion, and management of adverse events that are possibly attributed to therapy. The owner is responsible for the costs associated with the initial oncology consultation, lymph node aspirate, and diagnostic cytometry to confirm diagnosis."}, {"id": 15456, "name": "Treatment of feline gastrointestinal lymphoblastic lymphoma (“FGLL”) with cobalamin (vitamin B12), prednisone, lomustine, and 8 Gy", "url": "https://veterinaryclinicaltrials.org/s/treatment-of-feline-gastrointestinal-lymphoblastic-lymphoma-fgll-with-cobalamin-vitamin-b12-prednisone-lomustine-and-8-gy-242220/?ref=gallery", "status": "Completed", "tags": [{"tag_path": "financial-incentive_fully-funded-including-initial-screening-47", "label": "Fully funded including initial screening", "parent_label": "Financial incentive"}, {"tag_path": "species-20_feline-22", "label": "Feline", "parent_label": "Species"}, {"tag_path": "intervention-type_radiation-60", "label": "Radiation", "parent_label": "Intervention type"}, {"tag_path": "primary-field-19_oncology-1_lymphoma-or-leukemia-31", "label": "Lymphoma or leukemia", "parent_label": "Oncology"}, {"tag_path": "primary-field-19_oncology-1", "label": "Oncology", "parent_label": "Primary field"}], "description": "Purpose and Brief Explanation of Study Feline gastrointestinal (GI) lymphoblastic lymphoma (FGLL) is a debilitating disease of older cats. Chemotherapy for treatment of FGLL has been used with limited success and long-term survival is uncommon. Radiation therapy (RT) is used to treat localized lymphoma in humans and in two small studies of cats with lymphoma confined to the intestinal tract treated with RT, clinical signs improved in most cats. The purpose of this study is to determine whether the addition of abdominal cavity RT to oral chemotherapy (lomustine), daily oral prednisone, and weekly parenteral cobalamin will improve response to therapy, survival times, and quality of life of affected cats. If the addition of RT improves outcome, this therapy may be adopted as the standard of care for cats with FGLL and may be used to further study the use of RT for lymphocytic lymphoma and inflammatory bowel disease. What qualifies my cat for enrollment in this trial? To participate in this clinical trial your cat must: - Have been diagnosed with FGLL via needle aspirates of affected organs and/or histopathology of resected abdominal masses - Have ALT and total bilirubin  14 days prior to enrollment into the study - An expected survival of > 3 weeks regardless of therapy What does enrolling my cat in this trial involve? Once enrolled in the study, cats will receive 2 doses of RT and 4 doses of chemotherapy as part of the study. Cats will be expected to return to NC State at weeks 1, 2, 3, 6, 9 and 12 (a total of 6 visits after initial consultation and staging). You will be responsible for administering daily oral medications (prednisolone) and weekly vitamin B12 injections (under the skin) as part of the treatment for your cat's cancer. You will also be required to complete a written quality-of-life (QOL) survey at each visit.
