"label": "Canine", "parent_label": "Species"}], "description": "We greatly appreciate your interest in our clinical study to bank tissues from canine brain tumors, for shared use by investigators nationally, to better understand tumor behavior and develop new treatments. Your pets clinician will explain the disease characteristics of your pets brain tumor as well as available treatment options. If you choose to participate in this clinical study, this handout will provide you with some insight into the purpose of this study and will explain your responsibilities and patient procedures. What are clinical trials? Clinical trials are research studies. They are used in all specialties of medicine to evaluate new types of treatment. Clinical trials may be designed to determine the anti-cancer effects and side effects of new drugs, new surgical procedures, new radiation therapy procedures, or novel approaches to treatment (such as gene therapy or immunotherapy). In this case the clinical trial is to collect brain tumor and other tissues that will be used in numerous other future studies evaluating these topics. Your pets clinician and the Clinical Trials team will discuss standard treatment and clinical trial options with you. It is your decision whether or not you want your pet to participate in a clinical trial. You may discuss your pets participation with your family and your pets veterinarian. If you have any questions, please ask your pets clinician for additional information. Why is this clinical trial being conducted? Lack of access to good quality canine brain tumor tissues and tumor cell cultures is the biggest barrier in advancing the field of brain tumor investigation and therapeutic development. Very few veterinary institutions in this country have an actively-funded tumor biorepository, and fewer actively acquire and bank brain tumor tissues. Where canine biobanks exist, brain tumors remain strikingly underrepresented. Thus, there is a great importance to collecting and banking canine brain tumor tissues for shared use among comparative brain cancer researchers. Comprehensive information about tumor genetics, biology, and the molecular landscape of brain tumors, will allow specific determination of which pathways or tumor types/subtypes provide the best model for comparative and translational studies to advance human therapies. The availability of comprehensive data from the canine model will help promote identification and development of novel therapeutics that are targeted to molecular pathways or triggers for cancer development that co-occur in humans and dogs, and identify appropriate use of canine clinical trials that may promote more rapid approval of novel therapeutics through regulatory mechanisms. Tissues from the CSU Tissue Repository are made available to other institutions that wish to collaborate brain tumor studies, so the collection and banking of brain tumor tissues here at CSU will have far-reaching benefits to other institutions as well. The NIH National Cancer Institutes Comparative Brain Tumor Consortium (of which CSU is a member and active participant) already has in place collaborations among several key players in the area of brain tumor research, many of whom are in need of brain tumor specimens for their studies in tumor genetics, molecular biology, and therapeutic development. Which patients are eligible to participate in this clinical trial? Dogs must have a diagnosis of a brain tumor that is deemed surgically resectable/accessible based on MRI characteristics. They cannot have had any prior radiation therapy or chemotherapy for their tumor. They must have good function of the liver and kidneys, have acceptable blood counts, and be free of severe underlying disease that might affect safe administration of anesthesia. Dogs must undergo some diagnostic testing prior to starting the study to ensure that they are eligible, including blood work (complete blood count, chemistry profile), urinalysis, and brain MRI. What will happen if my pet participates in this clinical trial? After eligibility is confirmed, your dog will go under anesthesia for brain tumor resection. During surgery, the tumor tissue will be removed and evaluated by histopathology to obtain a diagnosis, as normally occurs with any clinical case. A portion of the tumor tissues collected will be processed and stored in the tissue biobank, for future use in various investigations of brain tumor biology or development of novel treatments. In addition to tumor tissue, blood, a small amount of cerebrospinal fluid, and a small sample of skin from the edge of the incision, will also be collected and banked. What side effects or risks may my pet experience while participating in this clinical trial? The act of tissue banking has no inherent risk, and this tumor tissue would normally be removed surgically; however, your pet may experience side effects associated with brain tumor surgery. The surgical technique has been used in veterinary brain tumor resection routinely. Nevertheless, surgery of any kind, and in particular surgery within the brain, does have risks associated with it, which could be mild or severe (including death). Your pets clinician will discuss possible side effects with you and help you manage them if they occur. If your pet experiences anything unusual during the clinical trial, please contact your clinician or Clinical Trials team. How long will my pet be in the clinical trial? After surgery is complete, your pets participation in the clinical trial is finished. Your pets clinician will discuss options for continued treatment and diagnostic testing once the trial has ended. Can my pet withdraw from the clinical trial? You may decide to withdraw your pet from the clinical trial at any time. Tell your pets clinician and/or the Clinical Trials team if you are considering withdrawing your pet. It is important to discuss withdrawal in order to determine a plan for continued treatment of your pets brain tumor. The clinician may stop your pet from continued participation in the clinical trial at any time if he/she believes it is in your pets best interest or if the trial is discontinued or if the trial protocol is not followed. What financial incentives will CSU provide for my pets participation? The study will apply a credit of up to $8000 to your VTH account to be put towards the costs of brain surgery. These credits can only be applied after your dog has been deemed eligible and you have chosen to enter the trial, and will be credited to your account after surgery is completed. What are my responsibilities during the clinical trial? You are responsible for any and all other costs relating to your dogs care not covered by the study, including the cost of the initial examination and pre-anesthesia testing required prior to entering the study or after the study ends, any costs of diagnostic testing or treatment beyond those covered by the credit, as well as any optional adjunctive cancer therapies you might elect. You are expected to make and keep all appointments, according to the clinical trial protocol. Questions? Please do not hesitate to obtain additional information from your pets clinician or the Clinical Trials team if you do not understand something about the study or your pets care and treatment. Previous research has found that feelinglymph nodes on examination can be an inaccurate assessment for cancer spread as they can be normal in size and still contain tumor cells. Needle aspirates of lymph nodes can be obtained to evaluate for evidence of spread at the cellular level, but there are several lymph nodes in the head and neck region which can be involved, and some are difficult to access on examination. Some of these lymph nodes are not generally found on physical examination, require advanced imaging to be detected, and can be challenging to acquire aspirates. Advanced imaging most commonly includes a neck ultrasound or a computed tomography (CT) scan of the region. This is part of the reason for the CT scan in your dog. This scan allows for better determination of the extent of the primary tumor, but also the lymph node appearance. As such, CTs are commonly used for surgical and/or radiation planning.As a diagnostic regularly utilized in current practice, we seek to determine whether CT is a sensitive and specific indicator for lymph node metastasis in dogs with oral malignant melanoma. In human medicine, staging for similar head and neck tumors also regularly includes the functional imaging positron emission tomography (PET) combined with CT, which assesses for regions of increased metabolic activity and has been found to correspond with cancer in the body. Currently, the accuracy for prediction of metastasis as well as for the local extent of disease is unknown for PET/CT in canine melanoma. In this study, palpation, CT, and PET appearance of lymph nodes of your dog will be compared to histopathologic (biopsy)results. We hypothesize that CT and PET will provide an increased sensitivity and specificity over palpation alone and will be accurate enough to eliminate unnecessary sampling or resection of lymph nodes in the future."}, {"id": 15499, "name": "Protocol for the Combined Use of TANOVEA™-CA1 (Rabacfosadine for Injection) and Asparaginase in Dogs with Relapsed Lymphoma: VC-01", "url": "https://veterinaryclinicaltrials.org/s/protocol-for-the-combined-use-of-tanoveatm-ca1-rabacfosadine-for-injection-and-asparaginase-in-dogs-with-relapsed-lymphoma-vc-01-912643/?ref=gallery", "status": "Completed", "tags": [{"tag_path": "financial-incentive_medication-costs-included-other-costs-go-to-owner-52", "label": "Medication costs included, other costs go to owner", "parent_label": "Financial incentive"}, {"tag_path": "intervention-type_drug-334", "label": "Drug", "parent_label": "Intervention type"}, {"tag_path": "species-20_canine-21", "label": "Canine", "parent_label": "Species"}, {"tag_path": "primary-field-19_oncology-1_lymphoma-or-leukemia-31", "label": "Lymphoma or leukemia", "parent_label": "Oncology"}, {"tag_path": "primary-field-19_oncology-1", "label": "Oncology", "parent_label": "Primary field"}], "description": "Lymphoma is a common cancer in dogs. Activation of melanocortin receptors in the brain leads to decreased food intake and increased metabolism. osteosarcoma to evaluate the safety and effectiveness of a new vaccine following standard of care therapy. Bone cancer or osteosarcoma (OSA) is a common, highly aggressive cancer that frequently affects the long bones of large breed dogs. Current standard of care therapy consists of surgical limb amputation plus 4 doses of chemotherapy, given in a vein, every 3 weeks. The immune system plays an important role in identifying and targeting cancer cells in the body. In this study, we aim to use a new approach to stimulate the bodys own immune system to attack remaining tumor cells in dogs that have undergone limb amputation and chemotherapy for the treatment of OSA. We will use a study vaccine, which has been modified to express a tumor protein (HER-2/neu) that is found in many cancer cells, including canine bone cancer cells and cancer stem cells. The hope is that when injected into the bloodstream, the vaccine stimulates the immune system to attack cells expressing the HER-2/neu tumor protein. This approach aims to delay and/or prevent the spread of cancer (metastases) following removal of the primary bone cancer tumor (limb amputation) and chemotherapy. Interactions with other drugs are unknown, so it is necessary to disclose any medications (and supplements) your dog is currently taking to the oncologist. It is strongly encouraged to eliminate all unnecessary medications. **Please note that all staging diagnostics (including but not limited to radiographs, ultrasound, and blood work) must be performed at Cornell University prior to surgery and chemotherapy. Full amputation surgery must also be performed at Cornell within 10 days of the initial staging diagnostics. Following surgery all chemotherapy and vaccine administration appointments must also be performed at Cornell. Please contact the clinical trials coordinator for more information."}, {"id": 15597, "name": "Using CT Imaging to Identify the Draining Lymph Node in Dogs with Mast Cell Tumors", "url": "https://veterinaryclinicaltrials.org/s/using-ct-imaging-to-identify-the-draining-lymph-node-in-dogs-with-mast-cell-tumors-319929/?ref=gallery", "status": "Completed", "tags": [{"tag_path": "financial-incentive_medication-costs-included-other-costs-go-to-owner-52", "label": "Medication costs included, other costs go to owner", "parent_label": "Financial incentive"}, {"tag_path": "intervention-type_diagnostic-57", "label": "Diagnostic", "parent_label": "Intervention type"}, {"tag_path": "species-20_canine-21", "label": "Canine", "parent_label": "Species"}, {"tag_path": "primary-field-19_soft-tissue-8", "label": "Soft tissue surgery", "parent_label": "Primary field"}, {"tag_path": "primary-field-19_soft-tissue-8_hemolymphatic-system-328", "label": "Hemolymphatic system", "parent_label": "Soft tissue surgery"}], "description": "Mast cell tumors are the most common malignant skin tumors in dogs and surgery is the treatment of choice for addressing these tumors. These tumors can spread (metastasize) to other areas and drain into the surrounding lymph nodes. If a tumor has spread into the lymph node it may also spread to the spleen, liver, and bone marrow and additional diagnostic tests may need to be performed. Identification and surgical removal of a draining lymph node (the sentinel lymph node) is used for determining local metastasis and can impact prognosis and treatment recommendation. As every dog and tumor is different, it has been shown that the node closest to the tumor is not necessarily the sentinel node. The goal of this study is to utilize computed tomography (CT) to identify the sentinel lymph node prior to surgical removal. collaboration with Varian Medical Systems, is currently accepting animals into a clinical trial to study the immune response of dogs that receive stereotactic radiation (SRS/SRT) to treat osteosarcoma, oral malignant melanoma, sino-nasal tumors, or thyroid carcinoma. All four of these tumor types are known to have the potential to spread (metastasize) to other parts of the body. This clinical trial was launched to evaluate specific immune cells found in the blood. These immune cells have been found to impact survival in people across several tumor types that also have metastatic potential. Early data collected by PetCure Oncology as well as other investigators suggests that SRS/SRT in dogs may have a positive effect on the immune cells responsible for attacking cancer, leading to longer survival times than a traditional treatment course centered around surgical tumor removal including amputation. The purpose of this trial is to test this theory. All trial-related blood draws will be free of charge, and pet owners will be provided $2,000 in compensation towards their treatment. As the tumor grows, it obstructs the flow of urine, which can become life-threatening. TCC can also spread to nearby lymph nodes, lungs, and bones. In most cases, TCC of the bladder cannot be cured. Common treatment options include nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), chemotherapy, stent placement, or radiation therapy. Most dogs with TCC of the bladder succumb to their cancer within 6 to 8 months of diagnosis. Recently, a tumor protein called V600E B-Raf has been identified in up to 87% of dogs with TCC. This clinical trial is evaluating a bacterial vaccine that encourages the immune system to target the V600E B-Raf protein. Paclitaxel is not water soluble and therefore needs to be formulated with a chemical that permits intravenous administration. Unfortunately, the chemical (cremephor) causes allergic reactions and limits the ability to use this drug in dogs. A new water soluble formulation of paclitaxel was developed (Paccal Vet) and tested in dogs with mast cell tumors, mammary tumors and oral squamous cell carcinoma tumors. While there were some responses to therapy, drug administration was limited by side effects to the bone marrow, primarily low white blood cell count. ART207 is a new formulation of paclitaxel in which the drug is encapsulated in a lipid (fat) protein complex designed to promote specific uptake of the complexes through cholesterol receptors that are expressed in tumors. An ongoing safety study in normal healthy dogs demonstrated that ART207 can be administered at doses over twice those used in the Paccal Vet study, with no side effects to the bone marrow. Therefore, the ART207 results in much higher exposures to paclitaxel than the previous formulations and may have greater anti-tumor activity in dogs with cancer. This will be an open label clinical trial in which all dogs will receive ART 207 every 21 days. Dogs with cutaneous mast cell tumors or solid tumorsare eligible to enroll. These dogs may have failed conventional therapy or the owners may not desire to pursue conventional therapy at this time. Dogs will receive ART 207 IV on an anticipated schedule of every 21 days for a total of 4 treatments. Response to therapy will be assessed 21 days after each treatment and ART 207 administration will continue in the setting of stable disease or partial/complete response to therapy. Those dogs with progressive disease will be removed from the study. Analysis of dogs for tumor response will be performed by caliper measurement of the tumor and photographic documentation. Standard clinical chemistries (CBC, chemistry panel, and urinalysis) will be performed during the study. Additionally, 24-hour pharmacokinetic analyses will be performed following the first dose of ART 207, and plasma will be collected at each study visit to assess basal paclitaxel plasma concentrations "Primary field"}], "description": "When a person or dog is diagnosed with cancer it is important to determine if the disease has spread throughout the body. This is called staging. Head and neck tumors usually go first to the local lymph nodes. Presently the only way to be sure if the cancer has spread there is to surgically remove the lymph nodes and look at them under the microscope. Imaging with CT or ultrasound can help, but is often not a very accurate way to tell if the cancer has metastasized. Iron nanoparticles (trade marked as a product called Feraheme) are taken up by normal cells in a lymph node. When cancer has infiltrated the lymph node there is no uptake. This can be visualized on MRI and in people has been shown to be a remarkably sensitive way to look for metastasis. The goal of this study is to determine if this novel, non-invasive imaging method utilizing iron nanoparticles is more sensitive than other types of imaging for diagnosing metastatic lymph nodes. On the first day of the study, dogs will receive an intravenous infusion of a medication called Ferumoxytol. This will be mixed with saline and given over 15-20 minutes after which we will monitor the dogs for any potential side effects. 48 hours later a CT and MRI will be performed. Dogs will then have several lymph nodes surgically excised so that they can be examined for presence of metastatic disease. In other cases, these treatments are likely to improve outcome but are inaccessible (e.g., financial, scheduling and/or geographical limitations). Thus, there is an immense need for treatments that offer effective tumor control and palliation, and that ideally can be given at low-cost in the primary care setting. We have recently demonstrated proof-of-concept for a low-cost effective option, called enhanced ethanol ablation. Ethanol ablation (intratumoral injectionof pure ethanol) was originally used for human liver cancer, achieving survival rates similar to surgical resection for small tumors. However, conventional ethanol ablation is ineffective for superficial, large, and/or poorly encapsulated lesions, and requires large injection volumes. Enhanced ethanol ablation involves controlled injection of an ethyl cellulose- ethanol mixture directly into the tumor. When mixed with ethyl cellulose, a water-insoluble ethanol-based gel is formed. We have shown this caused complete regression in 7 of 7 chemically-induced tumors in the hamster oral cavity while dramatically reducing the required injection volume. Now, we will perform a pilot study to evaluate safety and efficacy in feline oral squamous cell carcinomas, which serves as a model for other large, superficial and invasive tumors. Cats with oral squamous cell carcinoma (mandibular and maxillary) will be enrolled. They will have basic staging tests performed, and then undergo anesthesia for a intratumoral injection of ethyl cellulose-ethanol. The tumor will be imaged using CT, before and after injection. Cats will be hospitalized overnight for observation, after this first injection. They will then return for periodic recheck exams to evaluate for toxicity and changes in tumor size. Depending on response to the first injection, cats may be eligible for up to 2 booster injections. Cats will be dismissed from the study at the time of local disease progression, or after 6 months of follow-up."}, {"id": 15731, "name": "Preclinical Evaluation Of Combined CP-818 And Doxorubicin For Treatment Of Canine Multicentric T Cell Lymphoma", "url": "https://veterinaryclinicaltrials.org/s/preclinical-evaluation-of-combined-cp-818-and-doxorubicin-for-treatment-of-canine-multicentric-t-cell-lymphoma-428647/?ref=gallery", "status": "Completed", "tags": [{"tag_path": "financial-incentive_fully-funded-after-initial-screening-48", "label": "Fully funded after initial screening", "parent_label": "Financial incentive"}, {"tag_path": "intervention-type_drug-334", "label": "Drug", "parent_label": "Intervention type"}, {"tag_path": "species-20_canine-21", "label": "Canine", "parent_label": "Species"}, {"tag_path": "primary-field-19_oncology-1_lymphoma-or-leukemia-31", "label": "Lymphoma or leukemia", "parent_label": "Oncology"}, {"tag_path": "primary-field-19_oncology-1", "label": "Oncology", "parent_label": "Primary field"}], "description": "While conventional chemotherapy can induce remission in many dogs with lymphoma, relapse almost always occurs, and dogs with T cell lymphoma tend to have outcomes that are worse than average. Novel therapies for lymphoma, especially T cell lymphoma, are needed. CP-818 inhibits a novel cellular pathway that has been shown to induce cell death in some T cell lymphoma cells. Inhibitors of this pathway hold great promise for treating T cell lymphoma, and unpublished work suggests that a combination of CP-818 and the conventional chemotherapy drug doxorubicin are significantly more effective than either drug alone. CP-818 has been tested in rats at doses 10 times higher than the doses we plan to use, and in normal healthy dogs at the approximate dose we plan to use, without evidence of any adverse effects. CP-818 has been given to dogs with cancer and appears well tolerated. The dose of doxorubicin we are using has been used in dogs with cancer for decades, and has an acceptable and predictable likelihood of adverse effects. The primary objective of this study is to evaluate the safety and antitumor activity of this combination given to dogs with T cell lymphoma that have not yet been treated. Your dog will receive CP-818 orally twice daily, and will receive a conventional dose of doxorubicin once every 3 weeks for up to 5 treatments. He/she will be rechecked weekly for the first 4 weeks, then every third week thereafter. Visits where doxorubicin is given will generally take about 4 hours. He/she will be eligible to continue receiving treatment at no cost as long as the drugs are tolerated and your dog is experiencing clinical benefit (disease stabilization or meaningful tumor shrinkage). Analysis for tumor response will be performed by direct tumor measurement or through the use of imaging (X-rays, ultrasound, CT). Standard bloodwork will be performed at each visit. Additional tests to be performed include blood draws and 2 or 3 biopsies of the lymph nodes over the course of the study to determine how CP-818 is affecting the cancer cells. These biopsies will be performed using standard sedation/anesthesia protocols, the biopsy site will be sutured, and sutures removed 2 weeks later. The visits when biopsies are performed may require a longer time, approximately half a day. The total volume of blood involved in each collection is approximately 9 teaspoons. "Primary field"}], "description": "This is a multi-institutional consortium including UAB and veterinary colleges using an innovative immunotherapeutic approach to treating malignant glial brain tumors in pet dogs. Pet dogs share their environment (and oftentimes even their diet) with their owners. Dogs and humans develop sporadic benign and malignant brain tumors at about the same rate and with similar histopathology. Dogs are often euthanized due to the cost of care. Thus, the spontaneously occurring canine brain tumor represents an ideal opportunity to improve the lives of people and pets through comparative oncology and genomics and the One Medicine approach to research and direct clinical application. Malignant gliomas are the most common primary brain tumors in humans, accounting for 30% of all primary central nervous system (CNS) tumors in adults. With few major advances in decades, there has been no significant reduction in mortality and only a modest improvement in median survival. Recently, objective responses and long-term survivals have been observed in human glioma patients who have received oncolytic virotherapy and a Phase I trial is currently underway at UAB in patients using M032 alone. In this way, the human can served as a model for translation to the pet dog with malignant glioma. Following surgery to remove all or part of the tumor, a clinical grade oncolytic herpes simplex virus that expresses human interleukin-12 (currently being used in the concurrent human trial) will be injected into the resected tumor bed. Some dogs will also receive a drug called a checkpoint inhibitor. The dog is an ideal large animal model for diagnostic and therapeutic studies and can be used to translate successes to human patients while providing compassionate care to animals and advancing the field of veterinary medicine. One factor that has been showed to be potentially prognostic is the presence of a type of cell called a tumor associated macrophage (TAM). Despite the wide use of chlorambucil in cats, the pharmacokinetic parameters, i.e. how the body absorbs, metabolizes and eliminates the drug, have not been previously studied in cats. Dogs presenting with this disease often have spontaneous internal bleeding that results in sudden onset of weakness or collapse. Although this is a common consequence for hemangiosarcoma, any other tumor of the spleen can spontaneously bleed resulting in these same changes. Dogs who have a bleeding splenic tumor must undergo surgery to remove the spleen (called splenectomy). This procedure both removes the source of life-threatening hemorrhage and provides tissue samples for making a final diagnosis. Many of the remaining dogs will have hemangiosarcoma as the cause of their bleeding and will require chemotherapy following surgery to delay or prevent metastatic disease. For dogs with splenic hemangiosarcoma, the combination of surgery and chemotherapy has been estimated to provide median survival times of 4-9 months with only a small percentage of dogs surviving to 2 years. Furthermore, many dogs may present with disease that cannot be removed owing to size, location, or tumors that have already spread. Medical therapy for these patients needs improvement. However, the combination has not been scientifically tested for effectiveness. In veterinary medicine, this is typically accomplished with imaging techniques such as computed tomography (CT), or standard abdominal ultrasonography. However, these imaging studies often miss additional tumors or underestimate the severity of disease, and more extensive disease may be found at the time of open abdominal surgery, changing the treatment plan. This places emotional and financial burden on the owner, and puts the patient through a possibly unnecessary invasive, painful surgical procedure.In people, laparoscopic ultrasound (LUS) has been used successfully for staging of liver cancer and is now considered the gold-standard. Laparoscopic ultrasound is a minimally-invasive imaging technique that involves placing an ultrasound probe through a small incision into the abdomen, and directly placing the probe on the liver to acquire images. This is advantageous due to the ability to better visualize the liver without other organs in the way and by directly seeing the liver with the laparoscope (camera) at the same time. Additionally, LUS can be used to guide minimally-invasive surgery of the liver.The purpose of this study is to describe the use and feasibility of laparoscopic ultrasonography of the liver in healthy dogs. Our ultimate goal is to eventually apply this technique to dogs with liver cancer to advance the clinical management of these cases. Each dog will undergo a complete physical exam and have screening bloodwork performed to ensure they are healthy prior to undergoing anesthesia and surgery. Dogs will be placed under general anesthesia, and a small (2 cm) incision will be made into the abdomen, through which all procedures will be performed. One to two additional small incisions (0.5-1cm) may also be needed to provide adequate access to perform the spay and/or gastropexy. A laparoscope (camera) and special ultrasound probe intended for laparoscopic use will be inserted through the incision to perform thorough imaging and evaluation of the entire liver. No surgical procedure will be performed on the liver. "Primary field"}], "description": "Many sarcomas in both people and dogs can be resistant to the available treatment options. A new way of fighting these sarcomas is with immunotherapy, which helps the bodys own immune system fight the cancer. There is a type of immune cell in the body, called a macrophage, that normally helps fight bacteria and viruses, as well as helps heal wounds. However, it is also known that macrophages can help sarcomas grow and spread. There is a new drug, a small molecule called NCGC00413972 (NIH 972), which can re-program these macrophages to instead fight against the tumor. This has been shown to be successful in cells and in mice. There is also information that this drug is safe to give to healthy dogs. The primary goal of this trial is to evaluate the safety and biologic effects of NIH 972 in dogs with cancer. A secondary goal of this trial is to evaluate any anti-tumor effects it may have in dogs with sarcomas. If the exams, tests, and procedures show that your dog can take part in the study, and you choose to enroll them, then the following will happen as part of the study: On the first day your dog receives the new drug, they will have blood drawn at multiple time points and will be in hospital for close monitoring for at least 8 hours after their first dose. They will either need to stay overnight with us or come back for an additional blood draw 24 hours from their first dose. They will receive a tablet daily and be rechecked 1, 2, 4, and 6 weeks after starting then every 4 weeks thereafter, as long as their disease is not worsening, and the drug is well tolerated. On these follow-up visits, we will collect additional blood, both to assess how they are handling the drug and to store for research purposes. If needed to monitor their cancer, they will also have imaging performed at certain visits. Two weeks after starting the drug, they will have another biopsy of their tumor in addition to additional blood draws. Sedation will be required for the biopsies and imaging (if applicable to your dog). In the unfortunate event of your dog passing away or being humanely euthanized while in this trial, a necropsy will be performed to help understand the cause of death."}, {"id": 15933, "name": "Oral Melanoma Study in Dogs", "url": "https://veterinaryclinicaltrials.org/s/oral-melanoma-study-in-dogs-250949/?ref=gallery", "status": "Completed", "tags": [{"tag_path": "financial-incentive_fully-funded-including-initial-screening-47", "label": "Fully funded including initial screening", "parent_label": "Financial incentive"}, {"tag_path": "intervention-type_drug-334", "label": "Drug", "parent_label": "Intervention type"}, {"tag_path": "species-20_canine-21", "label": "Canine", "parent_label": "Species"}, {"tag_path": "primary-field-19_oncology-1_melanoma-26", "label": "Melanoma", "parent_label": "Oncology"}, {"tag_path": "primary-field-19_oncology-1", "label": "Oncology", "parent_label": "Primary field"}], "description": "Randomized, placebo-controlled clinical trial to assess a potential new treatment for oral melanoma in dogs. communication signal released from cells in dogs with soft tissue sarcomas after they are treated with non-invasive histotripsy ablation Background Soft tissue sarcomas are a common form of skin cancer in dogs. They tend to develop slowly and dont usually metastasize when they are low grade. A biopsy is needed to determine the tumor grade. Surgery is the treatment of choice, but if a minimal surgery (removal of only the tumor that can be seen or felt) is performed, the tumor is likely to grow back. Removal of the tumor and several centimeters of normal-appearing tissue is required for complete removal. However, this can be impossible without amputation or the addition of radiation therapy, particularly when the tumors are large or affect certain areas of the body like the limbs or face. Alternative treatments to surgery or radiation are needed. We have previously evaluated a non-surgical, non-radiation, non-thermal focused ultrasound treatment (histotripsy) to kill soft tissue sarcomas affecting pet dogs. This technology has also been used in humans with liver tumors. Histotripsy focuses microsecond-long soundwaves through the skin onto a precise target area of the tumor. This causes air bubbles in the tumor tissue to expand and collapse, mechanically disintegrating the surrounding tumor tissue. Research in rodents, pet dogs, and humans have shown that the liquified tissue stimulates the immune system to recognize cancer in other parts of the body. The purpose of this study is to evaluate one type of communication signal released from cells, termed extracellular vesicles (EVs). EVs carry protein and genetic messages that cause immediate changes in the receiving cell. EVs and their cargo can be used as a non-invasive way to diagnose a tumor or look for signals to predict response to treatment or prognosis. We will extract and measure EVs and their immune signal cargo from the liquified tumor tissue, the lymph nodes, and the blood after histotripsy treatment of soft tissue sarcomas. We hope to find that histotripsy increases the number and type of EVs in the blood, which would be the first step in developing a liquid biopsy for diagnosis; we also hope to find that histotripsy treatment changes the communication with the immune system, serving as a mechanism to explain the changes seen in the immune response after histotripsy. To determine how histotripsy may affect EVs, we are recruiting dogs with soft tissue sarcomas located in the skin to undergo histotripsy treatment of the tumor. An existing tumor must be present for treatment. The application of this experimental therapy has the potential to directly enhance the quality of life of dogs diagnosed with soft tissue sarcomas and defray the cost of treatment. At the same time, the results of our study may lead to improved liquid biopsy and treatment options for human cancer patients."}, {"id": 15911, "name": "Tolerability and clinical efficacy of "Primary field"}], "description": "Verdinexor is a chemotherapy drug that has been conditionally approved by the FDA for the treatment of canine lymphoma. Verdinexor is a selective inhibitor of nuclear export (SINE) compound, and this family of drug has demonstrated encouraging results in preclinical studies when combined with other chemotherapeutic drugs. These studies offer encouragement that these types of combinations and clinical results could be achieved in dogs. This study seeks to establish the tolerability of verdinexor in combination with doxorubicin in dogs with cancer. The results of this study could be used to advance the study of this combination of drugs in future clinical trials that focus on a specific cancer types. The study duration is 120 days and consists of a total of 10 hospital visits. The trial is fully funded with no costs to the owner. A 501(c)(3) nonprofit incubator of scientific innovation, Ethos Discovery has developed the most innovative scientific portfolio in the field of animal health and delivers answers to our clinical research questions through rigorous clinical trials made available to pet patients. The mission of Ethos Discovery is to improve health outcomes for humans and animals with complex medical problems. We are agnostic to the source of good ideas and uniquely positioned, with the support of Ethos Veterinary Health, to reach patients and doctors nationally and partner with key leaders in their field internationally. This flexibility provides us the opportunity to pursue impactful research that will make a difference where it is most important, at the point of care and for the benefit of patients and families in the community."}, {"id": 15950, "name": "Combination Trametinib and Sapanisertib Clinical Trial Pilot Study for Canine Malignant Neoplasia", "url": "https://veterinaryclinicaltrials.org/s/combination-trametinib-and-sapanisertib-clinical-trial-pilot-study-for-canine-malignant-neoplasia-400221/?ref=gallery", "status": "Completed", "tags": [{"tag_path": "financial-incentive_fully-funded-after-initial-screening-48", "label": "Fully funded after initial screening", "parent_label": "Financial incentive"}, {"tag_path": "intervention-type_drug-334", "label": "Drug", "parent_label": "Intervention type"}, {"tag_path": "species-20_canine-21", "label": "Canine", "parent_label": "Species"}, {"tag_path": "primary-field-19_oncology-1_multiple-tumor-types-343", "label": "Multiple tumor types", "parent_label": "Oncology"}, {"tag_path": "primary-field-19_oncology-1", "label": "Oncology", "parent_label": "Primary field"}], "description": "A large number of different canine and human cancers appear to rely on signaling through 2 important cellular pathways; the MAPK pathway and the PI3K/mTOR pathway. The drugs trametinib and sapanisertib, which target signaling through these 2 pathways, appear to have significant antitumor effects both in tissue culture and in mouse models. When these 2 drugs were given to laboratory dogs at the doses we plan to test, they were well tolerated and the amount of drug appearing in the blood was predicted to be enough to inhibit tumor growth. The primary objective of this study is to evaluate the safety, biologic effects, and antitumor activity of combined trametinib and sapanisertib given to dogs with measurable malignant tumors. Your dog will receive trametinib orally once daily and sapanisertib orally every other day. They will be rechecked 6 days, and 2, 4, and 8 weeks after starting then every 4 weeks thereafter, as long as their disease is not worsening and the drugs are well tolerated. Visits will generally take about 1 hour, except for the first visit and the Day 6 and Week 4 visits, which may take several hours or all day. They will be eligible to continue receiving treatment as long as the drugs are tolerated and your dog is experiencing clinical benefit (disease is stable or smaller). Analysis for tumor response will be performed by direct tumor measurement or through the use of imaging (X-rays, ultrasound). Standard bloodwork and urinalysis measurement will be performed at each visit. Additional tests to be performed include periodic extra blood draws to look at the amount of trametinib and sapanisertib appearing in the blood and for changes in other blood markers. The total volume of blood involved in each collection is approximately 5 teaspoons. Before starting treatment and after 6 days and 4 weeks, your dog will have a small sample of tumor tissue removed through a biopsy to look for changes in signaling in the tumor cells, if your dog’s tumor is in a location where it can be biopsied. This helps us know if the drugs are finding their targets in the cancer cells. This biopsy will require short acting sedation, and your dog may receive several days of oral pain medication after the procedure."}, {"id": 15958, "name": "TCC Probiotic", "url": "https://veterinaryclinicaltrials.org/s/tcc-probiotic-730565/?ref=gallery", "status": "Completed", "tags": [{"tag_path": "financial-incentive_fully-funded-after-initial-screening-48", "label": "Fully funded after initial screening", "parent_label": "Financial incentive"}, {"tag_path": "intervention-type_complementary-alternative-medicine-63", "label": "Complementary, alternative medicine", "parent_label": "Intervention type"}, {"tag_path": "species-20_canine-21", "label": "Canine", "parent_label": "Species"}, {"tag_path": "primary-field-19_oncology-1_carcinoma-other-30", "label": "Carcinoma, other", "parent_label": "Oncology"}, {"tag_path": "primary-field-19_oncology-1", "label": "Oncology", "parent_label": "Primary field"}], "description": "The purpose of this study is to determine if the addition of a probiotic (Escherichia coli Nissle 1917 (EcN)) can improve clinical outcomes when paired with a standard-of-care therapy (vinblastine / piroxicam) for canine bladder cancer also known as urothelial carcinoma. We will evaluate tumor response, clinical side effects, and quality of life as part of this study. Additionally, we will evaluate immune response and characterize the stool and urine microbiome and metabolome to understand the potential effects of the probiotic. Our broader goal is to improve cancer care and outcomes in dogs with bladder cancer."}, {"id": 15951, "name": "FOSCC Lattice", "url": "https://veterinaryclinicaltrials.org/s/foscc-lattice-929575/?ref=gallery", "status": "Completed", "tags": [{"tag_path": "financial-incentive_fully-funded-after-initial-screening-48", "label": "Fully funded after initial screening", "parent_label": "Financial incentive"}, {"tag_path": "species-20_feline-22", "label": "Feline", "parent_label": "Species"}, {"tag_path": "intervention-type_radiation-60", "label": "Radiation", "parent_label": "Intervention type"}, {"tag_path": "primary-field-19_oncology-1_squamous-cell-carcinoma-348", "label": "Squamous cell carcinoma", "parent_label": "Oncology"}, {"tag_path": "primary-field-19_oncology-1", "label": "Oncology", "parent_label": "Primary field"}], "description": "The goal of this study is to evaluate the feasibility, safety, efficacy and anti-cancer immune stimulation of a novel method of delivering radiation therapy, lattice radiation therapy, in cats with measurable oral squamous cell carcinoma. Lattice radiation therapy is special type of stereotactic radiation therapy utilizing a state-of-the-art linear accelerator that has on board advanced imaging capabilities and sophisticated software to deliver precisely-targeted radiation at much higher doses, in only a few treatments, as compared to traditional radiation therapy. This permits maximum dose delivery within the target while minimizing dose to the surrounding healthy tissue to minimize side effects. SBRT is used routinely to treat brain tumors in veterinary medicine and has been used to treat various cancers in cats."}, {"id": 15977, "name": "EFFICACY AND SAFETY OF A NOVEL ANTI-CANCER THERAPEUTIC FOR THE TREATMENT OF METASTATIC MAMMARY CARCINOMA IN CATS", "url": "https://veterinaryclinicaltrials.org/s/efficacy-and-safety-of-a-novel-anti-cancer-therapeutic-for-the-treatment-of-metastatic-mammary-carcinoma-in-cats-928987/?ref=gallery", "status": "Completed", "tags": [{"tag_path": "financial-incentive_fully-funded-after-initial-screening-48", "label": "Fully funded after initial screening", "parent_label": "Financial incentive"}, {"tag_path": "species-20_feline-22", "label": "Feline", "parent_label": "Species"}, {"tag_path": "intervention-type_genetic-gene-transfer-stem-cell-recombinant-dna-62", "label": "Genetic (gene transfer, stem cell, recombinant DNA", "parent_label": "Intervention type"}, {"tag_path": "primary-field-19_oncology-1_carcinoma-mammary-339", "label": "Carcinoma, mammary", "parent_label": "Oncology"}, {"tag_path": "primary-field-19_oncology-1", "label": "Oncology", "parent_label": "Primary field"}], "description": "Purpose of Study:Mammary tumors are a commonly encountered cancer in cats, particularly in females, with 80-90% of masses diagnosed as malignant (carcinoma). Mammary carcinoma in cats parallels breast cancer in humans with regards to receptor expression profile and propensity of metastasis. The median survival time in cats ranges from 6 months to several years, depending on tumor size and grade. Greater than 60% of cats have more than one tumor at diagnosis, with the majority being high grade. The objective of this study is to evaluate the safety and efficacy of a novel therapeutic targeting miR-10b, a molecule responsible for viability of metastatic cells in cats with mammary carcinoma. This multipurpose therapy has a previously demonstrated efficacy in halting breast cancer invasion and metastasis in mice. "parent_label": "Primary field"}], "description": "This clinical trial led by the National Cancer Institute (NCI) assesses the safety and effectiveness of a Vaccine Peptide Library (VPL) when given to dogs with cancer. This clinical trial conducted in pet dogs with cancer is designed to test whether the immune responses generated through routine vaccination against common viruses can be re-directed toward cancer cells. The approach appears to work in mouse models of cancer, and we are interested in evaluating it in pet dogs that have naturally occurring cancers that are very similar to humans. If successful, this research would help develop safe, effective, and low-cost ways of treating cancer that would benefit a wide variety of patients, especially those that live in communities with minimal access to cutting-edge cancer care (such as developing and low-resource countries). Studies in dogs with cancer will complement currently open human trials designed to test new doses and effects of this agent. As part of this study, your dog will be randomized to receive one of two vaccine protocols: either combination treatment with Shingrix/Garadasil vaccines or a rabies vaccine. Your dog will come to the Veterinary Teaching Hospital for the primer phase, which includes 1-3 weekly injections of the vaccines. Two weeks later, they will return to start weekly visits for injection of the VPL directly into the tumor for 8 weeks. Dogs will be treated with diphenhydramine (Benadryl) prior to the injection and then will be monitored for 4-6 hours post-injection.   One final visit will be required one week after the last injection (total length of study 12-14 weeks). Physical exam and blood collections for study purposes will be performed at each visit. A complete blood count will be performed every week during the treatment phase; blood and urine for serum chemistry profile and urinalysis will also be collected on Weeks 1, 5, and 9. Chest x-rays +/- abdominal ultrasound will be checked prior to the primer vaccine and at Week 9. Lymph node aspirates for study purposes will be obtained at Weeks 1, 5, and 9 of the treatment phase. Biopsies of your dogs tumor will also be collected prior to the first dose of the drug (pre-treatment), on Week 5, Week 5 at 24hrs, and Week 9 depending on how your dog has responded to therapy. Each of these biopsy sessions will occur under anesthesia, either local (sedation with anesthetic) or general."}, {"id": 15982, "name": "Novel Therapy with LSD1 inhibitor for Cats with Oral Squamous Cell Carcinoma", "url": "https://veterinaryclinicaltrials.org/s/novel-therapy-with-lsd1-inhibitor-for-cats-with-oral-squamous-cell-carcinoma-656488/?ref=gallery", "status": "Completed", "tags": [{"tag_path": "financial-incentive_fully-funded-including-initial-screening-47", "label": "Fully funded including initial screening", "parent_label": "Financial incentive"}, {"tag_path": "intervention-type_drug-334", "label": "Drug", "parent_label": "Intervention type"}, {"tag_path": "species-20_feline-22", "label": "Feline", "parent_label": "Species"}, {"tag_path": "primary-field-19_oncology-1_squamous-cell-carcinoma-348", "label": "Squamous cell carcinoma", "parent_label": "Oncology"}, {"tag_path": "primary-field-19_oncology-1", "label": "Oncology", "parent_label": "Primary field"}], "description": "Squamous cell carcinoma is the most common oral tumor in cats and this cancer shares many similarities with squamous cell carcinoma of the head and neck of people. This tumor is very aggressive in both cats and people and new treatments are greatly needed. This study is investigating a novel oral drug, called a lysine-specific demethylase 1 (LSD-1) inhibitor, that has been shown to slow the growth and metastasis of oral squamous cell carcinoma in people and mice in laboratory models. This medication has not been previously used in the treatment of oral squamous cell carcinoma in cats and the goals of this study are to establish the dosing, safety and anti-cancer properties when given to cats that have been diagnosed with oral squamous cell carcinoma. Cats participating in this study will have a low dose of the study medication administered in the hospital followed by collection of small amounts of blood throughout the day. These blood samples will be submitted to a lab to determine what dose of medication your cat will receive as part of this study. Once your cats dose of the study drug has been determined (approximately one week after the 1st study visit), your cat will return for tumor biopsies under either heavy sedation or general anesthesia. Some cats will also have a PET/CT scan performed at this visit. You will be dispensed the study medication to give at home once daily for the next three weeks. You cat will have weekly study visits for the next three weeks for examinations and blood collection to make sure they are tolerating the study medication. The use of a negative (i.e.,untreated) control group will allow for study conduct under masked    conditions and to determinethe time to disease progression for dogs receiving placebo tablets. Once enrolled in the study, dogs will be closely monitored for progression and may be removed from the study so that standard therapy may be initiated at the discretion  of the veterinarian and owner. If you elect to enroll your dog in the study, the study sponsor will provide the investigational treatment to be used during the  study and pay for the cost of the examinations and tests. If your dog has any adverse events that are study related and require treatment, the sponsor will cover the costs of reasonable treatment. Owner Participation / Commitment - Owners must be willing to commit to the clinic visit schedule over a 56-day duration.\n- Dogs will be randomized to receive the investigational veterinary product or a placebo treatment (tablets) to be administered with food twice weekly at least 72 hours apart for 8 weeks. \n- After receiving treatment in-hospital on Day 0, the dog will be required to return to the study site on Days 7, 14, 28, 42, and 56 for follow up evaluation visits.\n- Owners will be required to report and record abnormal daily observations and dosing using a phone app at home throughout the      study."}, {"id": 16057, "name": "Phase II - Multicenter Clinical Trial of Trametinib for Dogs with Histiocytic Sarcoma", "url": "https://veterinaryclinicaltrials.org/s/phase-ii-multicenter-clinical-trial-of-trametinib-for-dogs-with-histiocytic-sarcoma-591929/?ref=gallery", "status": "Suspended", "tags": [{"tag_path": "financial-incentive_fully-funded-after-initial-screening-48", "label": "Fully funded after initial screening", "parent_label": "Financial incentive"}, {"tag_path": "intervention-type_drug-334", "label": "Drug", "parent_label": "Intervention type"}, {"tag_path": "species-20_canine-21", "label": "Canine", "parent_label": "Species"}, {"tag_path": "primary-field-19_oncology-1_histiocytic-sarcoma-342", "label": "Histiocytic sarcoma", "parent_label": "Oncology"}, {"tag_path": "primary-field-19_oncology-1", "label": "Oncology", "parent_label": "Primary field"}], "description": "Canine histiocytic sarcoma (HS) is a highly aggressive and often fatal type of cancer that occurs more frequently in certain breeds, including Bernese mountain dog (BMD) (>25%), flat-coated retriever (36%), golden retriever, Rottweiler, and miniature schnauzer. Dogs with HS invariably carry a poor prognosis due to a rapid disease progression and limited effective clinical arsenal. First line conventional chemotherapy, Lomustine, provides a response rate of 29% for only a median of 96 days In this proposed trial, we will investigate a novel drug, Trametinib, to determine the antitumor activity (shrinkage of tumor) of the drug in dogs with histiocytic sarcoma using progression-free survival (PFS). PFS is defined as the percentage of dogs that are progression-free at 6-months post treatment initiation. Clinical Protocol: - Prior to treatment, a tumor biopsy, and a blood sample (less than one ounce) will be collected. \n- Upon enrollment, every patient will undergo a complete history, physical examination, laboratory analysis, blood pressure measurement, and diagnostic imaging. \n- Trametinib will be administered orally, once daily, indefinitely as long as progressive disease is not observed (i.e., stable, partial, or complete response). \n- The dog will need to return for evaluation of tumor response and/or monitoring of side effects at week 2, then every 4 weeks until week 14, and then every 8 weeks thereafter, until there is evidence of disease progression. \n- The dog will return for evaluation (physical examination, clinical laboratory assessment of blood, and tumor measurements) on week 2. \n- Starting on week 4, and every other 4 weeks until week 14, blood and urine sample will be taken, and x-rays and abdominal ultrasound will be repeated to monitor your dog’s response to treatment. \n- Cardiology consultations (Paid by owner)during Pre-treatment, week 6, week 14 and every 8 weeks till progressive disease.\n- Starting on week 14, the rechecks will be spaced out to every 8 weeks. Adverse Events (AEs) will also be evaluated at any unscheduled visit. Melanoma is also the most common oral cancer in companion dogs and like human melanoma, it is an aggressive cancer that spreads to lymph nodes, lungs, liver, brain, and kidney. Unfortunately, once melanoma spreads to distant sites, it is usually incurable. Despite advances in standard-of-care therapies (e.g., surgery, radiation therapy (RT) , and chemotherapy), the average survival in dogs with melanoma of advanced stage is less than one year after diagnosis, and less than 6 months if the melanoma has already spread. Therefore, as in human melanoma, new treatments for canine melanoma are needed to improve survival. Treatments that activate the patient's own immune system (immunotherapy) to fight the melanoma have worked very well in some human and dog patients. We are evaluating a combination of 3 types of therapy all of which have shown immune activation and anti-melanoma activity as single therapies in patients with melanoma. The three therapies include: administration of an immune stimulant directly into the tumor, radiation therapy targeted at the primary tumor, and intravenous administration of an antibody that potentially enhances the body's immune response to the melanoma. We hypothesize that by combining these therapies, we will be able to further extend the life of patients with melanoma. There are 3 parts to this study: Part 1 has been completed, and we have determined the dose of the immune stimulant to be administered directly into the tumor; In Part 2, the immune stimulant was combined with radiation therapy targeted at the same tumor, and; in Part 3 (Aim 1), the immune stimulant was administered to all sites of palpable disease in addition to the treatments in Part 2. Both Part 2 and Part 3 (Aim 1) are completed. In Part 3 the immune stimulant is administered directly into the tumor combined with intravenous (IV) Anti-PD1 monoclonal antibody (immune checkpoint inhibitor , [ICI]) and radiation therapy directed at the primary oral tumor. The information from this study will guide further clinical trials in both dogs and humans. Owner Responsibility The owner is expected to make and keep all appointments according to the study protocol. For many cancer types,\nmetastasis occurs via the lymphatic system and the status of the draining lymph nodes is an\nimportant part of the pre- and intraoperative evaluation. The sentinel lymph node (SLN) is the\nprimary lymph node draining the tumour and although one might expect that it is the first lymph\nnode downstream from the tumour, this is not always true. Failure to identify and assess the\nsentinel lymph node can lead to incomplete treatment, worse prognosis and poor patient outcome.\nCurrently in veterinary patients, there are not good protocols in place to identify sentinel lymph\nnodes. The development of these protocols could help us to decrease the number of lymph nodes\nwe remove, in addition to ensuring we are accurately evaluating the most important lymph node\nfor making follow-up treatment recommendations.\n\nYou will be responsible for bringing your pet to the OVC-HSC for both the CT scan and surgery\n(may occur during the same visit). This information will be\ncompared to our findings in surgery and on histopathology when the tissues are submitted.\nFollowing the procedure, your pet will be monitored for several hours to ensure they do not\ndevelop any complications from the injection. The most common non-radiation complications in dogs undergoing these longer radiation protocols include diarrhea, vomiting or regurgitation, and decreased appetite. When these complications happen in patients, both owners and clinicians attempt to offer a multitude of foods, home cooked diets, probiotics, appetite stimulants, anti-nausea medications, or antibiotics. Recently nutritionists and veterinarians at a well-known pet food manufacturer developed a prescription diet designed to specifically help nourish and support dogs that are fighting cancer. This diet is highly digestible and contains a proprietary blend of prebiotic fibers to help support a healthy gastrointestinal microbiome to provide consistent stool quality. The goal of this study is to evaluate the acceptance of the novel diet through food intake and eating enthusiasm data by dogs undergoing daily, definitive intent radiation therapy, and to examine the differences in body weight changes, muscle condition scoring, body condition scoring, body fat index, quality of life, and stool consistency over time in dogs receiving the novel vs control diet. If your dog participates in this study, he/she will have blood work, urine panel, fecal analysis, and will be randomized to receive one of the two study foods during radiation therapy. Blood work and fecal analysis will be performed prior to starting radiation therapy, half way through radiation, at the end of the radiation protocol and two weeks after completing radiation. Urine panel will be performed prior to starting radiation, at the final radiation dose, and at the two week recheck. We will assess intake of the diet and enthusiasm of the diet twice weekly. We ask that you also record food intake and eating enthusiasm twice a week, fecal scores at each defecation, and quality of life weekly with provided guides and questionnaires. You and your clinical team will be blinded to which diet your dog is receiving, but this will be revealed at the conclusion of the study period."}, {"id": 20710, "name": "Cell Therapy for Metastatic Osteosarcoma", "url": "https://veterinaryclinicaltrials.org/s/cell-therapy-for-metastatic-osteosarcoma-277843/?ref=gallery", "status": "Recruiting", "tags": [{"tag_path": "financial-incentive_fully-funded-including-initial-screening-47", "label": "Fully funded including initial screening", "parent_label": "Financial incentive"}, {"tag_path": "intervention-type_biologic-vaccine-58", "label": "Biologic/Vaccine", "parent_label": "Intervention type"}, {"tag_path": "species-20_canine-21", "label": "Canine", "parent_label": "Species"}, {"tag_path": "primary-field-19_oncology-1_osteosarcoma-or-bone-tumor-29", "label": "Osteosarcoma or bone tumor", "parent_label": "Oncology"}, {"tag_path": "primary-field-19_oncology-1", "label": "Oncology", "parent_label": "Primary field"}], "description": "In this study we will investigate the therapeutic potential of a type of white blood cell known as invariant natural killer T (iNKT) cells that are made from the blood of a healthy donor dog. iNKT cells are potent immune cells that kill cancer cells in mouse models and in some human cancer patients. In this study, we will use iNKT cells that express a cancer targeting receptor known as a chimeric antigen receptor (CAR). The CAR directs the modified iNKT cells to the cancer cells which are then killed. The CAR-iNKT cells also will further activate the patient's own immune system to help kill the cancer cells. The purpose of this study is to determine the safety of CAR-iNKT cells, their maximum tolerated dose, how long they will remain in the patient and their effectiveness against bone cancer that has spread to the lungs."}, {"id": 20713, "name": "CAR T Cell and Verdinexor Therapy for Treatment of Glioma Tumors in Dogs", "url": "https://veterinaryclinicaltrials.org/s/car-t-cell-and-verdinexor-therapy-for-treatment-of-glioma-tumors-in-dogs-802549/?ref=gallery", "status": "Recruiting", "tags": [{"tag_path": "intervention-type_biologic-vaccine-58", "label": "Biologic/Vaccine", "parent_label": "Intervention type"}, {"tag_path": "financial-incentive_partially-funded_partially-funded-owner-cost-between-501-1000-50", "label": "Partially funded (owner cost between $501 - 1000)", "parent_label": "Partially funded"}, {"tag_path": "financial-incentive_partially-funded", "label": "Partially funded", "parent_label": "Financial incentive"}, {"tag_path": "species-20_canine-21", "label": "Canine", "parent_label": "Species"}, {"tag_path": "primary-field-19_oncology-1_brain-or-spinal-tumor-338", "label": "Brain or spinal tumor", "parent_label": "Oncology"}, {"tag_path": "primary-field-19_oncology-1", "label": "Oncology", "parent_label": "Primary field"}], "description": "About the study Every year, about 3 out of every 100 dogs will be diagnosed with a brain tumor. Many of these dogs will be diagnosed with a glioma tumor, which is the second most common type of brain tumor and also, unfortunately, the most difficult to treat. One of the most promising developing areas of research for treating glioma tumors is immunotherapy, which is a type of intervention that uses the dog's own cells to fight the cancer cells. This study is looking at a specific type of immunotherapy called CAR T cell therapy. CAR T cells are created by doing a simple blood draw from the dog to extract the T cells (\"fighter\" cells), which are then infused with a Chimeric Antigen Receptor (CAR) protein. This \"upgrade\" allows the T cells to target and attack the glioma tumor cells. This intervention has been used in children with brain tumors but this study will be the first time it's being used in dogs with glioma tumors! In addition to the immunotherapy, we will be looking at a specific type of chemotherapy that has shown extremely promising results in canine lymphoma, along with human glioma tumors. This chemotherapy drug, verdinexor, will be used in combination with the CAR T cell therapy in an effort to produce the best possible outcome. Who qualifies Dogs who are over 10kg (22lb) in body weight who have already had a brain tumor diagnosed on MRI. Tumor must be surgically accessible to allow for biopsy and injection of CAR T cells directly into the tumor Dogs must be healthy enough to safely undergo anesthesia for the biopsy of the tumor Dogs cannot have previously received chemotherapy or radiation for this tumor Study activities and Timeline Visit 1 | Day-17 Exam Blood draw to create CAR T cells Begin verdinexor (chemo) therapy twice per week Visit 2 | Days -4 and -3 On both days, we will give a drug that temporarily depletes the immune system to prepare your dog's body for the CAR T cell injection Visit 3 | Days 0, 1, and 3 The first day will consist of the first CAR T cell injection while the next 2 days consist of recheck exams Visit 4 | Days 8 - 10 The visits throughout these days will consist of a brief planning scan followed by the brain biopsy surgery. During the surgery, a second injection of CAR T cells will be given directly into the tumor. Visit 5 | Month 3 We will do a recheck a MRI to evaluate the tumor response Verdinexor will continue to be given at home twice weekly until the tumor progresses based on neurological signs or growth seen on MRI."}, {"id": 20743, "name": "Electrochemotherapy for Nasal Cancer", "url": "https://veterinaryclinicaltrials.org/s/electrochemotherapy-for-nasal-cancer-126469/?ref=gallery", "status": "Recruiting", "tags": [{"tag_path": "financial-incentive_unfunded-53", "label": "Unfunded", "parent_label": "Financial incentive"}, {"tag_path": "species-20_canine-21", "label": "Canine", "parent_label": "Species"}, {"tag_path": "species-20_feline-22", "label": "Feline", "parent_label": "Species"}, {"tag_path": "intervention-type_other-65", "label": "Other", "parent_label": "Intervention type"}, {"tag_path": "primary-field-19_oncology-1_nasal-tumors-344", "label": "Nasal tumors", "parent_label": "Oncology"}, {"tag_path": "primary-field-19_oncology-1", "label": "Oncology", "parent_label": "Primary field"}], "description": "Nasal Cancers in dogs and cats are uncommon and standard treatment is external beam radiation therapy.  Side effects from radiation therapy may sometimes be severe and not every patient will qualify or respond to this therapy.  Plus, there are significant delays in accommodating patients for timely radiation therapy treatment due to the paucity of centers and available specialists. Nasal Electrochemotherapy has been used  predominantly outside of the United States (see below). Radiol Oncol 2017 Nov 1;51(4):422-430. doi: 10.1515/raon-2017-0043. eCollection 2017 Dec. Minimally Invasive Electrochemotherapy Procedure for Treating Nasal Duct Tumors in Dogs using a Single Needle Electrode Felipe Maglietti 1 2 3, Matías Tellado 4, Nahuel Olaiz 1 2 3, Sebastian Michinski 1 2 3, Guillermo Marshall 1 2 3 Abstract Background: Nasal cavity tumors are usually diagnosed late, when they already have infiltrated adjacent tissues thus requiring very aggressive treatments with serious side effects. Here we use electrochemotherapy (ECT), a well demonstrated treatment modality for superficial tumors. Materials and methods: In the case of deep-seated tumors, the main limitation of ECT is reaching the tumor with an appropriate electric field. To overcome this limitation we introduce the single needle electrode (SiNE), a minimally invasive device that can deliver an appropriate electric field with a simple procedure. Twenty-one canine patients with spontaneous tumors were selected, eleven were treated using the SiNE with ECT, and ten with surgery plus adjuvant chemotherapy as a control group. Results: In the SiNE group, 27% achieved a complete response, 64% had a partial response, and 9% had a stable disease. This means that 91% of objective responses were obtained. The mean overall survival was 16.86 months (4-32 months, median 16.5 months), with a survival rate significantly higher (p = 0.0008) when compared with control group. The only side effect observed was the inflammation of the treated nasal passage, which was controlled with corticosteroid therapy for one week. One year after the treatment, 60% of the canine of the SiNE group vs. 10% of the control group remained alive, and after the 32 months follow-up, the survival rate were 30% and 0%, respectively. Conclusions: ECT with the SiNE can be safely used in canine to treat nasal tumors with encouraging results. We now have a nasal electrochemotherapy electrode here in the United States. Clinical Protocol involves selected patients to receive a short sedation with IV propofol, +/- dexdomitor and O2 via intubation. Bleomycin IV 8 minutes prior to electrode placement into both nares providing a short pulse which opens the cell membranes driving chemotherapy to the region being treated.  In this case, we begin treatment at the deepest point of the nasal cavity just proximal to the region of the cribiform plate (end of nasal cavity).  After each treatment, the electrode is moved proximally until the entire region of both nasal cavities are treated.  Side effects are minimal and patients will go home on 3 days of anti-inflammatory medication.  This is an out-patient procedure."}, {"id": 20869, "name": "Autologous Cancer Vaccine with Checkpoint Inhibitor for Treatment of Canine Osteosarcoma", "url": "https://veterinaryclinicaltrials.org/s/autologous-cancer-vaccine-with-checkpoint-inhibitor-for-treatment-of-canine-osteosarcoma-565406/?ref=gallery", "status": "Completed", "tags": [{"tag_path": "intervention-type_biologic-vaccine-58", "label": "Biologic/Vaccine", "parent_label": "Intervention type"}, {"tag_path": "financial-incentive_partially-funded_partially-funded-owner-cost-1000-51", "label": "Partially funded (owner cost >$1000)", "parent_label": "Partially funded"}, {"tag_path": "financial-incentive_partially-funded", "label": "Partially funded", "parent_label": "Financial incentive"}, {"tag_path": "species-20_canine-21", "label": "Canine", "parent_label": "Species"}, {"tag_path": "primary-field-19_oncology-1_osteosarcoma-or-bone-tumor-29", "label": "Osteosarcoma or bone tumor", "parent_label": "Oncology"}, {"tag_path": "primary-field-19_oncology-1", "label": "Oncology", "parent_label": "Primary field"}], "description": "The purpose of this study is to evaluate the safety and efficacy of K9-ACV, an autologous killed tumor cell vaccine combined with a novel checkpoint inhibitor (CD200AR-L), compared to standard-of-care chemotherapy for the treatment of canine appendicular osteosarcoma (OSA). K9-ACV has safely been used in over 1,000 dogs and the vaccine has been shown to display safety in a previous study (without the addition of the checkpoint inhibitor). By evaluating K9-ACV, this trial aims to advance safer, immune-based treatment options for canine cancer that may offer comparable or superior outcomes to chemotherapy. Participating patients will be required to complete standard pre-enrollment screening that involves a physical exam, blood work, chest x-rays, and abdominal ultrasound. If the patient passes the screening, they will undergo limb amputation and be randomly assigned to the K9-ACV group or the carboplatin group. Patients in the K9-ACV group will receive an intradermal injection of the checkpoint inhibitor and then will return to the study site 24 hours later for the vaccine administration. Vaccines will be given every 3 weeks for a total of 3 treatments. Patients will return at 4, 6, and 8 months after initial vaccine administration for a physical exam, blood work, and x-rays. Patients in the chemotherapy group will be treated every 3 weeks for a total of 4 treatments. Patients will return at 4, 6, and 8 months after initial chemotherapy treatment for a physical exam, blood work, and x-rays."}, {"id": 20902, "name": "Librela/Beransa (bedinvetmab) Client Survey", "url": "https://veterinaryclinicaltrials.org/s/librelaberansa-bedinvetmab-client-survey-698124/?ref=gallery", "status": "Completed", "tags": [{"tag_path": "primary-field-19_orthopedics-7_osteoarthritis-284", "label": "Osteoarthritis", "parent_label": "Orthopedics"}, {"tag_path": "primary-field-19_orthopedics-7", "label": "Orthopedics", "parent_label": "Primary field"}, {"tag_path": "financial-incentive_unfunded-53", "label": "Unfunded", "parent_label": "Financial incentive"}, {"tag_path": "intervention-type_none-sample-collection-only-351", "label": "None - sample collection only", "parent_label": "Intervention type"}, {"tag_path": "species-20_canine-21", "label": "Canine", "parent_label": "Species"}], "description": null}, {"id": 21097, "name": "PSMA Ligand Based Theranostic to Treat Canine Prostatic Cancer", "url": "https://veterinaryclinicaltrials.org/s/psma-ligand-based-theranostic-to-treat-canine-prostatic-cancer-518451/?ref=gallery", "status": "Recruiting", "tags": [{"tag_path": "financial-incentive_fully-funded-including-initial-screening-47", "label": "Fully funded including initial screening", "parent_label": "Financial incentive"}, {"tag_path": "intervention-type_drug-334", "label": "Drug", "parent_label": "Intervention type"}, {"tag_path": "species-20_canine-21", "label": "Canine", "parent_label": "Species"}, {"tag_path": "primary-field-19_oncology-1_urogenital-tumors-349", "label": "Urogenital tumors", "parent_label": "Oncology"}, {"tag_path": "primary-field-19_oncology-1", "label": "Oncology", "parent_label": "Primary field"}], "description": "In this study, we will test a new research medication that combines a chemotherapy drug called MMAE (monomethyl Auristatin E) and a light-sensitive drug (Pc-413) and a laser light source (photodynamic therapy) to kill cancer cells in the prostate and in other areas of the body (metastatic disease). These two agents are linked to a molecule that binds to PSMA (prostate specific membrane antigen), a cell surface marker that is produced by prostatic cancer in large quantities. The research medication is inactive until it binds to PSMA. When the research medication binds to PSMA it is taken into the cell and activated. This means the research medication is targeted specifically to prostate cancer cells. The overall goal is to use this new research medication that is specific to prostate cancer cells to kill the cancer. This study will cover the specific study related diagnostics once your dog is enrolled: • Chest X-rays • Abdominal ultrasound • Prostate aspirate • Blood work (CBC and chemistry) • Urinalysis • Physical examination All costs associated with the theranostic infusions and laser will be covered by the study including the fees associated with hospitalization. The study will cover the cost of the recheck visits every 2 months following the treatments, including the physical examination, blood work, urinalysis, chest x-rays and abdominal ultrasound fees. If your dog needs sedation for any of the study related procedures, the study will cover the cost of the sedation as well."}, {"id": 21092, "name": "A dose-finding study of Paccal Vet in cats with spontaneous solid tumors", "url": "https://veterinaryclinicaltrials.org/s/a-dose-finding-study-of-paccal-vet-in-cats-with-spontaneous-solid-tumors-557870/?ref=gallery", "status": "Completed", "tags": [{"tag_path": "financial-incentive_fully-funded-including-initial-screening-47", "label": "Fully funded including initial screening", "parent_label": "Financial incentive"}, {"tag_path": "intervention-type_drug-334", "label": "Drug", "parent_label": "Intervention type"}, {"tag_path": "species-20_feline-22", "label": "Feline", "parent_label": "Species"}, {"tag_path": "primary-field-19_oncology-1_other-misc-tumor-33", "label": "Other/Misc tumor", "parent_label": "Oncology"}, {"tag_path": "primary-field-19_oncology-1", "label": "Oncology", "parent_label": "Primary field"}], "description": "No chemotherapies have been FDA-approved for use in cats despite a growing need for such therapies. Paclitaxel (Taxol®) is one of the most effective anticancer agents used in human cancer therapy today, with potent activity against a variety of cancers in people that also occur in cats. Paclitaxel has been found to kill cancer cell lines isolated from cat tumors in the laboratory, but only one small study has been published evaluating paclitaxel treatment of cats with cancer. In that study, 5 of 9 patients responded to paclitaxel therapy, with 4 of these patients experiencing stable disease and one patient experiencing a partial response. The current FDA-approved formulation of paclitaxel for use in people, which uses a cremophor-based agent to solubilize the drug for injection, causes allergic reactions in dogs and cats. This characteristic of the FDA-approved formulation has largely prevented its use in pets. The investigational drug to be used in this study, Paccal® Vet, uses a formulation that has been created to minimize allergic reactions and therefore improve tolerability. Several clinical trials have been performed or are ongoing with this formulation in dogs, but to date, no studies in cats using Paccal Vet have been undertaken. The primary purpose of this study is to test the tolerability of Paccal Vet in cats and to determine an acceptable dose. A secondary, exploratory goal is to see whether Paccal Vet may have anti-tumor activity in various tumors in cats. In this context, “exploratory” means that this study is not large enough to prove whether or not Paccal Vet is working in feline cancer. However, the results could help the drug developer determine whether the drug might have the potential to do so. The “investigational” part of the study is to test whether Paccal Vet is safe for use in cats and whether the drug may induce an anti-tumor response against their cancer. Current treatment strategies for canine glioma typically involve surgical resection when anatomically feasible, followed by adjuvant radiation therapy. Canine gliomas share many biological, imaging, and histopathological features with human glioblastoma (GBM), the most common and lethal primary brain tumor in adults. One promising frontier in glioma treatment is immunotherapy, particularly the use of chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-engineered immune cells. A pivotal safety study of CAR neutrophils in dogs was recently conducted at Purdue University, followed by preclinical efficacy testing in murine models of glioma. These genetically modified cells showed potential in targeting brain tumors with minimal off-target toxicity. Building upon these encouraging results, our current research proposes to evaluate the combined therapeutic effect of CAR immunotherapy and radiation therapy in dogs diagnosed with glioma.
