a high-precision ultrasound-based treatment that can non-invasively destroy tumor tissue without radiation or heat, on dogs with oral tumors. Background Histotripsy is an emerging technology that uses focused ultrasound waves to mechanically destroy tumor tissue. Histotripsy has the ability to precisely destroy tumors non-invasively and without using heat or radiation. Histotripsy also has the potential to stimulate the immune system into fighting off remaining or microscopic tumor. Our team’s previous research has evaluated the safety and efficacy of histotripsy for bone tumors, soft tissue sarcomas, and brain tumors in dogs. Additionally, histotripsy was FDA-approved for the treatment of liver tumors in humans in 2023, with promising clinical results. We are now interested in how histotripsy affects oral tumors in dogs. Study Design Dogs will undergo CT and/or MRI scans (if not obtained previously during diagnostics) to visualize the oral tumor and plan the histotripsy treatment. The histotripsy treatment approach will be patient-specific to accommodate for unique tumor sizes and locations. On the day of treatment, hair will be removed from the area overlying the tumor to allow for maximum transmission of the ultrasound waves. Histotripsy treatment will be delivered non-invasively through the skin to mechanically disintegrate the underlying tumor. Dogs will be maintained and monitored under anesthesia. After the treatment, images (CT and/or MRI) will be taken to assess the immediate effects of the ultrasound treatment. Most patients recover uneventfully and go home the same day. One day after the completion of histotripsy treatment, dogs will undergo standard-of-care surgical resection. This allows us to assess the effects of the ultrasound treatment. These locally invasive tumors lead to lesions that cause discomfort, pain, and functional limitations, significantly impacting a horse’s quality of life. Sarcoids are persistent and prone to recurrence, making their removal essential for preventing complications like infections or interference with tack. Current treatments, including surgery and cryotherapy, can be invasive, inconsistent, and have high recurrence rates, emphasizing the need for novel, effective solutions. Histotripsy is a non-invasive ultrasound therapy that uses focused ultrasound waves to create microbubbles that mechanically disrupt targeted tissue. Unlike thermal methods, histotripsy’s non-thermal mechanism ensures precise ablation with minimal damage to surrounding tissues. Developed for human medicine, histotripsy shows promise in veterinary applications due to its precision, real-time imaging, and adaptability. Non-invasive therapeutics like histotripsy are vital for improving animal welfare, minimizing recovery time, and reducing risks associated with invasive procedures. "parent_label": "Primary field"}], "description": "Although limb sparing for bone tumors has been performed for over 30 years in dogs, the complication rate for this surgery remains high. Risks of the surgery include infection, problems related to the implants, and local recurrence. Many factors are contributing to the high rate of complications and one of them is likely the material used to fabricate the implants. We hypothesize that if the implant used to replace the segment of bone with the tumor (i.e. endoprosthesis) was made of a material that the body could replace with its own viable bone, many of the complications would not occur or would be easier to treat. 3D-printing can create personalized implants made of a material that the body can replace with its own bone, namely anorganic (deproteinized) bone mineral (ABM). Over a period of time, the body can grow new viable bone while removing the ABM, such that the metal plate and screws used with limb sparing would be able to be removed after a period of time, leaving the dog with only its own tissues. The goal of this study is to evaluate a novel personalized implant system for limb sparing in dogs with primary bone tumors and identify complications associated with this surgical approach. Dogs will undergo imaging with a PET-CT scan, which is a special form of imaging that involves giving a small dose of a radioactive substance to help identify any areas of cancer spread. The data from this imaging will also be used to create the patient-specific implant and tools for surgery, which is anticipated to take 5 days or less. Once the supplies are ready, the limb sparing surgical procedure will be performed. Dogs will return two weeks after surgery for suture removal and to start carboplatin chemotherapy as long as the surgical site is well-healed. Carboplatin will be given every 3 weeks for 6 treatments, and dogs will be followed for up to 20 months after surgery. X-rays of the chest and limb will be performed every 8 weeks for the duration of the study, and force plate gait analysis will be done every 6 months. myeloid leukemia (AML). Trametinib is a medication used in people to treat some cancers. It works by blocking signals that help cancer cells grow. This drug is experimental for use in dogs with AML, and its safety and effectiveness for this condition are not yet known. In this study, all dogs will receive trametinib along with prednisone, which is commonly used to help dogs with leukemia feel better. About 13 dogs are expected to take part in this study. Treatment is done with your local oncologist. As part of this study, pets will have the following things done: •\tA physical exam by a veterinarian •\tBlood tests to check blood counts and organ health •\tUrine tests •\tA cheek (buccal) swab to collect DNA for future research studies related to leukemia and treatment response •\tRegular follow-up visits approximately 1 week and 2 weeks after starting treatment, approximately every 2 weeks through Week 12, and approximately every 4 weeks thereafter while dogs remains on study •\tDogs will take trametinib by mouth once daily at home •\tDogs will also take prednisone as directed by your veterinarian"}, {"id": 28470, "name": "Osteosarcoma- Targeted Bone Electrochemotherapy with Cementoplasty; Alternative to Amputation", "url": "https://veterinaryclinicaltrials.org/s/osteosarcoma-targeted-bone-electrochemotherapy-with-cementoplasty-alternative-to-amputation-334974/?ref=gallery", "status": "Recruiting", "tags": [{"tag_path": "financial-incentive_unfunded-53", "label": "Unfunded", "parent_label": "Financial incentive"}, {"tag_path": "species-20_canine-21", "label": "Canine", "parent_label": "Species"}, {"tag_path": "intervention-type_device-335", "label": "Device", "parent_label": "Intervention type"}, {"tag_path": "primary-field-19_oncology-1_osteosarcoma-or-bone-tumor-29", "label": "Osteosarcoma or bone tumor", "parent_label": "Oncology"}, {"tag_path": "primary-field-19_oncology-1", "label": "Oncology", "parent_label": "Primary field"}], "description": "Canine appendicular osteosarcoma is the most common primary bone tumor in dogs. sample collection only", "parent_label": "Intervention type"}, {"tag_path": "financial-incentive_partially-funded_partially-funded-owner-cost-1000-51", "label": "Partially funded (owner cost >$1000)", "parent_label": "Partially funded"}, {"tag_path": "financial-incentive_partially-funded", "label": "Partially funded", "parent_label": "Financial incentive"}, {"tag_path": "species-20_canine-21", "label": "Canine", "parent_label": "Species"}, {"tag_path": "primary-field-19_oncology-1_osteosarcoma-or-bone-tumor-29", "label": "Osteosarcoma or bone tumor", "parent_label": "Oncology"}, {"tag_path": "primary-field-19_oncology-1", "label": "Oncology", "parent_label": "Primary field"}], "description": "Osteosarcoma is the most common primary bone cancer in dogs, specially in large size breeds and it presents a high biological aggressiveness, in many cases at the time of diagnosis, metastatic dissemination has already occurred. Currently, the standard of care consists of surgical excision of the affected limb, followed by adjuvant chemotherapy. However, despite initial therapeutic response, patients develop treatment resistance, leading to the presence of metastasis, most commonly within the lungs, reducing life expectancy and quality of life of the patient. Recently the use of liquid biopsies, a minimally invasive sample collection from body fluids, such as blood, has been increasing, as they detect specific molecular biomarkers. Liquid biopsies can aid in the detection of certain pathologies, monitor disease progression or recurrence after the treatment, the latter can be achieved by measuring molecules such as proteins and microRNAs that are in the circulating blood. These proteins and microRNA might provide less invasive and faster detection than other techniques, such as computerized tomography (CT scan). For our research the main goal is to determine if this blood test is able to predict osteosarcoma recurrence, as these biomarkers may provide an earlier status of relapse, and could aid in designing more effective treatments. To support this, our team is developing a lab-on-a-chip platform that can measure the selected biomarkers using a minimal volume of blood. Purpose: The purpose of this study is to evaluate a new immunotherapy approach to treat osteosarcoma in dogs following limb amputation. Description of Procedures: Initial staging is to include a complete blood count (CBC), chemistry panel, urinalysis, cytologic or histologic diagnosis of osteosarcoma, thoracic radiographs and a bone scan (nuclear scintigraphy) prior to limb amputation. No follow up is necessary."}, {"id": 15250, "name": "Phase I study of KPT-9274 in dogs with lymphoma", "url": "https://veterinaryclinicaltrials.org/s/phase-i-study-of-kpt-9274-in-dogs-with-lymphoma-633984/?ref=gallery", "status": "Completed", "tags": [{"tag_path": "financial-incentive_fully-funded-including-initial-screening-47", "label": "Fully funded including initial screening", "parent_label": "Financial incentive"}, {"tag_path": "intervention-type_drug-334", "label": "Drug", "parent_label": "Intervention type"}, {"tag_path": "species-20_canine-21", "label": "Canine", "parent_label": "Species"}, {"tag_path": "primary-field-19_oncology-1_lymphoma-or-leukemia-31", "label": "Lymphoma or leukemia", "parent_label": "Oncology"}, {"tag_path": "primary-field-19_oncology-1", "label": "Oncology", "parent_label": "Primary field"}], "description": "Purpose and Brief Explanation of Study: PAK4 is a protein present in cells that is involved in helping to control the rate of cell growth. In normal cells, PAK 4 is tightly regulated so that growth occurs in a normal ordered manner. It is now known that abnormalities occur in PAK4 in cancer cells that contribute to driving uncontrolled tumor growth. In some cells there are mutations in PAK4 that cause it to be turned on all the time, and in others its expression is very high causing the tumor cells to divide uncontrollably. Based on the role of PAK4 in cancer there has been great interest in developing inhibitors of this protein that can be used to treat tumors and possibly halt their growth. Karyopharm Therapeutics has developed a drug called KPT-9274 that is given orally and binds to PAK4, thereby blocking its ability to drive cell growth. KPT-9274 has shown good activity against tumor cell lines in the laboratory and also inhibits tumor growth in mouse models of cancer. KPT-9274 has been tested in normal dogs and is well tolerated with no side effects when given at doses between1.5-6 mg/kg orally given on a Monday/Thursday or Monday/Wednesday/Friday schedule. KPT-9274 has also been tested in dogs with cancer, and doses ranging from 2-4 mg per given on a Monday/Wednesday/Friday schedule for 28 days were not associated with any side effects. Objective of the trial: The purpose of this clinical trial is to evaluate the activity of KPT-9274 when given in combination with doxorubicin chemotherapy for the treatment of canine lymphoma. What qualifies my dog for enrollment in this in this trial? To participate in this clinical trial your dog must have: - A diagnosis of lymphoma (T or B cell, newly diagnosed). - Dogs must be free of other diseases (heart, liver, and kidney) and be feeling good (playing, good appetite). - Your dog will be screened for eligibility based on bloodwork (complete blood count, biochemistry profile, urinalysis, chest x-rays, abdominal ultrasound) What does enrolling my dog in this clinical trial involve? If enrolled dogs will receive KPT-9274 for 4 doses (Monday/Wednesday/Friday/Monday followed by the administration of doxorubicin 24 hours after the last dose of KPT-9274. Recheck exams will be performed weekly (days 14, 21, and 28) for 1 month, then monthly thereafter. Routine bloodwork and urinalysis will be performed at these visits. Client Compensation All costs for the first 4 weeks of the clinical trial are covered, and a credit of $500 will be available for standard of care chemotherapy if/when your dog should fail treatment with the drug combination. The goal of this study is to determine if photodynamic therapy would be useful in treating dog and potentially human lung tumors. The steps of photodynamic therapy include injection of a photosensitizing agent into the blood. The drug is absorbed all over the body, but stays in cancer cells slightly longer than in normal cells. Two days after drug absorption, the tumor is exposed to a light source. Photosensitizer agents in the cells absorb the light and produce an active form of oxygen which destroys nearby cells. Patient Entry Criteria: Eligible patients include dogs having a single lung tumor greater than 2 centimeters in diameter. The patient will need to have a needle aspirate taken of the tumor which confirms a diagnosis of carcinoma prior to enrollment. Also recent chest radiographs, a complete blood count, a serum biochemistry panel, and a urinalysis are necessary prior to enrollment. The study is limited to dogs not having evidence of metastatic disease and who are in otherwise good health. What will happen if my pet participates in this clinical trial? Each dog will receive an intravenous injection of a photosensitizing agent on Day 0. Two days later on Day 2, each dog will be anesthetized for a chest CT scan and additional outpatient procedures. Following the CT scan while still anesthetized, a bronchoscopy (a flexible camera placed inside the trachea and lung airway branches) will be combined with fluoroscopy (a version of real-time chest xray imaging) to deliver a lighted wire through the bronchoscope for temporary placement into the lung tumor of each dog. Just prior to the lighted wire placement, a second photosensitizing agent acid will be given either orally or intravenously. Once the lighted wire has been activated to stimulate photosensitizing drugs within the lung tumor to cause cell death, the wire and scope will be removed. Two days later on Day 4, each dog will be readmitted to the hospital for routine surgical removal of the lung tumor via traditional thoracic surgery. Reevaluation with the Clinical Trials team at Colorado State University will be expected at two weeks, four weeks, and six weeks after the traditional thoracic surgery. Your pet will experience side effects. Specifically, dogs will experience light sensitivity, or photosensitivity, following administration of the photosensitizing drugs. The light sensitivity is expected to last from two to six weeks, the estimated amount of time for the drugs to be eliminated from the body. It is anticipated the ears may be the most sensitive to side effect, and will be a barometer for overall photosensitivity, but any exposed or lightly haired area of the body is susceptible including the belly, mouth, and eye tissues. Any strong light, including indoor as well as sunlight, could affect photosensitivity. Thus dogs will need to be kept mostly indoors during the time period of about one month, until the drugs are metabolized. Use of sunscreen products will not be of benefit. Dogs will need to be protected against unrestricted outdoor sunlight exposure in the first month following treatment by being supervised on a leash long enough to allow for urinations and defecations. If the ears become red or show signs suggestive of a 'sun burn' while a dog is being quarantined indoors, then less use of bright indoor lights will be recommended to reduce exposure effects. Importantly, controlled light exposure is the key for metabolism of the photosensitizing agents. Combined use of two photosensitizing agents in this study is anticipated to reduce the light sensitivity side effects in dogs. Owner Responsibilities: You are responsible for an initial examination, complete blood count, serum biochemistry profile, urinalysis, thoracic radiographs, and needle-aspiration diagnosis of your dogs tumor. You are also responsible for the costs associated with your dogs traditional thoracic surgery (minus the $1000 credit), for recheck fees at the fourth- and sixth-week visits following traditional thoracic surgery, and any other tests recommended by your pets oncologist. Financial Incentives: Enrollment in this clinical trial provides a $1000 credit to be used towards your pets traditional thoracic surgery for removal of the lung tumor. This trial is being conducted by the Comparative Oncology Trials Consortium. 180 dogs will be enrolled in this study. All dogs will receive surgical removal of their tumor and receive standard of care chemotherapy. Dogs will be randomized at time of enrollment to either receive standard of care alone or standard of care with orally administered rapamycin. Eligibility: Confirmed osteosarcoma diagnosis. Has not received any prior treatment for osteosarcoma. Osteosarcoma is the most common bone tumor in dogs. Amputation and chemotherapy significantly improves median survival times for dogs with this tumor type, from around 4-6 months to around 10-12 months. However, most dogs are not cured, and die due to the spread of their disease (metastasis) within 1-2 years. Better treatment options to treat cancer spread are needed to improve survival time for these patients. Rapamycin (sirolimus) is a drug that works through the blockade of mTOR, a cellular pathway that is associated with tumor spread. Preliminary studies have been performed in cell lines, in mice, and in dogs that demonstrate anti-tumor activity. Previous studies have also established a safe dose in healthy dogs and dogs with cancer. The addition of this drug to standard amputation followed by carboplatin chemotherapy is hoped to delay or prevent tumor spread, thus improving patient survival. All dogs receive the current recommended therapy for osteosarcoma (standard of care: SOC), consisting of amputation followed by 4 doses of carboplatin chemotherapy, given 3 weeks apart, initiated within 10-14 days of surgery. Your dog will then be randomly assigned to enter the study group that receives SOC alone, or the group that has the addition of the drug rapamycin (Rapa). All dogs in both groups will return every two months for monitoring for disease progression, including chest radiographs. Rapamycin is an oral drug, given at home, daily on Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, and Thursday of each week, with no drug administered on Fridays, Saturdays, or Sundays for a total of four months. Additional visits for the Rapa group of dogs includes 5 overnight stays (two the first month, then 3 additional monthly visits) for the purposes of a 24 hour blood collection to determine the levels of the drug in your dog's body. Standard of Care is defined as definitive surgery, being amputation of the affected limb, followed by 4 doses of intravenous carboplatin chemotherapy given on an every 21 day schedule. Carboplatin has been shown to safely and effectively improve survival in dogs with appendicular osteosarcoma for over 20 years. Rapamycin is a drug currently approved to induce immunosuppression in human patients receiving organ and bone marrow transplants. What qualifies my dog for enrollment in this trial? To participate in this clinical trial your dog must have: - Confirmed diagnosis of osteosarcoma - Primary appendicular osteosarcoma that is amenable to surgical removal via amputation (No evidence that the tumor has spread to the lung (metastasis) based upon physical exam, thoracic radiographs, and abdominal ultrasound). - ONLY newly diagnosed dogs are eligible with no prior therapy (conventional or metronomic chemotherapy, ionizing radiation, bisphosphonates) for osteosarcoma. - Dogs receiving analgesics including NSAIDs, gabapentin, tramadol, or other will be eligible for study inclusion. What does enrolling my dog in this clinical trial involve? To enroll in this study, you must sign informed consent allowing the surgical amputation of your dog's affected limb. Following amputation, your dog will return to the NCSU Veterinary Hospital every 3 weeks for 15 weeks for evaluation. On weeks 3, 6, 9 and 12 your dog will receive a dose of carboplatin. Precautions should be taken against contact with your dog's urine or feces for 48 hours after carboplatin treatment. Blood work will be done on your dog prior to carboplatin administration. After completion of SOC therapy, and depending upon initial study randomization, you might be required to administer oral rapamycin (PO) at home for 4 months. The schedule for rapamycin administration will be daily on Monday-Thursday (4 days on), with a drug holiday on Friday, Saturday and Sunday (no dosing, 3 days off). This will allow us to determine if oral rapamycin can be safely administered chronically and will require serial collections of blood on scheduled reevaluations to allow for measurements of rapamycin within your dog's blood. Your dog will have a total of five 24-hour serial blood draws completed over the course of 4 months. At the end of the each study cycle (Day 25), your dog must return to the NCSU Veterinary Hospital for reassessment and further blood collections. If your dog has been randomized to receive oral rapamycin, these visits are required for inclusion in the study. If your dog is in the Standard of Care arm only, you will be required to return to the NCSU Veterinary Hospital every 8 weeks for evaluation. Background HFIRE is a newer generation technology, similar to the NanoKnife system which is in clincial trial in humans for the destruction soft tissues (i.e. tumors or cancers) via irreversible electroporation (IRE). We have previously demonstrated the safety of IRE for the treatment of canine brain tumors and have safely performed HFIRE on soft-tissue tumors, including brian tumors, in client-owned dogs, cats, and horses. By placing thin electrodes within tissue, IRE uses electrical pulses to destroy tissues by disrupting cellular membranes. The IRE method is less invasive and disruptive than traditional methods of surgical tumor resection. HFIRE offers additional advantages over traditional IRE in that the high-frequency pulses do not result in electrically induced muscular contractions, eliminating the need for more anesthesic agents, and offering the potential to selectively kill cancer cells and spare normal, healthy cells based on the physical characteristics of the cells. Therefore, HFIRE is ideally suited to the treatment of cancers in anatomically sensitive areas, such as the brain. Our newest generation of HFIRE technology allows the neurosurgeon to perform the HFIRE treatment while the patient is in the magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scanner, which should improve the safety and efficacy of the procedure. Dogs will be cared for post-operatively using standard-of-care procedures for brain tumor patients, and monitored daily in the ICU for adverse events until discharge from the hospital. "intervention-type_other-65", "label": "Other", "parent_label": "Intervention type"}], "description": "Phase 1: The proposed study will develop and evaluate a series of protocols based on basic clinical information and simple diagnostics to aid the general practitioner in diagnosing and managing chronic diarrhea in dogs. Individualized diagnostic and therapeutic plans will be devised by Drs. Bryan, Cade, Sullivant and Mackin of MSU-CVM, in consultation with the patients primary veterinarian. Plans will be based on history, physical examination and results of simple diagnostic tests. In most cases, diagnosis and treatment will be performed at the local veterinary practice, by the dogs primary veterinarian, in consultation with MSU-CVM, without the need for the dog or pet owner travel to MSU-CVM. Each veterinarian will be provided funding support (up to $300) from MSU-CVM to fund reasonable diagnostic and therapeutic plans for management of chronic diarrhea for each individual dog enrolled. Diagnostic and therapeutic plans will be individualized based on the circumstances of each patient, but can be reasonably be expected to include: Diagnostic tests including fecal flotation, fecal cytology, fecal culture, rectal scrapings and fecal assays for infectious organisms. Therapeutic trials including food trials, parasiticides, antibiotic trials with drugs such as tylosin and metronidazole, and pre- and pro-biotics. Long-term advice and follow-up (minimum of 3 months) will be provided by Drs. Bryan, Cade, Sullivant and Mackin, in collaboration with the primary veterinarian. Prior to, and then monthly over the 3 month follow-up period, outcome surveys will be conducted, both with owners and with primary care veterinarians. For those dogs that fail to respond to reasonable diagnostic and therapeutic plans for the management of chronic diarrhea, subsidized referral to MSU-CVM for specialist-level investigation will be offered. Phase 2: The proposed study will entail specialist-level investigation of dogs with chronic diarrhea that have failed to respond to standard therapy. In dogs that still have chronic diarrhea despite appropriate therapy at their primary veterinarian or through the Mississippi State University College of Veterinary Medicine (MSU-CVM) Community Veterinary Services practice will be referred to the MSU-CVM Small Animal Medicine service, under the supervision of Drs. Sullivant and Mackin, for a full investigation. At the time of admission, Dr. Sullivant will develop (but not implement) a theoretical best guess aggressive treatment plan that would typically be instituted if owners declined referral work-up despite failure to respond to standard therapy. Individualized specialized-level diagnostic and therapeutic plans will then be devised by Dr. Sullivant. Each enrolled case will be funded for the amount needed for a full referral investigation and appropriate therapy (typically, $1,500 to $3,500). Diagnostic and therapeutic plans at MSU-CVM will be individualized based on the circumstances of each patient, but can be reasonably be expected to include: Diagnostic tests including blood tests (complete blood count and serum biochemistry), abdominal radiography and ultrasonography, and non-invasive gastrointestinal biopsy via endoscopy or, uncommonly, laparoscopy or, rarely, more invasive biopsies by exploratory surgery. Targeted therapy based on the final diagnosis, including aggressive immunosuppression for inflammatory bowel disease, antifungal drugs for fungal diseases such as histoplasmosis, and chemotherapy for cancers such as lymphosarcoma. Cancer vaccines represent a form of active immunotherapy, whereby they exert an antitumor effect by engaging the host immune response. Additional advantages of cancer vaccines are exquisite specificity, low toxicity, and the potential for a durable therapeutic effect / benefit as a result of the induction of immunologic memory. Autologous cancer vaccines, such as the K9-ACV (MediVet Biologics) utilized in this proposed project, are polyvalent therapeutic vaccines derived from whole tumor cells. Such vaccines are formulated on an individual case basis using tumor tissue biopsy samples from the actual patient. The vaccine system being employed in this project was developed by researchers at the University Of Kentucky College Of Medicine, in conjunction with MediVet Biologics, and was modeled on a vaccine system previously developed by the same research group at the University of Kentucky and investigated in human lung cancer patients. Objective: To evaluate the efficacy of a newly formulated anti-cancer vaccine (K9-ACV, MediVet Biologics) in dogs diagnosed with a spectrum of naturally-occurring cancers. We will be measuring the patients' systemic immunologic anti-tumor response to the vaccine. It is hypothesized that this vaccine will elicit an antitumor immunologic response resulting in improved disease-free intervals and median survival times in dogs with various tumor types without compromising quality of life. What does enrollment into this trial involve? After your dog is enrolled into this study, surgery will occur atVHC to remove ordebulk the primarytumor. Part of the tumor tissue will be submitted for histopathologic diagnosis, grading and surgical margin assessment, and the remainder (minimum 5g) for vaccine formulation by the team at the University of Kentucky/MediVet Biologics. While the vaccination series cannot start until 7-14 days after the initial surgery, as this is how long the vaccine formulation takes, approval of enrollment, accompanied by owner informed consent, is required prior to surgery. In all cases of enrolled dogs, the surgical procedure to be performed would be considered standard of care treatment of that particular tumor type. Following surgery, enrolled dogs will be placed into one of two treatment groups at the owners request; the first receiving simply the vaccination series, and the second receiving the vaccination series in combination with the appropriate standard of care chemotherapy.If post-operative chemotherapy is elected by the owners, it will be performed by VHC Oncology Service. Recheck exams and blood work are required for monitoring of the patients immune response to the vaccine, as well as periodic monitoring chest x-rays and ultrasound. All study activities must occur at the VHC. Client Compensation: This study covers the cost of vaccine formulation and administration, as well as recheck exams and blood work for enrolled dogs. Periodic monitoring chest x-rays and ultrasound are also covered by the study for up to one year. "label": "Canine", "parent_label": "Species"}], "description": "Canine Brain Tumor Vaccine Clinical Trial We greatly appreciate your interest in our clinical study evaluating the use of a vaccine in dogs with brain tumors, specifically glioma. Your pets clinician will explain the disease characteristics of glioma as well as available treatment options. If you choose to participate in this clinical study, this handout will provide you with some insight into the purpose of this study and will explain your responsibilities and patient procedures. What are clinical trials? Clinical trials are research studies. They are used in all specialties of medicine to evaluate new types of treatment. Clinical trials may be designed to determine the anti-cancer effects and side effects of new drugs, new surgical procedures, new radiation therapy procedures, or novel approaches to treatment (such as gene therapy or immunotherapy). Your pets clinician will discuss standard treatment and clinical trial options with you. It is your decision whether or not you want your pet to participate in a clinical trial. You may discuss your pets participation with your family and your pets veterinarian. If you have any questions, please ask your pets clinician for additional information. Why is this clinical trial being conducted? Gliomas in dogs are known to be a very aggressive cancer with relatively short survival times despite our best efforts at treatment. Because of this, we are always looking for new ways to treat this disease. Many new cancer treatments are aimed at activating the patients own immune system (called immunotherapy) to potentially make it more effective at fighting off the cancer. One form of immunotherapy is tumor vaccines. This vaccine was developed in the Dow Laboratory, and targets the cancer stem cells, which are the precursor cells that then migrate and mature into active tumor cells with appropriate biochemical signals. These cancer stem cells are thought to be responsible for the inevitable recurrence of gliomas. These cells are present in the subventricular zone of the brain, and as such are not accessible for resection with the primary tumor. As these precursor cells are not in active division and thus are resistant to chemotherapy and radiation therapy, immunotherapies are likely the key to achieving improved outcomes for gliomas. A successful vaccine that targets these cancer stem cells would be invaluable. The goal of this study is to evaluate preliminary tumor response to vaccination as well as vaccine tolerability. Which patients are eligible to participate in this clinical trial? To be eligible for this study, dogs must have a brain tumor that is presumed to be in the glioma family based on MRI characteristics. They must also have sufficiently stable clinical signs to allow likely survival of at least one month. The patients neurological status must be such that he/she is strongly ambulatory without assistance, and that seizures (if occurring) are controlled with anti-convulsant medication. Dogs must not be receiving prednisone, or must be on a dose <0.5 mg/kg/day for at least 72 hours prior to starting the vaccine series, and maintain below that threshold for at least 7 days post-final vaccine. Past radiation therapy patients and chemotherapy patients are not eligible. Dogs with preexisting allergic airway disease or low heart rate may not receive propranolol, which is one of two medications given in addition to the vaccine to enhance the vaccine effect, and may be excluded at the investigator's discretion. Dogs must undergo some diagnostic testing at CSU prior to starting the vaccines to ensure that they are eligible, including complete blood count, chemistry profile, urinalysis, and needle biopsy (not debulking) of the tumor (costs will be covered by the study). What will happen if my pet participates in this clinical trial? If enrolled, dogs will first have a needle biopsy of their tumor, and if confirmed glioma, then they will receive a vaccine under the skin once every other week for a total 6 vaccines, followed by once monthly vaccine boosters. Serial neurological exams will be performed at each visit during the study period, and recheck MRI scans of the brain will be done every 3 months after the first vaccine. Additional blood samples will be collected for study purposes prior to the first vaccine and then serially throughout the study to assess antitumor immune response. In addition to the vaccine, two additional medications (losartan and propranolol) will be given orally (by mouth) to enhance the effect of the vaccine. Once your pet has died or been euthanized, a post-mortem exam will be required for additional characterization of tumor type, growth, and cellular markers. What side effects or risks may my pet experience while participating in this clinical trial? Your pet may experience side effects. Possible side effects associated with the vaccine treatment include: Local vaccine site reactions (swelling, pain, redness, itching) Fever, mild loss of appetite, and/or lethargy for first 24 hours after vaccine injection Risk of anaphylaxis (rare) Cerebral edema and worsening of neurological signs (unlikely) due to peritumoral inflammation from exuberant response of tumor to vaccine Losartan may cause low blood pressure or lethargy; if this occurs the dosage will be decreased Propanolol may cause slow heart rate, low blood pressure, or lethargy; if this occurs the dosage will be adjusted Needle biopsy side effects may include: transient neurological decline, hemorrhage, infection, or less commonly permanent neurological decline or death The study is able to cover up to $500 in treatment costs for vaccine-associated adverse events if they occur. Adverse events are not anticipated, and most likely would involve simple local reactions that would require only oral medications to treat. Your pets clinician will discuss possible side effects with you and help you manage them if they occur. If your pet experiences anything unusual during the clinical trial, please contact your clinician. How long will my pet be in the clinical trial? The study period is 1 year. However, the length of your pets participation will depend on his/her response to the treatment. If your pets clinical signs are worsening or there is concern for tumor progression, your pet may be withdrawn from the study before it is completed. Your pets clinician will discuss continued treatment and diagnostic testing once the trial has ended. Can my pet withdraw from the clinical trial? You may decide to withdraw your pet from the clinical trial at any time. Tell your pets clinician if you are considering withdrawing your pet. It is important to discuss withdrawal in order to determine a plan for continued treatment of your pets cancer. Your clinician may stop your pet from continued participation in the clinical trial at any time if he/she believes it is in your pets best interest or if the trial is discontinued or if the trial protocol is not followed. What financial incentives will CSU provide for my pets participation? All required study activities once enrolled (not including the diagnostic tests to determine eligibility), will be performed at no cost. (Costs for medications or treatments that are not included as part of the study, are not covered by the study). There is no charge for the postmortem examination. In addition, up to $500 will be available for treatment of vaccine-related adverse events. What are my responsibilities during the clinical trial? You are responsible for the costs of any elective services, medications, or additional hospitalization fees not required by the study. In addition, any costs for treatment of adverse events beyond the $500 covered by the study will be your financial responsibility, as well as the cost and any other tests recommended by your pets neurologist that are not a required component of the study. You are expected to make and keep all appointments, according to the clinical trial protocol. Questions? Please do not hesitate to obtain additional information from your pets neurology clinician if you do not understand something about the study or your pets care and treatment. CSU Principal Investigator: Dr. Rebecca Packer, (970) 297-4543, email: Rebecca.Packer@colostate.edu Emergency Assistance: CSU VTH, (970) 297-5000. 2008, Animal Cancer Center, Colorado State University"}, {"id": 15382, "name": "Validation of a novel imaging device to detect cancerous vs normal cells during brain tumor resection", "url": "https://veterinaryclinicaltrials.org/s/validation-of-a-novel-imaging-device-to-detect-cancerous-vs-normal-cells-during-brain-tumor-resection-853184/?ref=gallery", "status": "Completed", "tags": [{"tag_path": "primary-field-19_neurology-neurosurgery-5", "label": "Neurology/Neurosurgery", "parent_label": "Primary field"}, {"tag_path": "primary-field-19_neurology-neurosurgery-5_central-nervous-system-neoplasia-251", "label": "Central nervous system neoplasia", "parent_label": "Neurology/Neurosurgery"}, {"tag_path": "intervention-type_diagnostic-57", "label": "Diagnostic", "parent_label": "Intervention type"}, {"tag_path": "financial-incentive_partially-funded_partially-funded-owner-cost-1000-51", "label": "Partially funded (owner cost >$1000)", "parent_label": "Partially funded"}, {"tag_path": "financial-incentive_partially-funded", "label": "Partially funded", "parent_label": "Financial incentive"}, {"tag_path": "species-20_canine-21", "label": "Canine", "parent_label": "Species"}], "description": "Which dogs can participate in this study? In this study, dogs that have been diagnosed with a surgically resectable brain tumor, based on MRI, are eligible for the study. Study Activities In this study, surgery would proceed according to normal standard of care; however, during surgery a novel imaging device will be used to record the chemical signal of the tissues visible during surgery. This imaging device is completely noninvasive, and will allow us to learn the differences in chemical signal of normal brain tissue compared to tumor tissue. This is important because visually some brain tumors look identical to tumor tissue, so improved methods of recognizing abnormal cells during surgery are vital to improving surgical accuracy. The readings obtained during surgery will be compared to the biopsy samples obtained as a normal component of tumor resection. This study only requires noninvasive acquisition of biochemical recordings during surgery. Carboplatin has been safely and effectively used to treat appendicular osteosarcoma in dogs for > 20 years, but the potential for unforeseen potentially life-threatening side effects from surgery, chemotherapy, and/or progressive cancer does exist. Rapamycin is a drug currently approved for immunosuppression during preparatory and maintenance regimens for organ and bone marrow transplant in human patients. Early work with rapamycin suggests that this agent might also have anti-cancer properties by inhibiting (reducing the effects of) an important pathway in cancer progression known as mTOR. Preclinical studies of rapamycin in mice, as well as recent data using analogous drugs in human patients (rapalogs), suggest that mTOR blockade might be effective in the treatment of several cancers. Studies in mice have shown rapamycin to be safe when used to treat experimental cancers. In a recently completed study of rapamycin in dogs with cancer, a dose and schedule for rapamycin administration have been defined which appears to be safe and tolerable by most dogs. Affected individuals are genetically predisposed to developing inflammatory skin disease with characteristic clinical features associated with lgE antibodies directed against environmental allergens, such as house dust mites, pollens, and molds. Current treatment options for canines include antihistamines , corticosteroids , cyclosporine A, oclacitinib , and allergen specific immunotherapy (ASIT) administered subcutaneously or sublingually, as well as adjunctive treatments such as topical and systemic antimicrobial therapy . Avoidance of implicated allergens is impractical or impossible in most cases. These approaches to treatment are not entirely reliable, have potential for adverse reactions, or they come with significant financ ial burden. Our primary goal is to investigate the safety and biological activity of canine placental (fetal) derived MSCs (Wharton's Jelly MSC = WJ-MSC) in alleviating the clinical signs associated with canine AD. Our secondary goal is to investigate the feasibility of this protocol for future applications in larger scale randomized controlled double-blinded clinical trials. We are studying genetically modified Vesicular Stomatitis Virus (VSV-IFN-NIS) which has been shown to be effective against cancer in the laboratory and in a pilot study of eight dogs. The study will treat dogs with VSV intravenously, followed by amputation of the affected limb 10 days later, then followed by chemotherapy with carboplatin. February 2018: expanded trial to placebo-controlled. Dogs will be screened for acceptability, including a CT scan under anesthesia. Once enrolled, dogs typically spend the week at the Veterinary Medical Center (VMC). We will perform a tumor biopsy under anesthesia and take baseline samples of blood, cheek, urine and stool on Monday. On Tuesday dogs receive the treatment with VSV-IFN-NIS or saline placebo and will be housed in isolation, closely monitored by our team, for a period of time (6-24 hrs). We will sample blood, cheek, urine and stool periodically to detect virus shedding and immune responses. On Wed - Fri, we will monitor the dog and take additional samples. Dogs go home on Friday. Recheck visits are weekly for 1st month. Day 10 is the amputation surgery. Chemotherapy begins about Day 21, and will continue for six treatments (standard protocol through the Oncology Service). Study rechecks are at months 3, 6, and one year. "Primary field"}], "description": "Many brain cancers are not accessible to surgical excision, and use of chemotherapy drugs is limited by the blood brain barrier. In an effort to deliver chemotherapy drugs directly into a cancer, novel polymeric microcylinders have been developed using poly (lactic-co-glycolic acid (PLGA) as a biocompatible drug delivery system. These novel microcylinders have been designed to be amenable to stereotactic implantation, allowing for a minimally-invasive implantation procedure. The polymer can be adjusted for various degradation times, allowing the associated drug to be delivered over a prescribed period of time. Because the drug can be placed directly into the cancerous tissue, the blood brain barrier is bypassed entirely. This enables a high dosage of chemotherapy to be delivered into the cancer without the risk of systemic side effects associated with high-dose chemotherapy including myelosuppression or gastrointestinal upset. Temozolamide is a chemotherapy drug that has been FDA approved for the treatment of glioblastoma multiforme (GBM) in humans, and was shown to provide a statistically significant benefit to 2-year survival and progression-free survival time in humans as part of multimodal therapy for GBM. Temozolomide has been demonstrated as safe in dogs with lymphoma, but there have been no studies evaluating its clinical efficacy for any type of brain tumor in dogs. The current objective is to study implantation of temozolomide and gadolinium-infused PLGA microcylinders in dogs with gliomas. Our preliminary studies confirm that PLGA microcylinders infused with both temozolomide and gadolinium are clinically well-tolerated in healthy dogs."}, {"id": 15473, "name": "Novel gene therapy for the treatment of canine brain tumors", "url": "https://veterinaryclinicaltrials.org/s/novel-gene-therapy-for-the-treatment-of-canine-brain-tumors-447900/?ref=gallery", "status": "Completed", "tags": [{"tag_path": "financial-incentive_fully-funded-including-initial-screening-47", "label": "Fully funded including initial screening", "parent_label": "Financial incentive"}, {"tag_path": "species-20_canine-21", "label": "Canine", "parent_label": "Species"}, {"tag_path": "intervention-type_other-65", "label": "Other", "parent_label": "Intervention type"}, {"tag_path": "primary-field-19_oncology-1_brain-or-spinal-tumor-338", "label": "Brain or spinal tumor", "parent_label": "Oncology"}, {"tag_path": "primary-field-19_oncology-1", "label": "Oncology", "parent_label": "Primary field"}], "description": "This project is a collaborative effort between Celsion, Corporation and veterinarians at Veterinary Referral & Critical Care (VRCC) of Manakin-Sabot, VA evaluating a novel gene therapy (GEN-1) for the treatment of brain tumors. The goal of this project is to evaluate the safety and feasibility of intra-cranially administering GEN-1 following tumor resection surgery. The results of this study will be used to support the initiation of clinical trials aimed at treating human patients with glioblastoma multiforme. The following treatment design will be used: Surgery to remove as much of the tumor as possible. Subcutaneous implantation of a reservoir device with access to the resection cavity Repeated administration (3x) of the gene therapy (GEN-1) through the device directly into the resection cavity. What dogs are eligible for the project? Any dog that is approximately 10 Kg in weight or greater with an intra-axial brain tumor and that is healthy enough to undergo resection surgery can be included in this study. The specific tumor type will not be an eligibility requirement although there will be requirements regarding the location of the tumor that will inform a final eligibility decision. How much does it cost? All project related treatments, analytical work and followup will be performed at no cost to the dog's owners. Owners will be responsible for transportation to and from VRCC for treatments and follow-up visits. What is the therapy? In this study, GEN-1, a nanoparticle formulation that contains the IL-12 gene will be repeatedly delivered intra-cranially into dogs following tumor resection surgery. IL-12 protein is known to have very potent anti-tumor properties that work by stimulating the bodys own immune response to help kill tumor cells. In addition, IL-12 can also help to prevent the formation of new blood vessels that are required for tumor growth. Use of GEN-1 is currently being evaluated in human clinical trials for treating ovarian cancer and has shown in animal models that it can slow and/or eliminate a wide variety of tumor types, including glioblastomas. Although this study is designed to evaluate the feasibility and safety of repeatedly administering GEN-1 into the resection cavity in the brain that has resulted from surgically removing a brain tumor, it has the potential to reduce or eradicate the remaining tumor in dogs suffering from brain cancer. Please contact Dr. Jeff Clarke, DVM, DACVIM or Dr. Anna Aman, DVM, DACVS at VRCC for more information. This investigational drug inhibits a very important pathway that has been shown to induce cell death in lymphoma cells holding great promise for treating lymphoma and possibly other cancers. What qualifies my dog for enrollment in this in this trial? To participate in this clinical trial your dog must have: - A diagnosis of cancer (Lymphoma) -Minimum weight of 20 kg or 44 pounds. -Prior chemotherapy or radiation must be completed 2 weeks prior to study entry -Dogs must have gross/measurable disease (approximately 2 cm) -Dogs must be free of other diseases (heart, liver, and kidney) and be feeling good (playing, good appetite). -Your dog will be screened for eligibility based on bloodwork (complete blood count, biochemistry profile, urinalysis, chest x-rays, abdominal ultrasound) What does enrolling my dog in this clinical trial involve? Your dog will receive the investigational drug intravenously (IV) two times given 48 hours apart while hospitalized in the Veterinary Medical Center (VMC). Your dog will be discharged later that day after the second treatment and then will return to the VMC one week after the first treatment for re-evaluation.Analysis for tumor response will be performed by direct tumor measurement or through the use of imaging (radiographs, ultrasound, CT). Standard bloodwork will be performed periodically throughout the study. Additional tests to be performed include blood draws, collection of peripheral blood cells (PBCs), fine needle aspirates (FNAs) and biopsies of the lymph nodes to determine how the investigational drug is affecting the cancer cells.During the two drug treatments your dog will stay in the hospital overnight so that blood samples can be drawn to assess how the investigational drug blood levels change during the course of the day. The total volume of blood involved in this collection is approximately 6 tablespoons. Client Compensation Following your dogs completion of the clinical trial, you will receive a credit of $2000 for continued treatment of your dog at the VMC.The clinical trial will cover the costs associated with trial screening for dogs that are eligible for the trial and enroll in the study. Screening costs will not be paid for ineligible dogs. For eligible, enrolled dogs, the clinical trial will cover all costs associated with screening prior to study entry, all treatments, and treatment of any side effects associated with the treatment. These samples will be used in future studies to investigate issues like what mutations cause brain tumors, how brain tumors grow or whether they cause any abnormalities in the blood or urine. The hope is that one day we will find new avenues for treatment of brain tumors, or new laboratory tests that will help us know whether pets have a brain tumor or whether the tumor is responding to treatment. Eligibility: To be eligible for participation in this study, dogs must have been preliminarily diagnosed with a brain tumor. Only dogs that are having surgery to remove the tumor, as part of their veterinary care, are eligible for this study. Procedures: During surgery, after enough tumor has been sampled to provide a clear diagnosis, any additional brain tumor tissue will be stored in our Brain Tumor Bank. Blood and urine samples will also be sampled and stored in our Brain Tumor Bank. These samples will be drawn while your pet is under anesthesia and being prepared for the brain tumor surgery. If we are sampling blood or urine to prepare your animal for the surgery, additional blood / urine may be drawn at that time. Associated Risks: There will be no additional risk to the pet by having your pet enrolled in this study. The brain tumor surgery risks will be no different than any other brain tumor surgery. The risk of harm from having the urine and blood sampled is extremely low. There can be bleeding or infection of the site where blood or urine is drawn, but this is uncommon. Sampling urine from the bladder can cause urine to leak into the abdomen, but this is very rare. Compensation: There is no compensation for participating in this study, however the owner will not be charged for the particular urine or blood sample taken for the Brain Tumor Bank and only $500 of the surgery cost. It destroys the bone it is originating from and causes pain. In treating dogs with this cancer, some form of therapy is typically directed at the tumor itself. It can be a limb amputation, radiation therapy, or limb sparing surgery. As the name implies, limb sparing surgery is a surgical procedure where the tumor is removed while preserving the function of the limb. For tumors that are located close to the wrist, many different techniques are possible but the risk of complication remains relatively high. The 3 main complications are infection, implant-related problems, and recurrence of the tumor in the limb. With currently-available techniques, the risk of an infection developing in the limb following limb sparing surgery can be as high as 75%, the risk of implant related problem as high as 60% and local recurrence is seen in 15%-25%. Many deficiencies exist with the currently available implants used for limb sparing in dogs. With the advent of 3D-printing, we have developed a process that allows us to manufacture an implant specifically designed for each individual dog that undergoes limb sparing. With these improved implants, we predict the risk of implant-related complications will significantly decrease and may also help decrease the risk of an infection. Novel therapies for lymphoma, especially T cell lymphoma, are needed. This investigational drug inhibits a novel cellular pathway that has been shown to induce cell death in some T cell lymphoma cells. Inhibitors of this pathway hold great promise for treating T cell lymphoma. The investigational drug has shown good activity against lymphoma cell lines in culture. This drug has been tested in rats at doses 10 times higher than the doses we plan to use, and in normal healthy dogs at the approximate dose we plan to use, without evidence of any adverse effects. The primary objective of this study is to evaluate the safety and antitumor activity of this investigational drug given to dogs with cutaneous T cell lymphoma that have not yet been treated. Dogs will receive this drug orally twice daily. There are weekly recheck visits for the first 4 weeks, then every other week thereafter. Each of these visits will generally take approximately 1 hour. Dogs will be eligible to continue receiving treatment at no cost as long as the drug is tolerated and the dog is experiencing clinical benefit (disease stabilization or meaningful tumor shrinkage). Analysis for tumor response will be performed by direct tumor measurement or through the use of imaging (radiographs, ultrasound, CT). Standard bloodwork will be performed at each visit. Additional tests to be performed include blood draws and 2 or 3 biopsies of the skin lesions over the course of the study to determine how the investigational drug is affecting the cancer cells. These biopsies will be performed using standard sedation/anesthesia protocols, the biopsy site will be sutured, and sutures removed 2 weeks later. The visits when biopsies are performed may require a longer time, approximately half a day. For the seventh/eighth day of the study your dog may stay in the hospital overnight one night so that blood samples can be drawn over 24 hours to assess how drug blood levels change during the course of the day, and a biopsy can be performed. "parent_label": "Species"}], "description": "Purpose and Brief Explanation of Study: In people, hypovitaminosis D has been shown to be a negative prognostic factor associated with disease progression, development of renal secondary hyperparathyroidism, and mortality. We are currently investigating this relationship in dogs with chronic kidney disease (CKD). It has yet to be investigated if supplementation with some form of vitamin D can improve vitamin D status and/or if this will have a positive effect on disease progression and survival. Objective of the trial: The purpose of this study is to determine how supplementation with vitamin D affects serum concentration and parathyroid hormone (PTH) concentrations in dogs with chronic kidney disease (CKD). What qualifies my dog for enrollment in this in this trial? To participate in this clinical trial your dog must: - Be diagnosed with CKD, specifically International Renal Interest Society (IRIS) stage 2 or 3, which is based predominantly on serum creatinine. - Be at least one year of age and weigh at least 10 kg (22 pounds). - Have a serum 25(OH)D concentration   2.0. - Not be diagnosed with any other disease known to affect vitamin D or PTH concentrations (e.g., protein-losing enteropathy, primary hyperparathyroidism, primary hypoparathyroidism, hyperadrenocorticism). - Not have cancer. What does enrolling my dog in this clinical trial involve? First your dog will have a physical examination and blood pressure measurement. Then your dog will have blood and urine collected to evaluate his/her suitability for enrollment. This will include a complete blood count (CBC), serum biochemistry profile, ionized calcium, urinalysis, urine protein:creatinine (UPC) ratio and serum 25(OH)D concentration.If your dog meets the enrollment criteria, then your dog will receive a vitamin D (25\"OH\"D) supplement to be dosed once daily by mouth. Your dog must return for recheck examinations monthly for 3 months, at which time complete physical examinations and blood pressure measurements will be performed. Blood and urine will be collected.After the first month, based your dogs response to the supplement, we will determine if the dose requires adjustment. If so, your dog will need to return for one additional recheck visit (4 months after enrolment). Client Compensation The study will cover over $3000 of appointment fees and diagnostic tests (including vitamin D metabolite, ionized calcium, and parathyroid hormone concentrations, as well as biochemistry profiles) over the study period. Standard of Care is defined as amputation surgery, followed by 4 doses of intravenous carboplatin chemotherapy given on a q21 day schedule. Explanation: Bone cancer or osteosarcoma (OSA) is a common, highly aggressive cancer that frequently affects the long bones of large breed dogs. Current therapy consists of limb amputation plus chemotherapy. However, despite therapy, most patients die as a result of the cancer spreading to other parts of their bodies. The immune system plays an important role in identifying and targeting cancer cells in the body. In this study, we aim to use a new approach to stimulate the bodys own immune system to attack remaining tumor cells in dogs that have undergone limb amputation and chemotherapy for the treatment of OSA. We will use a vaccine, referred to as ADXS31-164c, made from the bacteria Listeria monocytogenes, which has been genetically modified to express a tumor protein (HER-2/neu) that is found in many cancer cells, including canine bone cancer cells and cancer stem cells. When injected into the bloodstream, the modified Listeria stimulates the immune system to attack cells expressing the HER-2/neu tumor protein. This approach aims to delay and/or prevent the spread of cancer (metastases) following removal of the primary bone cancer tumor (limb amputation) and chemotherapy. What does enrollment into this trial involve? Within this study, we ask that you permit surgical amputation of your dogs affected limb. Your dog will return to KSU VHC every 3 weeks for 15 weeks for evaluation. On weeks 3, 6, 9 and 12 your dog will receive a dose of carboplatin. Blood work will be done on your dog prior to carboplatin administration. After completion of standard of care, your dog will be administered 3 doses of ADXS31-164c. Doses will be administered every 3 weeks for a total of 3 doses. These visits are required for inclusion in the study. Your dog may be required to stay overnight after receiving ADXS31-164c. This will be determined by your clinician. Owner Compensation: Once your dog has been enrolled, the study will cover the cost of the initial oncology consultation and chest radiographs, as well as most of the cost associated with the 4 doses of ADXS31-164c. "Primary field"}], "description": "Vinblastine has been used in feline cancer patients mostly as a component of multi-drug treatment protocols for lymphoma. Response rates, progression-free survival and lymphoma-specific survival are similar between cats receiving vinblastine or vincristine as part of a multi-drug protocol for lymphoma. However, cats receiving vinblastine may have a lower incidence of gastrointestinal toxicity, and this can be a deciding factor in choosing vinblastine over vincristine for treatment of lymphoma in cats. The incidence of neutropenia in cats following administered vinblastine versus vincristine does not appear to differ and dose reductions due to neutropenia are sometimes required during vinblastine therapy. No pharmacokinetic data exist for vinblastine in the cat. In other species, vinblastine demonstrates either a bi- or tri-exponential decline in plasma concentrations with abundant distribution to tissues that occurs rapidly after dosing. Vinblastine readily accumulates within the cellular component of blood, as it binds to tubulin within platelets and blood cells; up to 50% of drug may distribute to the cellular compartment of blood within 20 minutes of administration. Consistent with the findings of abundant tissue distribution, vinblastine has a large volume of distribution for and plasma protein binding values ranging from 43-99% depending on the species studied. Extensive hepatic metabolism of vinblastine leads to formation of one major metabolite, 4-desacetylvinblastine, suggested to have equal or greater antitumor activity to the parent molecule in dogs and humans. It is unknown if metabolism in cats also produces this active compound. Of note, pharmacokinetic studies in all other species have identified substantial inter- and intra-individual variability in pharmacokinetics which is noted clinically by the equally large variability in neutropenia following equivalent doses.It is important to understand the pharmacokinetics of vinblastine in the population of patients that are receiving this drug; older, cancer-bearing cats that may have other co-morbid diseases that can affect pharmacokinetic profiles, i.e. hepatic or renal disease. Variability in pharmacokinetics is likely to be larger in this population when compared to younger, healthy cats. This study is designed to obtain the information required to describe the pharmacokinetics of vinblastine in cats and associate the variability in pharmacokinetic parameters with patient variables."}, {"id": 15624, "name": "Evaluation of a recombinant, attenuated Listeria monocytogenes expressing a chimeric human HER2/neu protein in dogs in the adjuvan", "url": "https://veterinaryclinicaltrials.org/s/evaluation-of-a-recombinant-attenuated-listeria-monocytogenes-expressing-a-chimeric-human-her2neu-protein-in-dogs-in-the-adjuvan-797336/?ref=gallery", "status": "Completed", "tags": [{"tag_path": "intervention-type_biologic-vaccine-58", "label": "Biologic/Vaccine", "parent_label": "Intervention type"}, {"tag_path": "financial-incentive_partially-funded_partially-funded-owner-cost-1000-51", "label": "Partially funded (owner cost >$1000)", "parent_label": "Partially funded"}, {"tag_path": "financial-incentive_partially-funded", "label": "Partially funded", "parent_label": "Financial incentive"}, {"tag_path": "species-20_canine-21", "label": "Canine", "parent_label": "Species"}, {"tag_path": "primary-field-19_oncology-1_osteosarcoma-or-bone-tumor-29", "label": "Osteosarcoma or bone tumor", "parent_label": "Oncology"}, {"tag_path": "primary-field-19_oncology-1", "label": "Oncology", "parent_label": "Primary field"}], "description": "Standard therapy for dogs diagnosed with osteosarcoma has long been amputation of the affected limb followed by chemotherapy to delay the spread of cancer. Treatment has been limited to external beam radiation therapy at significant expense and often multiple days of anesthesia needed. Median survival is about 1 year and side effects are common. Electrochemotherapy is the use of electrical impulses to open cell membranes driving chemotherapy locally, i.e. a targeted therapy. We now have an electrode that may be used for nasal tumors based on published material below:. Radiol Oncol.2017 Nov 1;51(4):422-430. doi: 10.1515/raon-2017-0043. eCollection 2017 Dec. Minimally InvasiveElectrochemotherapyProcedure for TreatingNasalDuct Tumors inDogs using a Single Needle Electrode. Maglietti F,Tellado M,Olaiz N,Michinski S,Marshall G Nasal cavity tumors are usually diagnosed late, when they already have infiltrated adjacent tissues thus requiring very aggressive treatments with serious side effects. Here we useelectrochemotherapy(ECT), a well demonstrated treatment modality for superficial tumors. MATERIALS AND METHODS:In the case of deep-seated tumors, the main limitation of ECT is reaching the tumor with an appropriate electric field. To overcome this limitation we introduce the single needle electrode (SiNE), a minimally invasive device that can deliver an appropriate electric field with a simple procedure. Twenty-one canine patients with spontaneous tumors were selected, eleven were treated using the SiNE with ECT, and ten with surgery plus adjuvant chemotherapy as a control group.RESULTS:In the SiNE group, 27% achieved a complete response, 64% had a partial response, and 9% had a stable disease. This means that 91% of objective responses were obtained. The mean overall survival was 16.86 months (4-32 months, median 16.5 months), with a survival rate significantly higher (p = 0.0008) when compared with control group. The only side effect observed was the inflammation of the treatednasalpassage, which was controlled with corticosteroid therapy for one week. One year after the treatment, 60% of the canine of the SiNE group vs. 10% of the control group remained alive, and after the 32 months follow-up, the survival rate were 30% and 0%, respectively. CONCLUSIONS: ECT with the SiNE can be safely used in canine to treatnasaltumors with encouraging results. Those clients not electing to participate with this therapy will be followed and data used for comparison. Rechecks may also be done with RDVM but advanced imaging post treatment would be necessary to follow response. While the study is for canine patients, there is no reason not to look at feline and wildlife with the same or similar diagnosis. The procedure involves a short general anesthesia and is generally an outpatient procedure.  Minimal side-effects have been noted and anti-inflammatory pain management may be necessary for a few days post procedure For more information: LINK TO TEXTBOOK: https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-3-030-80668-2 https://www.vetspecialists.com/vet-blog-landing/animal-health-articles/2024/01/23/electrochemotherapy-cancer-treatment"}, {"id": 15645, "name": "Dogs with bladder cancer (Transitional Cell Carcinomas-TCC)", "url": "https://veterinaryclinicaltrials.org/s/dogs-with-bladder-cancer-transitional-cell-carcinomas-tcc-357974/?ref=gallery", "status": "Completed", "tags": [{"tag_path": "financial-incentive_partially-funded_partially-funded-owner-cost-expected-500-49", "label": "Partially funded (owner cost expected <$500)", "parent_label": "Partially funded"}, {"tag_path": "financial-incentive_partially-funded", "label": "Partially funded", "parent_label": "Financial incentive"}, {"tag_path": "intervention-type_drug-334", "label": "Drug", "parent_label": "Intervention type"}, {"tag_path": "species-20_canine-21", "label": "Canine", "parent_label": "Species"}, {"tag_path": "primary-field-19_oncology-1_urogenital-tumors-349", "label": "Urogenital tumors", "parent_label": "Oncology"}, {"tag_path": "primary-field-19_oncology-1", "label": "Oncology", "parent_label": "Primary field"}], "description": "Purpose and Brief Explanation of Study: The investigational drug (PLX4720) is a novel small molecule inhibitor of the BRAF, which is a gene involved in sending signals in cell growth, this gene is altered in many types of cancer. PLX 4720 is closely related to vemurafenib (Zelboraf, PLX4032), another BRAF inhibitor approved for the treatment of human melanoma carrying activating mutations in BRAF. It was recently determined that approximately 80% of canine bladder cancer (transitional cell carcinomas-TCC) carry activating mutations in BRAF identical to those found in human melanoma. Unfortunately, vemurafenib has unfavorable oral bioavailability in dogs, necessitating the use of another analog with better pharmacokinetic properties. Recently, healthy volunteer client owned dogs were enrolled into a clinical trial to evaluate the pharmacokinetics of a single dose of PLX4720 given orally. This was well tolerated and provided critical data regarding expected pharmacokinetic variability and likely dosing necessary to reach biologically relevant blood levels of drug for the current clinical trial. Objective of the trial: To evaluate the biologic activity associated with oral administration of PLX4720 to dogs bladder cancer and with BRAF mutation, and to assess adverse events associated with chronic PLX4720 dosing. What qualifies my dog for enrollment in this in this trial? Eligible patients (any breed of dog) must meet all of the following criteria: Be greater than 1 year of age Weigh at least 5 kg Have a diagnosis of transitional cell carcinoma of the bladder with measurable disease Be medically healthy with no clinically significant physical findings Prior chemotherapy or radiation must be completed 2 weeks prior to study entry Be able to receive oral medication on a daily basis Urine must be positive for the BRAF mutation What does enrolling my dog in this clinical trial involve? All dogs will receive PLX4270 once per day, dogs will receive PLX4270 for 28 days at which time an assessment of response to therapy will be performed. If biologic activity is evident, owners will be given the opportunity to continue on therapy in a compassionate use setting. Recheck exams will be performed at Days 7, 14 and 28 (the final visit). Analysis of dogs for tumor response will be performed by ultrasound examination of the bladder. Standard clinical chemistries (CBC, chemistry panel, and urinalysis) will be performed during the study. Additionally, plasma will be collected at each visit to assess trough blood levels of PLX4270. The initial dose of PLX4270 for dogs will be 30 mg/kg, with dose escalations in 30 mg/kg increments until a maximum tolerated dose (MTD) is identified or until biologic activity in 50% or more dogs is documented or until pharmacokinetic analysis determines that no benefit would be obtained by continuing to increase the dose. Client Compensation If your dog participates in this research, he/she will have the following benefits: complete blood work, urinalysis, and abdominal ultrasound at the initial visit and at conclusion of the study at no charge to you. In addition, the cost of the recheck exams for Day 0, 7, 14 and 28 will be covered. It is an aggressive tumor with local bone destruction and severe pain where it originates and early metastasis (spread) to other sites within the body. The primary site of metastasis is to the lungs with >90% of dogs having at least microscopic metastasis at the time of diagnosis. Therefore, although surgical removal of the tumor via amputation of the affected limb provides palliation, these patients will eventually die from the development of multiple tumors within the lungs in only a few months. The addition of chemotherapy to address these secondary tumors increases survival over amputation alone and has been the accepted standard of care (SOC) for decades. However, the average survival still does not exceed a year and only a small percentage of dogs survive two years or longer. Thus, more effective treatment protocols are desperately needed. In human oncology, an approach that has been previously investigated is the delivery of low-dose radiation to the lungs (total lung irradiation; TLI) in the hopes of killing the microscopic cancer cells that are present. In these human studies, low-dose TLI, alone or combined with chemotherapy, was found to be safe but clinical benefit varied. Although safety data exists for TLI in healthy and tumor-bearing dogs, its effect on survival in dogs with OSA has been studied on a very limited and non-optimized basis and never in conjunction with SOC: amputation and chemotherapy. Therefore, the aim of this study is to investigate TLI plus SOC for dogs with OSA in a prospective clinical trial. After undergoing amputation (either here at NC State or at another institution) dogs will be enrolled and starting within 3 days following surgery will begin a protocol of 10 daily fractions of TLI followed by 6 doses of carboplatin chemotherapy (as per our protocol for the adjuvant treatment of canine OSA; may be performed here at NC State \"preferred\" or with another veterinarian if the clients cannot pursue chemotherapy here). Following completion of the carboplatin protocol dogs will then be monitored with serial thoracic radiographs performed every 2 months (our standard practice) to assess for metastatic disease and any potential adverse effects of TLI. Our primary objective is to evaluate the effect of adding TLI to SOC on metastasis-free interval (MFI; the time from amputation to development of the aforementioned lung nodules or spread elsewhere, e.g. bone) and overall survival time (ST; the time from amputation to death or euthanasia). Our secondary objective is to obtain short- and long-term safety data by using serial bloodwork, chest x-rays, and respiratory (client-provided history, physical exam) assessments. We hypothesize that the addition of TLI will significantly improve patient outcome and will be well-tolerated with minimal to no hematologic or respiratory toxicity."}, {"id": 15700, "name": "Novel
