"Species"}], "description": "The Veterinary Medical Center at the University of Minnesota is conducting a study in dogs with high-grade glioma including glioblastoma (GBM), common primary malignant brain tumors, to develop novel immunotherapy strategies that are more effective than current treatments. These tumors are uniformly deadly in both dogs and people with median survival times of two months in dogs and ~ 14 months in people after standard of care treatment. This work aims to evaluate novel combinations of immune therapies in dogs with previously untreated brain tumors to determine the combination that provides the longest remission times with minimal adverse effects. Our ultimate goal is to develop a safe and effective postoperative treatment that avoids the standard therapy with chemotherapy and radiation therapy that can be translated to human GBM patients. Dogs with clinical signs (symptoms) that suggest the presence of a brain mass or tumor will be eligible for participation. Each dog should have a magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) study of the brain to determine the location, size, and imaging characteristics of the mass. A small sample of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) may be collected for analysis after the MRI. Dr. Pluhar, the Principal Investigator, will examine the MRI to determine whether the characteristics of the mass are consistent with a diagnosis of glioma that is amenable to surgical removal, which would make your dog eligible to participate in the treatment study. Thorough physical and neurological examinations, blood screening tests, and imaging of the chest and abdomen should be done to make sure that your dog is healthy enough to undergo general anesthesia. If your dog is in adequate physical condition based on these tests, he/she can be enrolled in the study. Inclusion criteria will be: (i) any dog with an intracranial mass and MRI consistent with diagnosis of GBM that is (ii) suitable for surgical resection; (iii) is healthy enough to undergo chemotherapy; and (iv) informed consent provided by the dogs owner. Note: Dogs that do not display a GBM diagnosis upon surgical biopsy will not continue in the trial, but will be treated by standard care. The Exclusion criteria for our trial will be (i) severe neurologic dysfunction, especially changes in level of consciousness that may indicate pending brain herniation; (ii) tumor not amenable to surgical resection; (iii) existence of concomitant disease that would affect the dogs long-term prognosis and preclude completion of chemotherapy or vaccine therapy, and (iv) French bulldogs, which we have found do not respond to vaccine-mediated immunotherapy. Study: All dogs that meet the requirements listed above will have a surgical biopsy to definitively identify the specific tumor type and grade at the time of surgical removal of as much of the tumor as possible. All dogs will be randomly assigned to receive one of the three additional immunotherapies as described above to enhance anti-tumor immunity. The vaccine used for immunotherapy will be created from the dog's own tumor cells grown under special conditions that will improve how they stimulate the dog's immune system. The vaccines should cause the dog's immune system to recognize and kill any tumor cells that were not removed during surgery. The gene therapy has been shown to be effective in killing primary brain tumors in rats and mice and safe in a previous study in dogs that was conducted by the PI. Each dog will be placed under general anesthesia supervised by a board-certified anesthesiologist during the surgical procedure that will be performed by Dr. Pluhar, with assistance from an MD neurosurgeon. After approaching the dog's brain with the appropriate craniotomy, as much of the tumor mass as possible will be removed. A portion of the tumor will be submitted for histopathology to get a definitive tumor type and grade and the remainder will be used to create the vaccines. Dogs in the gene therapy groups will have injections of the vector in the brain tissue around the site of tumor removal. A brain MRI will be performed immediately after surgery to assess how much of the tumor was removed. Each dog will recover from anesthesia and have postoperative care in the intensive care unit until discharged from the Veterinary Medical Center. Each dog will receive (1) several doses of a vaccine created from their own tumor cells with the CD200 inhibitor, or a drug used to activate the gene therapy with (2) or without (3) the CD200 inhibitor, according to a color-coded calendar that summarizes the treatment schedule. In general the vaccines and/or CD200 inhibitor will be given once a week for 3 weeks starting about 10 days after surgery, then once a month for 3 months, then once every 8 weeks until there is MRI evidence of tumor recurrence. Each dog will have regular follow up examinations during the 12-month period of the study or until euthanasia, when necessary. The follow up protocol including timing and exams is as follows: Complete physical and neurological examinations and quality of life assessment at each vaccination starting at suture removal about 10 days after surgery. "Oncology", "parent_label": "Primary field"}], "description": "Osteosarcoma is a common cancer in dogs. Current treatment options include surgery, radiation therapy and various types of chemotherapy; however, there are few efficacious therapy options for dogs with osteosarcoma that has spread to the lungs. Cancer vaccines, directed against a variety of different tumor antigens, can generate T cell responses, yet alone typically fail to control or reverse tumor growth. Among the morest important reasons why cancer vaccines fail is their inability to overcome the immune suppressive effects of the tumor microenvironment (TME). Therefore, combining cancer vaccines with immunotherapy approaches that modify the TME is an attractive option for improving vaccine efficacy. The drugs losartan and propranolol have both been shown to modify the tumor microenvironment and reduce immune suppression caused by the tumor. The goal of this study is to evaluate an osteosarcoma tumor lysate vaccine in combination with losartan and propranolol in dogs with metastatic osteosarcoma The tumor vaccine will be given every 2 weeks for six treatments and then monthly for up to one year. Dogs will also be sent home with oral losartan and propranolol to be given twice daily. Rechecks will be required every 2 weeks following the start of treatment until the vaccine therapy is completed, and every 4 weeks thereafter if tumors are stable or better. This study is not randomized and there is no placebo group all dogs will receive all study treatments. The study covers all costs related to the trial for thefirst 6 months (including examinations, blood work, chest radiographs, the vaccine, and the losartan and propranolol). "Primary field"}], "description": "Xerostomia, or dry mouth, affects over 8 million people in the U.S and occurs as a result of salivary dysfunction due to autoimmune disease, medication usage, smoking, aging, and radiation therapy for head and neck cancer. Absence of saliva severely compromises the oral health and quality of life of patients: saliva protects the oral mucosa, facilitates food digestion and articulation, and aids in the re-mineralization of dental hard tissues. There are no viable long-term treatments for salivary dysfunction, driving a need for new, translatable solutions. We have devised a new promising therapy for improving salivary function and saliva flow that is based on stem cell-mediated regeneration via local delivery of a novel drug delivery system within a gel (alginate) that will enable uniform distribution within the tissue and controlled release of the drug (cevimeline). Testing in mice has shown that the drug is efficacious in promoting stem cell proliferation within the salivary glands in a fashion consistent with controlled release. Based on these exciting data, we seek to enroll dogs who will be undergoing radiation therapy to see if the same treatment that worked in mice will work in dogs. If we are successful, this therapy could help many people with dry mouth from radiation therapy and may be used to treat radiation side effects in dogs in the future. To understand if the therapy will work in dogs, we will give a dose of radiation to one salivary gland. Because dogs have multiple salivary glands, we do not anticipate that this dose will cause dry mouth in your pet. Once dogs are enrolled into the study, they will be assigned to one of four treatment groups: alginate (carrier) only, cevimeline only, alginate + cevimeline, or no injections (control). A single dose of radiation therapy will be administered to one salivary gland. The radiation protocol for treatment of your pets tumor will then be completed. Dogs that are assigned to one of the treatment arms will have injections of the assigned treatment into a salivary gland 14 days after radiation therapy. Saliva, a small amount of blood, and biopsies of the salivary gland will be collected prior to injection and at 7, 14, and 30 days post-treatment. This type of cancer can be difficult to diagnosis due to its small size and vague symptoms caused by the tumor. Insulinomas can also spread (metastasize) to other parts of the body and this spread can also be difficult to detect. Locating and removing the insulinoma along with any spread to other organs is very important to improve clinical signs and possibly cure patients. The purpose of this study is to compare the ability of multiple imaging procedures to detect insulinoma tumors in dogs. The goal of this study is to determine how well these imaging procedures can identify the tumor and if any of these procedures has an advantage over the other. These imaging procedures include CT, MRI, and PET-CT. CT uses x-rays and MRI uses a large magnet to produce detailed images of the body. PET is a form of nuclear imaging that uses injected radiopharmaceuticals to help detect subtle diseases/changes in the body at the cellular level. PET produces a much lower quality image than CT and MRI, but PET can be combined with CT to increase the detail of the image without losing the ability to detect subtle disease processes. This radiopharmaceutical emits a low dose of radiation. Following the imaging procedures, your dog will remain in-hospital until the radiation levels are low enough that they can go home without any risk to the people around them. This is almost always by the end of the day. If it is more convenient your pet can stay overnight in the hospital at no cost to you. "parent_label": "Primary field"}], "description": "This study is for dogs with bone cancer in their leg who are interested in amputation and have not yet received chemotherapy. The study aims to evaluate how effective Flash Proton Radiation Therapy can be as a treatment for osteosarcoma in future studies; however, this study does not offer flash proton radiation as a treatment. One dose of radiation is preformed for study purposes whereas typical radiation as a treatment for osteosarcoma consists of multiple radiation treatments. We hope to find out if flash proton radiation is more effective than standard radiation therapy for dogs with osteosarcoma by studying how the bone and tissue react to the radiation following amputation. The flash proton therapy may decrease normal tissue damage, increase a dog's ability to recognize and kill cancer cells, and decrease pain at the site of the tumor until amputation. An initial screening visit is required at the Veterinary Hospital at the University of Pennsylvania for a physical examination, bloodwork, chest x-rays, limb x-rays if not previously done, and an aspirate of the lesion. If you agree to have your dog participate in this study, your dog will have the radiation therapy study visit approximately 5 days before his/her scheduled amputation procedure. At this visit, your dog will be anesthetized and will be randomly assigned (like flipping a coin) to receive either standard or flash proton RT. An area of the tumor will be treated with one of these two methods of radiation. An adjacent area of healthy bone, still within the affected limb to be amputated, will also be treated with the opposite method of radiation. Approximately 5 days after radiation, your dog will have the scheduled amputation according to standard of care. Background Osteosarcoma (OS) is the most common bone cancer in dogs. Typically, OS is treated with a combination of surgical removal of the primary tumor and chemotherapy for metastatic disease. Surgical removal of the tumor usually involves limb amputation or limb salvage surgery. Limb salvage surgery can have high complication rates, and not all dogs are suitable for limb amputation. Even though chemotherapy delays metastatic disease development, most dogs with OS ultimately succumb to metastasis. Histotripsy is a novel treatment that mechanically breaks down tissues and can potentially induce the immune system to attack cancer cells. This study aims to evaluate the efficacy of histotripsy to treat dogs with OS, to ultimately advance the development of histotripsy as a non-surgical limb salvage treatment option for OS and an immunotherapy treatment against metastatic disease for OS. Study Design Dogs will be evaluated for eligibility at either theAnimal Cancer Care and Research Center in Roanoke, VAor the mainVeterinary Teaching hospital in Blacksburg, VA. Qualifying dogs will undergo a non-invasive histotripsy treatment of the tumor 1-5 days prior to standard-of-care limb amputation surgery. Travel will be required to the Veterinary Teaching Hospital in Blacksburg for the histotripsy treatment. Tumor samples will be obtained after limb amputation and evaluated by a pathologist at Virginia Tech. Results from this routine evaluation will be provided to you. Enrolled patients will need to return for recheck visits at 2 weeks and one month after completion of chemotherapy, and at 6, 9, and 12 months after surgery. With advanced notice, these recheck visits may be performed by your local veterinarian. If the rechecks are done remotely, the visit costs are not covered by the study. "parent_label": "Primary field"}], "description": "While surgery, radiation therapy and conventional chemotherapy can be useful for the management of osteosarcoma in dogs, improvement is often short-lived and not all dogs may be candidates for treatments like surgery or radiation therapy. New forms of treatment are needed for both dogs and people with osteosarcoma for this reason. The new drug GEM-IB combines a bone-targeting drug (ibandronate) with a potent cancer drug (gemcitabine) to increase the concentration of cancer drug exactly at the site of the tumor. This drug has shown good activity against osteosarcoma in mice, and laboratory studies suggest that combining this drug with the conventional chemotherapy drug docetaxel (DTX) significantly improves effectiveness. Pilot studies in normal dogs with the starting doses of both drugs in this study have demonstrated excellent tolerability. The primary objective of this study is to evaluate the safety and antitumor/anti-pain effects of this combined treatment given to dogs with osteosarcoma that have not yet been treated with surgery, radiation therapy or chemotherapy. Dogs will receive both drugs intravenously once every 21 days. Recheck visits will be required 1, 3-4, 7, 14 and 21 days after the first treatment, then every three weeks thereafter. Dogs will be eligible to continue receiving treatment at no cost as long as the drug is tolerated and dogs are experiencing clinical benefit (pain control and lack of tumor worsening). Analysis for tumor change will be performed through the use of imaging (X-rays), and limb use will be measured through gait analysis. Standard bloodwork will be performed at each visit. Additional tests to be performed include blood/urine collection over the course of the study to determine how the investigational drug is affecting changes in bone turnover. Imaging will be performed using standard sedation/anesthesia protocols."}, {"id": 15767, "name": "Use of papaverine to reduce low tumor oxygen in dogs with soft tissue sarcoma", "url": "https://veterinaryclinicaltrials.org/s/use-of-papaverine-to-reduce-low-tumor-oxygen-in-dogs-with-soft-tissue-sarcoma-266235/?ref=gallery", "status": "Completed", "tags": [{"tag_path": "financial-incentive_fully-funded-including-initial-screening-47", "label": "Fully funded including initial screening", "parent_label": "Financial incentive"}, {"tag_path": "intervention-type_drug-334", "label": "Drug", "parent_label": "Intervention type"}, {"tag_path": "species-20_canine-21", "label": "Canine", "parent_label": "Species"}, {"tag_path": "primary-field-19_oncology-1_soft-tissue-sarcoma-28", "label": "Soft tissue sarcoma", "parent_label": "Oncology"}, {"tag_path": "primary-field-19_oncology-1", "label": "Oncology", "parent_label": "Primary field"}], "description": "Purpose: This clinical trial evaluates the safety and efficacy of papaverine (PPV) as a method to reduce tumor hypoxia (low oxygen) in dogs with soft tissue sarcoma. Tumor hypoxia is a barrier to effective radiation therapy of solid tumors, so elimination of hypoxia will enhance effectiveness of radiation to treat cancerous tissue in dogs and humans.Radiation therapy involves the application of electromagnetic radiation to an area of interest using a linear accelerator (radiation-generating machine). This study will not involve radiation, but evaluate a drug that may make radiation therapy more effective. The drug papaverine has been given to humans for over 100 years with an excellent safety profile. Researchers at Ohio State have identified an unknown effect of papaverine that reduces oxygen consumption in tumor cells. Studies in rodent tumors have shown that the effect of papaverine on reducing oxygen consumption reduces hypoxia and increases the effectiveness of radiation therapy.We are now asking if papaverine can reduce hypoxia in canine sarcoma. The current study will be an addition to the regular treatment of your dog's tumor, and will not affect how that therapy is given. What qualifies my pet for this trial? To be included in the trial, dogs must fulfill the following criteria: 1.Body weight of at least 5 lbs or 2.27 kg 2.Adequate organ function as indicated by standard laboratory tests 3.Skin or subcutaneous soft tissue sarcoma as diagnosed by cytology or histopathology. Tumor can be new or recurrent. 4.Minimum tumor size of 2cm diameter. 5.Able to undergo general anesthesia and surgery for treatment of soft tissue sarcoma Exclusion Criteria Dogs with the following criteria or conditions will be excluded from the study: 1.Evidence of underling disease conditions such as clinically significant abnormalities in their labwork that would indicate renal, cardiac, or hepatic dysfunction. 2.Result of diagnostic testing (cytology and/or histopathology) are not clearly documented. 3.History of prior radiation therapy to tumor. What does enrolling in this clinical trial involve? Prescreening (Day -3 to -7): Pre-Treatment Diagnostics and ScreeningAfter signature of Owner Informed Consent, the dog will have a medical history completed and undergo a physical examination. Blood and urine samples will be collected and submitted for complete blood count (CBC), serum chemistry panel, and urinalysis. Visit 1 (Day 0): General anesthesia and pre-treatment MRI, PPV Administration and post-treatment MRI.Each dog will undergo a physical examination. Prior to general anesthesia, the patient will have been fasted 10 hours before admission or overnight during hospitalization but can receive water ad libitum until the morning of the planned general anesthesia. The dog will be premedicated using a protocol developed by the board-certified anesthesiologist. The dog will have an MRI of the tumor. Following completion of MRI the dog will have papaverine administered IV and be monitored. General anesthesia will be maintained and sixty minutes following completion of papaverine administration the dog will be transported back and have a repeat MRI of the tumor. Visit 2 (Day 7): Pimonidazole treatment, general anesthesia, and surgical excision of soft tissue sarcoma.One week following general anesthesia and MRIs, the dog will be readmitted to the hospital and a physical examination performed. Following a catheter placement, 2-4 hours prior to surgery pimonidazole will be administered. Premedication will be given then shortly after general anesthesia will be induced and maintained. The soft tissue sarcoma will be surgically removed. A small sample will be taken from the tumor for testing and the rest of the tumor will be submitted for pathology. Following recovery from surgery the dog will receive pain medications as needed and be discharged from the hospital following recovery. Client Compensation The study is funded by a National Institutes of Health (NIH) research grant. The study costs will be covered by the research grant. Drugs (pimonidazole and papaverine), bloodwork (study blood draws), processing of tumor sample to measure hypoxic regions, MRIs for oxygenation measurements (including anesthesia for 2 hours) will all be covered by the research grant. The study will cover all the required appointment charges and contribute $1049 towards surgery and anesthesia for tumor removal. The study will not cover any other costs or cost of the treatment to your dog's tumor or hospitalization due to any other reason. Current treatment options include surgery, radiation therapy and various types of chemotherapy; however, there are few efficacious therapy options for dogs with osteosarcoma that has spread to the lungs. Recent studies indicate that certain immune cells such as monocytes and regulatory T lymphocytes play an important role in tumor metastasis in diseases such as osteosarcoma. Certain anti-tumor drugs, such as toceranib, have been show to suppress these cells and help the immune system better recognize cancer. Toceranib (PalladiaTM) is an oral drug that inhibits the function of a group of proteins important for cancer growth called receptor tyrosine kinases. Toceranib is approved by the FDA for the treatment of canine mast cell tumors, but there is preliminary evidence that some dogs with osteosarcoma may benefit from toceranib as well. In recent studies, we have determined that treatment with the combination of the tyrosine kinase inhibitors, such as toceranib, together with losartan exerts significantly greater antitumor activity than either drug alone. The drugs losartan and propranolol have both been shown to modify the tumor microenvironment and reduce immune suppression caused by the tumor. The goal of this study is to evaluate the anti-tumor effects of a 3-drug combination of toceranib, losartan, and propranolol in dogs with metastatic osteosarcoma. Initially your pet will undergo a series of diagnostic tests, which may include blood tests, urinalysis, blood pressure, and chest x-rays. The results of these initial tests will determine if your pet is eligible to enter this clinical trial. These tests are part of the routine testing done in patients with osteosarcoma and may be performed even if you decide that your pet will not participate. Your dog will be sent home with oral losartan and propranolol to be given twice daily and oral toceranib to be given every other day. Rechecks will be required every 2 weeks following the start of treatment until the week 12 visit, and every 4 weeks thereafter until week 24 if tumors are stable or better. Chest x-rays will be performed every 8 weeks while on study. At the week 2 visit, your dog will need to stay in the hospital all day for serial blood collections following propranolol administration. Background Primary brain tumors (PBT) are a significant cause of illness and death in dogs. Surgery remains a common treatment for canine PBT, with the goal of removing as much of the tumor as possible. However, significant numbers of canine PBT are considered inoperable due to their location in the brain, and conventional, invasive surgical techniques can cause serious side effects. Even when surgery goes well, the tumor may regrow after surgery. New treatments, particularly for PBT that cant be removed by surgery or that have regrown after surgical removal, are needed to improve quality and quantity of life of affected dogs. This proof-of-concept of study will provide data necessary to refine histotripsy technology and explore new, non-invasive techniques. The techniques we are developing have the potential to allow precision image-guided, non-invasive treatment of PBT using ultrasonographic equipment and treatments that are currently in use in the majority of small animal veterinary practices, which may make treatment cheaper and more accessible.Please note that while our eventual goal is to be able to offer histotripsy as a non-invasive option, for this study we need to be able to surgically remove the patient's brain tumor and test it. Cryoablation is a freezing technique that may kill or shrink the tumor, alleviate pain, and assist the body in rejecting cancer. Cryoablation is performed by advancing a small needle through the skin into a tumor and freezing the tumor in place. The hypothesis of this study is that cryoablation can be used as a minimally invasive alternative to surgical removal of mammary masses. Cryoablation can generally be performed without significantly affecting the pets overall health while maintaining the pets appearance cosmetically. Pets can typically resume their usual activities within a few days with minimal side effects. The study will test a new device being developed for veterinary medicine. There is some data that support cryotherapy as a means to also kill tumor cells that have escaped the primary mass, e.g., metastasis. Background Soft Tissue Sarcomas are a common form of cancer in dogs that can invade tissues vital to normal function. As in humans, complete surgical removal remains the treatment of choice, with aggressive surgery recommended to ensure the best outcome. Surgical removal can sometimes be impossible without leg amputation or radiation therapy. In some cases, a tumor may be surgically resectable, but it could still recur at the surgical site or spread in a distant site like lymph node or lung. Radiation therapy is often recommended when surgery cannot completely remove the tumor, to help reduce the risk of local recurrence. Unfortunately, these therapeutic approaches can be unsuccessful and associated with significant discomfort, disfigurement, and financial burden to the owner. Thus, there is a need for novel, less invasive, and more effective therapeutic options. High intensity focused ultrasound (HIFU) is a non-invasive, outpatient ablative technique that has the potential to answer these unmet needs. "primary-field-19_oncology-1", "label": "Oncology", "parent_label": "Primary field"}], "description": "When a person or dog is diagnosed with cancer it is important to determine if the disease has spread throughout the body and to monitor them carefully to see if the chemotherapy they are getting is working. The vast majority of dogs that have been diagnosed with lymphoma and receive chemotherapy do great they feel better, their lymph nodes go back to a normal size and they honestly dont know they are sick. But is it not uncommon for some cancer cells to remain in the body in spite of the medications. The testing performed in this clinical trial is being looked at to see if we can figure out which dogs still have cancer. If we can do that our next step in a future clinical trial would be to try and figure out how to also get rid of those cells. On the first day of the study your pet will be placed under anesthesia for imaging. Initially we will do an F18-FDG PET/CT. This is a special form of imaging that involves giving your pet a small dose of a radioactive substance. The radiation dose is small enough that we expect no harm to be associated with it, and it is a substance that weve given to many dogs without problems. They will be under anesthesia for a few hours for the imaging then recovered in a special area of the hospital until the radioactive substance is almost completely gone. When your dog is discharged from this procedure, he or she will be safe for you to pet and touch. In almost every case that we have done this on (>350 dogs and counting) the dog will be able to go home the same night they had the imaging. While your pet is under anesthesia there will be some samples taken with a small needle from a few lymph nodes. As well we may decide to do a similar sample from other regions if there are areas we see on the F18 FDG PET/CT that make us concerned that the cancer has spread to them. These areas may include certain organs such as the liver or spleen. If we need to sample these organs we will use an ultrasound to guide us to limit risks as much as possible. We will also collect a blood sample for analysis prior to anesthesia and imaging. After the initial imaging your pet will be treated with any chemotherapy protocol you and your oncologist have agreed on. Your pet will need to have the same imaging and sampling performed after halfway through the chemotherapy protocol, then again 1-3 weeks after your pet has finished the chemotherapy. If your pets lymphoma is determined to have recurred during chemotherapy, additional imaging and sampling will be required at that time."}, {"id": 15866, "name": "Evaluation of new methods to identify With this form of treatment, survival times of dogs diagnosed with osteosarcoma is on average about 10 to 12 months with little improvement in survival occurring over the past two decades. The purpose of this study is to evaluate the addition of immunotherapy with an inhaled IL-15 (an immune stimulatory molecule called a cytokine) to the standard treatment in patients with osteosarcoma to see if it improves outcome. Our group, as well as others, have found that immunotherapy with inhaled cytokines can cause large osteosarcoma tumors in the lungs of dogs to shrink. Because the lungs are most often the first site for these tumors to spread, we believe that treating earlier when fewer cells are in the lungs could improve the outcomes seen with chemotherapy alone."}, {"id": 15844, "name": "A preclinical feasibility study evaluating the use of Deep CIVO, a novel intra-tumoral micro-injection device, in canine patients ", "url": "https://veterinaryclinicaltrials.org/s/a-preclinical-feasibility-study-evaluating-the-use-of-deep-civo-a-novel-intra-tumoral-micro-injection-device-in-canine-patients-620493/?ref=gallery", "status": "Completed", "tags": [{"tag_path": "financial-incentive_fully-funded-after-initial-screening-48", "label": "Fully funded after initial screening", "parent_label": "Financial incentive"}, {"tag_path": "species-20_canine-21", "label": "Canine", "parent_label": "Species"}, {"tag_path": "intervention-type_device-335", "label": "Device", "parent_label": "Intervention type"}, {"tag_path": "primary-field-19_oncology-1_other-misc-tumor-33", "label": "Other/Misc tumor", "parent_label": "Oncology"}, {"tag_path": "primary-field-19_oncology-1", "label": "Oncology", "parent_label": "Primary field"}], "description": "This is a multi-site prospective 6-9 patient escalation study with 3 canine patients per group, each group having progressively more difficult to access tumors that measure >5cm in diameter. The first group will consist of canine patients with tumors that are superficial, just below the skin; the second group will consist of canine patients with tumors that are submuscularorlocated such that there is > 3.5 cm of intervening normal tissue between the tumor and the skin surface; and the third group will consist of canine patients with tumors that are intra-cavitary (i.e., intra-abdominal). The Deep CIVO injection system consists of (1) five custom-designed 25-gauge stainless steel hypodermic needles multiplexed into a single cylindrical 12-gauge outer cannula and triggered to extend up to 4 cm beyond the end of the cannula into the tumor by the action of a single lever; (2) a cartridge magazine with up to 5 loaded vials containing saline and fluorescent tracking microspheres; and (3) visualization lights and glasses which enable visualization of the fluorescent tracking microspheres during surgical excision of the injected mass. Ultrasound-guidence helps target the CIVO device to the optimal location and depth within the tumor. Following insertion of the needles into the tumor, microliter volumes of saline and/or drug, mixed with the fluorescent tracking microspheres, will be injected in a columnar fashion through each needle into a single solid tumor. Following the injection procedure, the tumor will be excised either immediately following the injection or within 1-3 days according to standard of care surgical oncological principles.Adverse events will be monitored on an ongoing basis throughout the study. When the first group of patients has been enrolled, an interim analysis may be conducted to evaluate safety and feasibility. After the second group of patients has been enrolled, a second interim analysis may be conducted. Risks of the surgery include infection, problems related to the implants, and local recurrence. Many factors are contributing to the high rate of complications, and one of them is likely the material used to fabricate the implants. 3D-printing can create personalized implants made of a material that the body can replace with its own bone, namely tricalcium phosphate. Over a period of time, the body can grow new viable bone while removing the tricalcium phosphate, such that the metal plate and screws used with limb sparing will be able to be removed after a period of time, leaving the dog with only its own tissues. We hypothesize that if the implant used to replace the segment of bone with the tumor (i.e. endoprosthesis) was made of a material that the body could replace with its own viable bone, many of the complications would not occur or would be easier to treat. Following entry into the study, dogs will have a CT scan of the affected limb prior to surgery. The images obtained with the CT scan will be used to make the 3D-printed implants that will be used in the limb-sparing surgical procedure. We hope that the limb-sparing surgery will be able to occur 5-7 days after the CT scan. In the event that this needs to be delayed due to technical difficulties with the implant production, we may recommend that your dog receive a dose of intra-arterial chemotherapy in the time between the CT scan and surgery. Two weeks after surgery, dogs will begin carboplatin chemotherapy, administered every three weeks for a total of 6 treatments. Follow-up bloodwork, orthopedic exams, gait analyses, and chest and limb x-rays will be performed at various points throughout the chemotherapy protocol and every 2 months thereafter until 18 months post-op, then every 4 months indefinitely."}, {"id": 15862, "name": "Treating feline sarcomas with high-intensity focused ultrasound", "url": "https://veterinaryclinicaltrials.org/s/treating-feline-sarcomas-with-high-intensity-focused-ultrasound-271095/?ref=gallery", "status": "Completed", "tags": [{"tag_path": "financial-incentive_partially-funded_partially-funded-owner-cost-1000-51", "label": "Partially funded (owner cost >$1000)", "parent_label": "Partially funded"}, {"tag_path": "financial-incentive_partially-funded", "label": "Partially funded", "parent_label": "Financial incentive"}, {"tag_path": "species-20_feline-22", "label": "Feline", "parent_label": "Species"}, {"tag_path": "intervention-type_device-335", "label": "Device", "parent_label": "Intervention type"}, {"tag_path": "primary-field-19_oncology-1_soft-tissue-sarcoma-28", "label": "Soft tissue sarcoma", "parent_label": "Oncology"}, {"tag_path": "primary-field-19_oncology-1", "label": "Oncology", "parent_label": "Primary field"}], "description": "THIS STUDY IS NOW CLOSED Purpose To determine if high-intensity focused ultrasound (HIFU), a treatment that can destroy tissue using sound waves, will result in tumor cell death and immunologic activation in cats with sarcomas. Background Soft tissue sarcomas are a common form of cancer in cats, and are sometimes associated with injections or vaccines. They can invade tissues that are vital to normal function, and complete surgical removal can be impossible without amputation or radiation therapy. In some cases, a tumor may be removable by surgery, but it could still recur at the surgical site or in a distant site like lymph node or lung. One attractive option for such cases is immunotherapy. We propose using mechanical high-intensity focused ultrasound (HIFU) to kill tumor cells and release antigens from tumors, stimulating the patients anti-tumor immune response. We hope to find out if HIFU application can both kill tumor cells and activate the immune system in cats. To determine if the treatment is effective, we are recruiting cats with soft tissue sarcomas located in the skin to undergo HIFU treatment prior to surgical removal of the tumor. Study Design Prior to enrolling in the study, your cat must undergo cancer staging, including a complete physical exam, lab work, tumor biopsy and a CT scan. These procedures are at owner expense. If your cat meets the eligibility criteria, s/he will be scheduled for the HIFU treatment within ten (10) days of enrollment. HIFU will be applied to the tumor under general anesthesia. Your cats fur/hair will be clipped over the tumor as is standard for any ultrasound in cats. The treatment will be delivered in a series of bursts of sound that will be focused on the tumor to kill the cancerous cells through unbroken skin surface. The HIFU treatment is expected to take 30-60 minutes, but may take longer for some patients. Your cat may be sent home the same day, or if due to timing of the treatment or for the safety of your pet, s/he may need to stay overnight while recovering from anesthesia. Your cat's surgery will take place at the Veterinary Teaching Hospital in Blacksburg, VA 4-6 days following treatment. Your cat will be discharged according to standard procedures, based on the surgeons discretion. Your cat will return for a recheck 2 weeks after the surgery. Compensation The screening (eligibility) tests, surgery, and post-surgery recheck visits are not fully covered by the study. Your total out of pocket costs are estimated to be between $2900 and $3400. Screening: Lab work and chest x-rays cost, approximately $900 if performed at ACCRC. If performed by your regular veterinarian, they can be sent to ACCRC to begin the screening process. Tests and images of insufficient quality will not be accepted. An exam and CT scan with the oncologists at ACCRC will be necessary to fully determine whether your cat is eligible to enroll. Current treatment options include surgery, radiation therapy and various types of chemotherapy; however, there are few efficacious therapy options for dogs with osteosarcoma targeted to treat macroscopic OS metastases to the lungs. Recent studies show that certain immune cells, such as monocytes and regulatory T lymphocytes, play an important role in tumor metastasis in osteosarcoma and other cancer types. Certain anti-tumor drugs, like toceranib (PalladiaTM), have been show to suppress these cells and help the immune system better recognize cancer. Toceranib is an oral drug that inhibits the function of a group of proteins (receptor tyrosine kinases) important for cancer growth. "Oncology"}, {"tag_path": "primary-field-19_oncology-1", "label": "Oncology", "parent_label": "Primary field"}], "description": "Lymphoma comprises approximately 25% of all canine cancers. Up to 40% of these cases are caused by T lymphocytes, known as peripheral T cell lymphoma (PTCL). The vast majority of lymphoma cases cannot be addressed with surgery and instead warrant chemotherapy. The standard of care chemotherapy protocol for lymphoma is abbreviated CHOP, which stands for the 4 drugs involved. Generally, dogs with PTCL treated with CHOP chemotherapy tend to experience shorter remission durations and overall survival than dogs with diffuse large B cell lymphoma (DLBCL). When treated with CHOP chemotherapy, PTCL dogs have a median survival time of 4-9 months while DLBCL dogs have a median survival time of 11-13 months. Previous studies have questioned whether other, non-CHOP protocols may be better suited for dogs with PTCL in hopes of increasing remission and survival times. One protocol that has been repeatedly investigated is LOPP chemotherapy. This protocol uses two of the same drugs as CHOP and two that are different. Recent studies have demonstrated with dogs with PTCL treated with LOPP can experience survival times closer to 11-17 months. While these findings are promising, none of these investigations have had a control arm of dogs receiving CHOP chemotherapy. The purpose of this study is to provide a direct comparison between the outcomes for dogs with peripheral T cell lymphoma (PTCL) treated with CHOP or LOPP chemotherapy. The findings of this study could help veterinarians understand if one protocol is truly superior to the other for dogs with PTCL. In this study, your dog will be randomly selected to receive either CHOP or LOPP chemotherapy. At each visit, their lymph node size, blood work, and overall wellbeing will be assessed. Both protocols involve treatments every 7-14 days and take 4-6 months to complete. The therapy is rapid and involves the placement of electrodes followed by the delivery of electrical pulses. This results in the destruction of tumor cells within a well-defined space, leaving a margin of healthy, viable tissue. IRE has been used to treat human tumors for the last decade. Currently, a variant of IRE (electro-chemotherapy) is used to treat horses with squamous cell carcinoma and melanoma tumors. Background Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) and low-grade intestinal T-cell lymphoma (LGITL) are two common diseases affecting cats. Both diseases can cause diarrhea, vomiting, pain, and malabsorption of food. However, recent data indicate that those two conditions may represent a continuum, and more studies are necessary to better understand the conditions. Since the diseases are similar and the symptoms overlap and are nonspecific, diagnosis can be challenging, and may require expensive and invasive procedures. In addition, although the general treatment for both conditions is similar, treatment may mask more aggressive and potentially costly diseases. Thus, developing better diagnostic approaches is essential to provide better care to feline patients. In this study, we will analyze blood and small fragments of the intestines ofcats with each disease and perform comprehensive genetic studies evaluating the differences. This broad approach has not been applied to studying IBD and LGITL before. We believe it can provide valuable data, indicating what differentiates and causes each disease. Our long-term goal is to identify and develop blood-based diagnostic tests to differentiate IBD from LGITL. We hope our study will improve the health care and well-being of cats who suffer from these conditions. Study Design We will screen cats who have clinical suspicion of having IBD or LGITL and who require endoscopic evaluation for final diagnosis. Once diagnosis of IBD or LGITL is confirmed, the cat will be enrolled. Aiming to cause minimal distress to enrolled cats, we intend to minimize the collection of extra samples. Thus, we will use leftover samples collected for diagnostic purposes (i.e., mucosal biopsies during endoscopy, and whole blood submitted for complete blood count) during routine clinical workups, not material collected for this studys sole purpose. Overall tolerability and biological activity will be based on clinical and pharmacodynamic endpoints."}, {"id": 15973, "name": "Fully Canine Anti-PD1 for Urothelial Carcinoma in Dogs: Safety and Tolerability", "url": "https://veterinaryclinicaltrials.org/s/fully-canine-anti-pd1-for-urothelial-carcinoma-in-dogs-safety-and-tolerability-534418/?ref=gallery", "status": "Completed", "tags": [{"tag_path": "financial-incentive_fully-funded-including-initial-screening-47", "label": "Fully funded including initial screening", "parent_label": "Financial incentive"}, {"tag_path": "intervention-type_drug-334", "label": "Drug", "parent_label": "Intervention type"}, {"tag_path": "species-20_canine-21", "label": "Canine", "parent_label": "Species"}, {"tag_path": "primary-field-19_oncology-1_urogenital-tumors-349", "label": "Urogenital tumors", "parent_label": "Oncology"}, {"tag_path": "primary-field-19_oncology-1", "label": "Oncology", "parent_label": "Primary field"}], "description": "Urothelial carcinoma (also known as transitional cell carcinoma) is the most common type of bladder cancer to affect dogs. Treatment often involves a combination of surgery, chemotherapy, and radiation therapy, with the aim being to reduce the size of the tumor, alleviate symptoms, and improve the dog's quality of life. In recent years, immunotherapy has emerged as a promising treatment approach for many types of cancer, including canine urothelial carcinoma. Immunotherapies aim to harness the body's immune system to recognize and attack cancer cells. They can be particularly attractive for treating cancers that are difficult to access surgically or that have metastasized (spread to other parts of the body).This study seeks to evaluate a novel immunotherapy when used in dogs with urothelial carcinoma. The therapy specifically targets an important molecule primarily expressed on immune cells, which usually turns off the immune cells and prevents overactive immune responses. However, it also turns off anti-cancer immune responses and prevents the immune system controlling and killing cancer cells. Immunotherapies that are able to inhibit this molecule on immune cells that recognize cancer cells could make it possible for the immune system to recognize and attack the underlying cancer more effectively.Urothelial carcinoma in dogs shares many biological and molecular features with human urothelial carcinoma, including their ability to be shielded from the immune system. Human clinical trials in urothelial carcinoma investigating similar immunotherapies have shown these therapies to be more effective than traditional chemotherapies in some cases. Development of an immunotherapy that is safe and beneficial in canine urothelial carcinoma patients will advance veterinarians ability to treat this disease and will provide an important model to inform future canine and human clinical trials in this area. This study seeks to evaluate the tolerability and efficacy of this novel immunotherapy in dogs with urothelial carcinoma."}, {"id": 15978, "name": "Flourescence Lifetime Imaging for real time surgical guidance in oral tumors", "url": "https://veterinaryclinicaltrials.org/s/flourescence-lifetime-imaging-for-real-time-surgical-guidance-in-oral-tumors-293511/?ref=gallery", "status": "Completed", "tags": [{"tag_path": "intervention-type_diagnostic-57", "label": "Diagnostic", "parent_label": "Intervention type"}, {"tag_path": "financial-incentive_partially-funded_partially-funded-owner-cost-1000-51", "label": "Partially funded (owner cost >$1000)", "parent_label": "Partially funded"}, {"tag_path": "financial-incentive_partially-funded", "label": "Partially funded", "parent_label": "Financial incentive"}, {"tag_path": "species-20_canine-21", "label": "Canine", "parent_label": "Species"}, {"tag_path": "primary-field-19_dentistry-14", "label": "Dentistry", "parent_label": "Primary field"}, {"tag_path": "primary-field-19_dentistry-14_oral-surgery-114", "label": "Oral surgery", "parent_label": "Dentistry"}], "description": "The goal of oral cancer surgery is to remove all cancer cells to prevent local recurrence and distant spread to other organs. However, there is currently no pre-operative or intraoperative diagnostic test that is capable of accurately identifying all cancer cells, especially at the leading tumor edge where there is only microscopic disease. Thus, to ensure no cancer cells are left behind, a border of grossly normal appearing tissue (up to 2 cm) is also removed during surgery. Yet, in the oral cavity, removal of bordering healthy tissue is typically associated with severe structural, functional and cosmetic side effects. Most notably, the ability to eat may be compromised. There is an urgent need for intraoperative diagnostic tests that can delineate healthy from cancer tissue in real-time. The aim of this study is to evaluate the use of florescence lifetime imaging with Protophoryin IX (a natural intermediate in the iron pathway that fluoresces under blue light) to accurately diagnose cancer versus normal tissue during surgery. We will also characterize the tissue changes that drive differences in florescence emission between the tumor, peritumoral region (area of potential pre-malignant cells), and healthy tissue with spatial transcriptomics. This will allow us to also create biomarkers for early diagnosis of cancer and decide when florescence imaging is most likely to be helpful. If successful, the use of florescence lifetime imaging with PpIX during surgery would ensure the surgeon successfully removes all cancer cells while simultaneously sparing normal healthy tissue."}, {"id": 15979, "name": "Lattice radiation therapy’s effect on the immune response in canine sinonasal carcinoma", "url": "https://veterinaryclinicaltrials.org/s/lattice-radiation-therapys-effect-on-the-immune-response-in-canine-sinonasal-carcinoma-445681/?ref=gallery", "status": "Completed", "tags": [{"tag_path": "financial-incentive_partially-funded_partially-funded-owner-cost-1000-51", "label": "Partially funded (owner cost >$1000)", "parent_label": "Partially funded"}, {"tag_path": "financial-incentive_partially-funded", "label": "Partially funded", "parent_label": "Financial incentive"}, {"tag_path": "species-20_canine-21", "label": "Canine", "parent_label": "Species"}, {"tag_path": "intervention-type_radiation-60", "label": "Radiation", "parent_label": "Intervention type"}, {"tag_path": "primary-field-19_oncology-1_nasal-tumors-344", "label": "Nasal tumors", "parent_label": "Oncology"}, {"tag_path": "primary-field-19_oncology-1", "label": "Oncology", "parent_label": "Primary field"}], "description": "Sinonasal cancer is smaller subgroup of head and neck cancers; however, sinonasal carcinoma is an important cancer globally, as it has the second highest occupational attributable fraction of all types of cancer. Despite improvements in the fields of surgery and radiation therapy, the prognosis remains poor for human patients diagnosed with this tumor type as most succumb to local tumor recurrence. Using the dog as a model for the human disease may help speed progress in developing new approaches to treatment of this cancer. Sinonasal carcinoma occurs commonly in dogs and is primarily treated with radiation therapy. Like humans, most dogs succumb to local tumor recurrence. With these clinical similarities, dogs could fill an unmet need for an effective model for human sinonasal carcinoma. In this study, we aim to evaluate a new radiation treatment known as Lattice Radiation Therapy (LRT). A current method of radiation therapy used to treat canine sinonasal carcinoma (SC), called stereotactic body radiotherapy therapy (SBRT), distributes a high dose of radiation uniformly across the tumor. Lattice radiation therapy (LRT) differs from SBRT in that instead of administering that uniform high dose of radiation throughout the tumor, several small spheres of high dose radiation are administered within the tumor and the rest of the tumor receives a lower dose of radiation. LRT has shown promise in early studies to provide tumor control with low normal tissue toxicity, suspected to be due to improved blood flow and immune responses compared to uniform, high dose radiation therapy. Our goal is to look at the differences in the tumors immune response during and after treatment as well as the clinical response with LRT compared to our standard SBRT. Dogs enrolled into this study will be treated with LRT. Prior to starting treatment, all dogs will have a CT scan and a nasal flush under anesthesia. The following procedures will be performed in all dogs enrolled in the study: CT scan for radiation therapy planning Lattice radiation therapy; 3 treatments given once daily over consecutive business days under general anesthesia Nasal flush, 5 time points: prior to LRT, following 3rd fraction of LRT, 2 weeks following LRT, 3 months following LRT, and 6 months following LRT Blood collection (9-19 mL), 5 time points: prior to LRT, following 3rd fraction of LRT, 2 weeks following LRT, 3 months following LRT, and 6 months following LRT Tumor biopsy at the 2 week post-LRT time point under general anesthesia Recheck CT scan 3, 6, 12 months, and 18-months post-LRT under general anesthesia."}, {"id": 15986, "name": "An indication-seeking pilot study of Paccal Vet in dogs with splenic hemangiosarcoma following splenectomy", "url": "https://veterinaryclinicaltrials.org/s/an-indication-seeking-pilot-study-of-paccal-vet-in-dogs-with-splenic-hemangiosarcoma-following-splenectomy-752456/?ref=gallery", "status": "Completed", "tags": [{"tag_path": "financial-incentive_fully-funded-including-initial-screening-47", "label": "Fully funded including initial screening", "parent_label": "Financial incentive"}, {"tag_path": "intervention-type_drug-334", "label": "Drug", "parent_label": "Intervention type"}, {"tag_path": "species-20_canine-21", "label": "Canine", "parent_label": "Species"}, {"tag_path": "primary-field-19_oncology-1_hemangiosarcoma-341", "label": "Hemangiosarcoma", "parent_label": "Oncology"}, {"tag_path": "primary-field-19_oncology-1", "label": "Oncology", "parent_label": "Primary field"}], "description": "Hemangiosarcoma (HSA) is a highly aggressive and malignant vascular tumor occurring most commonly in dogs. Dogs with splenic hemangiosarcoma have a poor prognosis, with fewer than 20% of dogs surviving 9 months with surgery and adjuvant doxorubicin chemotherapy. Paclitaxel is one of the most effective anticancer agents used in human cancer today, with potent activity against a wide variety of tumors. Paclitaxel interferes with normal microtubule function during cell division and induces cell cycle arrest. In addition, several studies have shown that paclitaxel has antiangiogenic properties. Paclitaxel targets both the tumor stroma and the vasculature, and it has been shown to inducetumor control in human patients with soft tissue angiosarcomas. The conventional formulation of paclitaxel (Taxol) has been associated with acute adverse events in dogs, which has largely precluded the use of paclitaxel as a chemotherapeutic in veterinary oncology. The investigational drug to be used in this study, Paccal Vet, uses a proprietary formulation based on retinol derivatives (XR-17), which encapsulate paclitaxel to form nanosized micelles. Previous studies with Paccal Vet have demonstrated a tolerability profile that is generally similar to other chemotherapy drugs used in veterinary oncology. Moreover, anti-tumor activity in selected cancers in dogs, including mast cell tumors, squamous cell carcinoma, and mammary cancer has also been reported for Paccal Vet. These findings suggest that Paccal Vet may be a promising treatment option for dogs with hemangiosarcoma. It is important to note that none of the chemotherapeutic agents commonly used in veterinary oncology clinics for the treatment of hemangiosarcoma have been approved for veterinary use."}, {"id": 15987, "name": "Combining Traditional and Multi-omic Approaches to Elucidate the Cause and Mechanisms of Canine Dysautonomia", "url": "https://veterinaryclinicaltrials.org/s/combining-traditional-and-multi-omic-approaches-to-elucidate-the-cause-and-mechanisms-of-canine-dysautonomia-148406/?ref=gallery", "status": "Completed", "tags": [{"tag_path": "primary-field-19_neurology-neurosurgery-5_peripheral-nervous-system-disorders-256", "label": "Peripheral nervous system disorders", "parent_label": "Neurology/Neurosurgery"}, {"tag_path": "primary-field-19_neurology-neurosurgery-5", "label": "Neurology/Neurosurgery", "parent_label": "Primary field"}, {"tag_path": "financial-incentive_unfunded-53", "label": "Unfunded", "parent_label": "Financial incentive"}, {"tag_path": "intervention-type_none-sample-collection-only-351", "label": "None - sample collection only", "parent_label": "Intervention type"}, {"tag_path": "species-20_canine-21", "label": "Canine", "parent_label": "Species"}], "description": null}]}

{"content": {"id": 24792, "headline": "Repurposing Vaccine Immunity to Treat Cancers in Dogs", "tagline": "COTC033: Help us test a new approach to treat cancer by using vaccine immunity in dogs.", "description": "

This study is for dogs that have cancer. Veterinarians and researchers want to see if common vaccines can be repurposed to help a dog’s immune system fight cancer. Dogs in the study will be randomly chosen to receive either vaccines normally used for people (Shingrix or Gardasil) or a rabies vaccine.


At first, dogs will receive 1 to 3 weekly vaccine injections to boost immune response. After that, they will receive weekly injections directly into the tumor for 8 weeks. During the study, doctors will collect small samples from the tumor and nearby lymph nodes at certain times to see how the cancer is responding. Blood samples will also be taken at each visit. The clinical and research team will closely watch how each dog’s tumor changes during treatment.

", "requirements": "
  1. Dogs must weigh between 33–132 lbs (15–60 kg)
  2. Dogs must have a confirmed cancer diagnosis (but not mast cell tumors, thyroid cancer, lymphoma, or skin hemangiosarcoma)
  3. Tumor must be 2–8 cm in diameter and accessible for biopsy
  4. Blood tests must show the dog is healthy enough for the study
  5. Dogs must stop chemotherapy or radiation at least 2 weeks before, and steroids 7 days before starting the study
  6. All study visits must take place at Colorado State University (CSU)
", "who_can_participate": "

Dogs may join the study if they:

  1. Have a confirmed cancer diagnosis that meets study rules
  2. Meet the size and health requirements
  3. Have a tumor that meets the specified size requirements and can be safely sampled
  4. Are not currently receiving restricted cancer treatments (chemotherapy, radiation, and/or steroids)
  5. Can travel to CSU for all visits


", "benefits_and_risks": "

Benefits:

  1. All study-related costs are covered, including:
  2. Exams, blood and urine tests
  3. X-rays and ultrasounds
  4. Tumor biopsies and lymph node tests
  5. Study treatments
  6. When your pet completes or is removed from the study, you will receive a $3,000 VHS credit for additional treatment at CSU
  7. Your dog may benefit from a new cancer treatment approach


Possible Risks

  1. Your dog will have multiple injections, blood draws, and tumor biopsies
  2. There may be side effects from the vaccines or procedures
  3. The treatment may not help every dog

{"content": {"id": 24778, "headline": "Immunotherapy (CAR-T) treatment for canine glioma tumors", "tagline": "Help us test CAR T cells and verdinexor, a new chemotherapy for gliomas in dogs.", "description": "

About 3 in 100 dogs are diagnosed with brain tumors each year, and gliomas are among the hardest to treat because they can escape traditional treatments. This study is focused on finding new treatment options for dogs with brain tumors, specifically gliomas, which are one of the most difficult types to treat. Researchers are exploring a new approach called immunotherapy, which helps the body’s own immune system fight cancer.


In this study, a small blood sample is taken from your dog to collect immune cells (called T cells). These cells are then modified in the lab to better recognize and attack cancer cells. The upgraded cells (called CAR T cells) are given back to your dog to target the tumor.


Dogs in this study will also receive a chemotherapy drug called verdinexor, which may help improve the effectiveness of the treatment.


Additionally, dogs can receive radiation therapy, which is currently the gold-standard for treating gliomas in dogs. We hope that by attacking the tumor through immunotherapy, radiation therapy, and chemotherapy, we will give dogs the best chance at success.


This is the first study to test this type of therapy in dogs, building on promising results seen in children with brain tumors.

", "requirements": "
  1. A 5-month study period with frequent visits
  2. Initial MRI (for eligibility)
  3. Blood collection to create CAR T cells
  4. CAR T cell injections (two treatments)
  5. Radiation therapy
  6. Brain biopsy (case-dependent, not required)
  7. Follow-up MRI at month 1 and month 4 following initial CAR-T treatment
  8. Ongoing oral chemotherapy
", "who_can_participate": "

Dogs may qualify if they:

  1. Have a glioma confirmed on MRI
  2. Weigh over 10 pounds
  3. Have not received prior chemotherapy or radiation
  4. Are healthy enough for anesthesia
  5. Have owners willing to give chemotherapy at home and follow study requirements
", "benefits_and_risks": "

Benefits:

  1. Access to a cutting-edge, first-in-dogs treatment
  2. Study covers the cost of biopsy, treatments, and medications
  3. Study covers the cost of radiation therapy, which is currently the gold-standard for treating glioma tumors
  4. Chemotherapy costs covered for the rest of your dog’s life
  5. Contribute to research that may improve cancer treatment for dogs and humans

Risks:

  1. Risks associated with anesthesia, brain biopsy, and MRI
  2. Possible side effects from chemotherapy and immunotherapy
  3. Frequent visits and time commitment
  4. Treatment may not be effective for some dogs

What we do
The Veterinary Clinical Investigations Center (VCIC) at the University of Pennsylvania’s School of Veterinary Medicine is an internationally recognized clinical research organization.
In collaboration with industry sponsors, Penn Vet clinicians, and partner academic centers, the Penn Vet VCIC team supports the design, coordination, and efficient implementation of veterinary clinical trials designed to identify novel approaches to disease diagnosis, management, and prevention.
The Center has long-established relationships with leaders in the veterinary pharmaceutical industry and maintains collaborative partnerships with other innovative academic centers. In addition to performing clinical trials, the VCIC offers an extensive range of clinical research operations services, including clinical trial project management, recruiting and marketing strategies, trial site selection and monitoring, record auditing, and data quality assurance and control.
Our Services
The VCIC works closely with corporate sponsors, individual clinicians, clients, and patients, offering services ranging from recruitment, study design, protocol compliance, quality assurance, data capture, and reporting, conducting clinical trials at both Penn Vet hospitals.
Targeted Marketing & Recruitment Strategies
The VCIC has demonstrated an ability to recruit significant sample sizes in a wide array of disease models over more than 14 years of managing veterinary clinical trials. Ryan Hospital’s large case load combined with its extensive referral network of more than 3,000 veterinary practices make it uniquely suited for clinical trial recruitment and enrollment.
When a trial requires more animals with a specific condition than would normally be presented in the 34,000 pets that come to Ryan Hospital annually, the VCIC has a proven record for targeted recruitment of animals at over 400 percent above baseline presentation rate.
VCIC understands and employs recruitment modalities that are most effective for a given target population and can guide sponsors on the most efficient means to enroll the desired number of animals in a specified period of time for a given study, pain management, and disease specific recommendations.
Clinical Trial Design and Study Protocol Development
Penn Vet has the expertise to implement and manage all aspects of veterinary clinical trials, from study set-up and recruitment to data collection and analysis, final study reporting and closeout. The center works closely with faculty members trained in epidemiology and trial design to ensure that projects are powered appropriately with a robust plan for statistical analysis in order to yield meaningful results.
Study Site Selection, Training & Management
The VCIC has the clinical research experience to identify and oversee clinical trial sites that are familiar with the international standards set forth in VICH GL-9 Good Clinical Practice as well as perform training for GCP.
Study Monitoring
Veterinary research nurses with extensive clinical and monitoring experience work on campus as well as with remote study sites to ensure protocol and regulatory compliance.
Quality Assurance & Control
The implementation of a robust audit plan is vital to the success of any clinical trial. The VCIC at Penn Vet has developed business processes to optimize data capture rates and ensure protocol adherence so that a research question may be answered utilizing the most complete information set possible.
Data Capture Form, +/- Electronic Data Capture Management
The center has extensive experience in the creation of data capture forms and competency using a number of commercial, governmental, and private electronic data capture modalities.
Final Study Reporting
Final study reports are formatted according to FDA/CVM Guidance #85 Good Clinical Practices with technical recommendations provided in Guidance #104.
Frequently Asked Questions
Here are commonly asked questions and answers about clinical trials, which might help you better understand clinical investigations, their benefits, and what clinical trials entail.
What is Translational Research
Translational research bridges laboratory science and clinical medicine to develop new treatments. At Penn Vet’s Veterinary Clinical Investigations Center, we conduct clinical trials with client-owned pets and large animals, providing insights that closely resemble human conditions. This approach benefits both pets and humans by studying naturally occurring diseases in a real-world environment.
The Veterinary Clinical Investigations Center facilitates high-quality investigations in companion animals with diseases similar to human conditions. This intermediate step helps screen for efficacy and complications before human trials.
Advantages of Studying Human Diseases in Companion Animals:
Similar biological and clinical conditions
Complex tissue interactions
Shared environment with humans
Diverse pet population
Comparable drug metabolism
Ethical advantages over induced disease models
Useful clinical and preclinical data
What are Clinical Trials?
Clinical trials investigate new methods of prevention, diagnosis, and/or treatment of various diseases and conditions.
They also explore new avenues in surgical technique, nutrition, drug/medicinal therapies, and alternative medicine such as acupuncture.
All of these approaches to prevent and treat disease are not only used in veterinary medicine but in human medicine as well and they all came out of successful clinical trials.
Many of the naturally occurring diseases that affect our animal friends closely resemble those suffered by humans. As a result, animal clinical trials have a profound impact on not only our furry friends but ourselves as well.
Although some consider the treatments/methods used in clinical trials to be “untested” they have actually been previously conducted using not only laboratory animals but also healthy volunteer animals before they are moved on to this stage.
As part of a clinical trial, once owner’s permission is given, samples of blood, urine, or even tissue samples for biopsies may be taken from the pet depending on the trial protocol. This is done so the investigator can gain further information that may benefit present as well as future patients. In a nutshell clinical trials help us push the science of medicine into other realms and advance the way we care for our pets and our fellow humans.
Who benefits from Clinical Trials?
Everyone, both human and animal!
Clinical trials offer hope and new solutions to human and animal patients. They can be very rewarding for the pet, their family, the veterinary investigator, and most importantly future patients.
Many of the effective and commonly used treatments, surgical procedures, and medications are available today because of the participation of patients enrolled in clinical trials.
Clinical Trial participants may also benefit from reduced cost or even free services, treatments, and medications depending on the particulars of the trial.
But most importantly, all patients benefit from the compassionate and professional care provided by our veterinarians and veterinary nurses.
Why should I enroll my pet in a Clinical Trial?
One of the main benefits to enrolling your pet into a clinical trial is that the medicine, treatment, or surgical procedure being studied could help alleviate your pet’s pain and suffering.
Also, since your pet would be enrolling in a clinical trial at Penn Vet you can have the peace of mind knowing that your special friend will be getting the best possible care from our licensed, professional and caring veterinarians and veterinary nurses.
Some of our trials may offer free or discounted services, medicine, or treatments for your pet.
The greatest benefit of all is the fact that through your pet’s participation they will help advance many facets of medicine and help countless other patients.
What are my and my pet’s rights as a volunteer in a Clinical Trial?
You have many rights should you decide to volunteer your pet as a trial participant.
First and foremost, you have the right to know and understand all of the risks and benefits associated with the study. These along with a thorough explanation of the trial’s goals and procedures will be discussed with you in detail by the veterinary investigator or the trial nurse before your consent is given.
You have the option to withdraw from the trial at anytime. Once the trial or your participation is complete you have the right to be informed of the trial’s end results if available.
Finally, your pet will not be enrolled in a trial unless all aspects have been completely explained and an “informed owners consent” document is signed stating that you have received all the information relevant to the trial. Then and only then will your pet be enrolled.
What regulations are there to ensure the safe and ethical conduct of a trial and of the safety of my pet?
Clinical trials are regulated at many levels. The Federal Government requires that all trials involving animals be approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC). This committee includes physicians, researchers, veterinarians, and lay personnel who are not involved in the medical field.
At the hospital level, the Clinical Sciences & Advanced Medicine Academic Department, which runs the Matthew J. Ryan Veterinary Hospital at Penn Vet, has an internal committee that reviews all clinical trials conducted at the hospital. The committee helps ensure that patients involved in clinical trials receive the same high level of quality care that all patients at the Ryan Veterinary Hospital are given.
All staff involved in the various trials are required to participate in courses and pass examinations on safety, ethics, and animal care before they can work with a study patient.
The VCIC Team
The VCIC staff is comprised of clinical research operations professionals, veterinarians and clinical research nurses. The operations staff assists with contracts, proposals and business related matters. Veterinarians with advanced training in epidemiology, biostatistics and clinical trial design assist clinicians and principal investigators with protocol development and study design. The veterinary clinical research nurses in the center provide clinician support and project management while also providing high quality patient care.

Clinical Trials FAQ
Canine Lymphoma Trials
We are currently recruiting dogs with multicentric lymphoma for multiple ongoing clinical studies.
Canine B-cell or T-cell Lymphoma
We are currently enrolling dogs in a study investigating high-intensity focused ultrasound (HIFU) to treat dogs with lymphoma.
Learn more about our high-intensity focused ultrasound (HIFU) trial
.
Veterinary Referrals
If you are a veterinarian interested in referring a canine patient with lymphoma for treatment, or if you would like additional information about these studies, please call the Purdue Veterinary Hospital at
765-494-1107
and ask to speak with Araynna Holland, RVT, or Dr. Michael Childress.
A Note on Prednisone
Please note that treatment of canine lymphoma with prednisone prior to initiation of multidrug chemotherapy has been associated with increased chemotherapeutic drug resistance and reduced remission and survival times.
Therefore, dogs previously treated with prednisone are unfortunately not eligible for some of the ongoing trials.
If you are a veterinarian interested in referring a canine patient with lymphoma to the Purdue University Veterinary Hospital for treatment, please do not prescribe prednisone for that patient.
We realize that lymphomas may progress rapidly and that prompt treatment is imperative for optimal patient care. We therefore make every effort to receive patients with a confirmed or tentative diagnosis of lymphoma as quickly as possible. Usually, appointments are available within 7 days of our receiving the referral. Patients with severe lymphoma-related illness can usually be seen within 24 hours.

Evan and Sue Ann Werling Comparative Oncology Research Center
The Werling Comparative Oncology Research Center conducts research and clinical trials to further our understanding and treatment of cancer, improving the outlook for pet animals and people.
About
The Evan and Sue Ann Werling Comparative Oncology Research Center (WCORC) in the Purdue University College of Veterinary Medicine was formed to transform and grow research to improve the outlook for pet animals and humans facing cancer.
Learn More About Us
Bladder Cancer Screenings
Certain dog breeds, including Beagles, West Highland Terriers, Shetland Sheepdogs, and Scottish Terriers, are at higher risk for bladder cancer—particularly transitional cell carcinoma (TCC). Early detection is key to improving outcomes, and a bladder ultrasound is a non-invasive, effective way to identify potential abnormalities before symptoms appear.
If your dog is 6 years or older and belongs to a high-risk breed, consider scheduling a screening to prioritize their health. The screening includes a bladder ultrasound as well as blood and urine sample collection. No referral is required.

Cancer Research
Our ongoing cancer research with canines is leading to new and innovative treatments that benefit both canines and humans.

Clinical Trials
Participate in one of our many ongoing clinical trials to help us better understand how to diagnose and treat cancer in both canines and humans.

Clinical Trials FAQ
Current Oncology Clinical Trials
Although we are making considerable progress in the fight against cancer, we still have a long way to go. Often, the best new information about cancer comes from animals participating in a clinical trial.
If you do not live in our region of the country, you could check with the
Veterinary Cancer Society
to learn about clinical trials in your area.
Emerging Canine Cancer Studies
We are currently recruiting for Emerging Canine Cancer Studies
High Intensity Focused Ultrasound (HIFU) for Lymphoma in Dogs
High Intensity Focused Ultrasound (HIFU) for Osteosarcoma in Dogs
Immunotherapy Trial of New Cancer Vaccine
Learn more about our Emerging Canine Cancer Studies
Canine Urinary Bladder Cancer
For dogs with urinary bladder cancer (TCC) affecting the bladder and/or urethra. The study is aimed at learning how the dog’s immune system can be stimulated to attack the cancer.
Learn more about our Canine Urinary Bladder Cancer Trial
Canine Osteosarcoma
The WCORC and Purdue Institute for Cancer Research have recently launched a research program in canine osteosarcoma to identify new, effective therapies in dogs that will improve cure rates for both dogs and humans with this cancer.
Our current focus is on collecting tumor tissues from dogs undergoing amputation to analyze them for susceptibility to novel drugs. A financial incentive of $500 per dog is available to help offset the cost of amputation to the owners of dogs contributing to this research.
We are excited to announce a new clinical trial for osteosarcoma that studies the clinical, molecular, and immune characterization of this tumor type. Eligible dogs must have a confirmed diagnosis, no evidence of metastasis, or spread, to other parts of the body, and received no prior treatment.
Learn more about our Clinical, Molecular, and Immune Characterization of Naturally-Occurring Osteosarcoma Clinical Trial
Tumor Ablation Studies
H-FIRE Liver Cancer Study
is evaluating the safety and immune effects of High-Frequency Irreversible Electroporation (H-FIRE) for dogs diagnosed with liver cancer.
The goals of this study are to evaluate the safety and feasibility of H-FIRE in dogs with liver cancer, measure local and systemic immune responses after H-FIRE treatment, analyze tumor biopsies, blood immune cells, and cytokines before and after treatment, and determine whether a single H-FIRE treatment can stimulate a meaningful anti-tumor immune response.
Learn more about our H-FIRE Liver Cancer Study
Emerging Immunotherapy Study
Purdue is evaluating new immunotherapy approaches designed to help a dog's own immune system better recognize and fight cancer.  Currently, studies include evaluating MO29, a new drug that blocks SHP-1, a protein that can limit the immune system's response to cancer.
Learn more about SHP-1 inhibitor study

Clinical Trials
Improving care through clinical trials
Clinical trials help doctors in the medical and veterinary fields discover new ways to improve the detection, diagnosis, ​and treatment of illnesses, all while enhancing the quality of care each patient receives. Clinical trials are critical to our groundbreaking research, may provide access to cutting-edge care, and result in discoveries that help people and animals in the future, all while providing your pet with the highest level of personalized care.
biotech
Participate in a clinical trial
When your pet participates in a clinical trial, they help our veterinarians discover disease prevention methods and find new ways to improve detection, diagnosis, and treatment of animal illnesses.

Frequently asked questions
Why should my pet participate?
+
Clinical trials help us evaluate new diagnostics, treatments, or devices to better understand their safety and how well they work. We carefully design studies with strict ethical oversight and ensure you understand the trial’s purpose and any risks. Clinical trials often offer benefits, including access to cutting-edge treatments or financial incentives. All pets enrolled in clinical trials receive unparalleled care from their veterinary team, just like all other VHS patients.
What should I expect during a clinical trial?
+
When you inquire about a clinical trial, the clinical trial team will review your pet’s medical history. If they appear to be a good fit, you may be contacted to move to the screening step, which may include a review of your veterinarian’s records and an in-person visit. You will have time to review the client informed consent documents and ask questions related to participation in the trial. You will also be presented with alternatives to participating in the clinical trial. You will learn about the study requirements, including any treatments and follow-up visits that are required. You can decide not to enroll in the trial or withdraw at any time without any negative impact on the care you and your pet will receive.
Are clinical trials safe?
+
All clinical trials undergo extensive review before starting, including review of any potential risks. Just as many aspects of veterinary care carry inherent risks or potential side effects, clinical trials may also have these. The care team will discuss any potential risks with you prior to enrollment.
Does it cost anything to participate in a clinical trial?
+
There may be some associated costs to establish a diagnosis before clinical trial enrollment. Each study will have different associated costs and this will be outlined in the client informed consent document.
How many visits are required and how long does a trial last?
+
This is variable depending on the study, ranging from a single visit to lifelong follow-up.
How do I know if my pet qualifies for a clinical trial?
+
Enrollment criteria are established for each clinical trial and may include factors such as size, breed, age, or diagnosis. These will vary for each clinical trial. Please inquire for an individual clinical trial to see if your pet may qualify.
Will my primary veterinary be updated if I enroll my pet in a clinical trial?
+
Yes, your care team will send updates to your veterinarian regarding the care your pet receives as a part of the clinical trial.
